Later, Mohinder Singh withdrew his complaint by filing affidavit dated 28.11.1980 stating that the complaint filed by him is based on wrong information and he feels regret for the same. However, the Director, Health Services, U.T. Chandigarh served a show-cause notice dated 7.1.1981 seeking explanation of the petitioner on the complaint filed by Mohinder Singh. Petitioner filed a detailed reply and affidavit dated 1.1.1981 explaining that there is no difference between the income and expenditure. It has been averred by the petitioner in his petition that the Director, Health Services as well as the Chief Commissioner were not satisfied with the reply filed by him and therefore, the Chief Commissioner ordered the Vigilance Cell. U.T. Chandigarh to hold preliminary enquiry to look into the allegations of corruption. It is the case of the petitioner that Vigilance cell made an enquiry and submitted its report to the Director, Health Services in the year 1981-82, but the report of the preliminary enquiry was not supplied to the petitioner. Petitioner was reverted to the State of Punjab. The record of the enquiry proceedings was handed over to the parent State. Respondent No. 1 issued charge-sheet to the petitioner vide memo dated 22.11.1983 under rule 8 of the Punjab Civil Services (Punishment and Appeal) Rules, 1970. Petitioner filed interim reply dated 17.12.1984 to the charge- sheet, giving details of his income and expenditure during the year 1980. In his reply, petitioner also requested that the departmental file be summoned and he be allowed to inspect the same. Respondent No. 1 was not satisfied with the reply filed by the petitioner and decided to hold departmental enquiry into the charges. On 8.1.1985, one Gurdial Singh, Deputy Director, was appointed as an Enquiry Officer and later on, on 22.4.1985 the enquiry was entrusted to Enquiry Officer, Vigilance, Punjab. After enquiry, the Inquiry Officer submitted his report to respondent No. 1 in November, 1986. On 11.5.1990, respondent No. 1 ordered the dismissal of the petitioner from service. Petitioner was served with the order along with copy of the enquiry report. Petitioner filed representation to respondent No. 1 for review of the said order, but no decision was taken by respondent No. 1. Per force the petitioner filed Civil Writ Petition No. 11786 of 1990 in this Court, challenging the enquiry report and the charge-sheet and also the dismissal order. The writ petition was disposed of by the Division Bench with a direction to the competent Authority to decide the review petition of the petitioner expeditiously, preferably within a period of three months by passing a well-reasoned and speaking order. Pursuant to the order passed in the writ petition, petitioner filed another review petition on 12.9.1990 giving all the details, for consideration by the competent Authority. Respondent No. 1 vide order dated 10.1.1991 dismissed the review petition. Order of dismissal and also the order dismissing the review petition are being challenged in this petition inter alia on the ground that the same are illegal, arbitrary and violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution of India.  3. In his written statement, respondent No. 1 has admitted that a copy of the enquiry report was sent to the petitioner for the first time along with the dismissal order. Order dismissing the petitioner from service is being defended on the ground that on finding the reply of the petitioner to the charge-sheet as unsatisfactory, an enquiry under rule 8 of the 1970 Rules was ordered to be held against the petitioner. The Inquiry Officer after giving sufficient opportunity to the petitioner gave his report in which charges levelled against the petitioner have been proved and therefore, it has been averred that the order of dismissal is not illegal as alleged by the petitioner. As regards the order passed in review, respondent No. 1 has averred that the review petition was examined at an appropriate level and was rejected by the Governor of Punjab under Rule 21 of the 1970 Rules.  4. Learned counsel for the petitioner has made the following submissions:  i) That the Disciplinary Authority on receipt of the enquiry report was of the view that only punishment of reduction in time scale for two years should be imposed but the order of dismissal has been passed at the insistence of Punjab Public Service Commission (in short the Commission) and therefore, respondent No. 1 having not applied its mind before passing the order, the order deserves to be quashed on this score alone; ii) that the impugned orders have been passed in the name of respondent No. 1 against which no appeal lies to any appellate Authority. According to the counsel, in view of the drastic consequences which ensue a non-appealable order the rules of natural justice have to be fully complied with. He also contended that although this court had directed respondent No. 1 to pass a speaking order on the review petition filed by the petitioner, but the order passed is again a laconic and non-speaking one; iii) that the enquiry report submitted in this case is not an enquiry inasmuch as the Inquiry Officer has failed to examine, analyse and appraise the evidence before him, rather the enquiry report is based on surmises and conjectures. In answer to these submissions, the learned counsel for the State has submitted that the disciplinary proceedings were initiated against the petitioner as it had come to the notice of the Authorities that he was in possession of assets disproportionate to known source of income during the period he had worked with the Union Territory, Chandigarh. He further contended that the enquiry was held in accordance with rules and regulations and is not illegal, arbitrary or violative of principles of natural justice, as has been contended by counsel for the petitioner.  5. As regards the first contention of counsel for the petitioner, it is to be noticed that the Inquiry Officer submitted his report to respondent No. 1 in November 1986. However, it remained pending with respondent No. 1 till 14.8.1987 when respondent No. 1 wrote letter No. 18/43/84/4HBI/19235 seeking advice of the Commission on the basis of enquiry report. Respondent No. 1 in its letter to the Commission informed that this was a case of reduction to a lower scale for a period of two years. The Commission did not agree with the views of respondent No. 1 and vide letter dated 19.10.1988 recommended the punishment of dismissal. Respondent No. 1 again recommended to the Commission vide letter dated 24.1.1989 reiterating that it is not a case of disproportionate assets but a case in which no prior permission was taken before the property was sold/purchased and so, the penalty of reduction of pay scale is appropriate. However, the Commission again wrote back to respondent No. 1 that punishment of dismissal is appropriate. Respondent No. 1 in the written statement has admitted that the competent Authority decided to award the major penalty of reduction to a lower stage in the time scale for a period of two years, but when the matter was referred to the Commission, the Commission did not accept the recommendation. It has also been averred that the advice/approval of the Commission is binding on the State Government and therefore, the competent Authority passed an order on 26.4.1990 that "Considering the facts and circumstances of the case Government may accept the recommendations of the Punjab Public Service Commission and award the punishment of dismissal from service to the petitioner". Reply of the Government as stated in paras 11 and 12 of the written statement has, thus, revealed that respondent No. 1 on the basis of enquiry report and material on record was satisfied that it is not a case of disproportionate assets and for that matter, it recommended that penalty of reduction of pay scale is appropriate, but since the Commission did not approve of the recommendation, the order of dismissal came to be passed against the petitioner. Rules do not provide that advice of the Commission is binding on the Disciplinary Authority. Rather, in law, the Disciplinary Authority is not bound by the advice of the Commission but has to consider the evidence before him and though he has to consider Inquiry Officer's report, but he is not bound by the latter's finding as well. What is provided under clause (ii)(a) and (b) of sub-rule 4 of rule 9 of 1970 Rules is that where the Punishing Authority finds it necessary to consult the Commission, the record of the enquiry together with a copy of notice given to the Government and representation made in pursuance of such notice shall be forwarded by the Punishing Authority to the Commission for its advice and the Punishing Authority after considering the representation made by the Government employee and the advice given by the Commission, shall determine as to what penalty should be imposed upon the Government employee and shall make such order as it thinks fit. Rule does not provide that the advice of the Commission is binding on the Disciplinary Authority and therefore, the stand taken by respondent No. 1 that the advice of the Commission is binding is not correct. It, thus, stands established that respondent No. 1 was influenced by the opinion of the Commission with whom he consulted with a view to obtain its advice on the case. The conclusion of respondent No. 1 is based on the advice tendered by the Commission and thus, was not arrived at independently on the basis of the charges and relevant material placed before the Inquiry Officer in support of the charges and defence of the petitioner. In fact the final conclusion of the Disciplinary Authority was so much at variance with the advice of the Commission that it is impossible to say that respondent No. 1 was not in any manner influenced by the advice tendered by the Commission. Respondent No. 1 having not applied its independent mind to the material before it, the order deserves to be quashed on this score alone.  6. Coming to the second contention of counsel for the petitioner, viz, the impugned orders have been passed in utter disregard to the principles of natural justice as at no stage the petitioner was given any opportunity to challenge the enquiry report. It is the admitted case of the parties that copy of enquiry report was supplied to the petitioner for the first time along with the order of dismissal. In the case of orders from which appeal lies, the delinquent has an opportunity to challenge the findings of the Disciplinary Authority in appeal. There the delinquent can attack the conclusions of the Inquiry Officer and the procedure followed in the departmental enquiry. Furthermore, he has the opportunity to satisfy the Disciplinary Authority about his innocence. For this purpose, a copy of the enquiry report is supplied to the delinquent along with order of punishment. However, in the present case, the impugned orders, Annexures P-10 and P-15 were passed in the name of the President of India by respondent No. 1. Rule 14 provides that no appeal shall lie against the order made by the Governor. Therefore, obviously there is no appeal from the said orders and for that matter when the petitioner was supplied with a copy of the enquiry report along with the order of dismissal, he made representation on 18.6.1990 against the order of dismissal, but no decision was taken by respondent No. 1 on his representation. Petitioner per force had to file Civil Writ Petition No. 11786 of 1990 and on 6.9.1990 the Division Bench directed the Competent Authority to decide the representation by passing a well-reasoned and speaking order. This course was adopted by the Division Bench as the Division Bench was alive to the grievance made by the petitioner that no opportunity had been provided to him to attach the report of Inquiry Officer. Despite the directions of the Division Bench to respondent No. 1 to pass a well-reasoned and speaking order, Annexure P-15 which has been passed has not dealt with the detailed review petition which runs into 15 pages. The order only states "And whereas, after considering carefully, there has been found no reason or justification to accept the review petition filed by Dr. Avtar Singh. Various charges have been established beyond doubt and the evidence has been conclusive. It has been established beyond doubt that Dr. Avtar Singh violated the conduct rules as he had possessed assets disproportionate to his known sources of income and he acquired/purchased property violative of the conduct rules." The order gives no indication that the Disciplinary Authority was alive to the grounds taken in the review petition, rather it shows that respondent No. 1 did not apply its mind at all though he was required to do so under the orders of this court passed in Civil Writ Petition No. 11786 of 1990. The order passed in review suffers from the defect of non-application of mind and thus, not only the order passed in review but also the order of dismissal have to be set aside because the petitioner at no stage was given any opportunity to challenge the enquiry report. For this view, I am supported by a judgment of Apex Court in Surjit Ghosh v. The Chairman and Managing Director, United Commercial Bank and others, 1995(2) SCT 352(SC) : 1995(2) S.C.C. 474, wherein it has been held that when there is a provision of appeal against the order of Disciplinary Authority and when the appellate Authority or the higher authority against whose order there is no appeal, exercises the powers of the Disciplinary Authority in a given case, it results in discrimination against the employee concerned. This is particularly so when there are no guidelines in the Rules/Regulations as to when the higher authority or the appellate Authority should exercise the powers of the Disciplinary Authority.  7. Before considering the third contention of counsel for the petitioner, it would be appropriate to notice few judgments on the subject. In Union of India v. H.C. Goel, A.I.R. 1964 S.C. 364, it has been held that if the conclusion, upon consideration of evidence, reached by the Disciplinary Authority is perverse or suffers from patent errors or is based on no evidence at all, a writ of certiorari could be issued. In Anil Kumar v. Presiding Officer and others, A.I.R. 1985 S.C. 1121, it has been held that the enquiry report must show the application of mind on the part of Inquiry Officer and further, the Inquiry Officer must disclose the reasons for relying on the evidence of prosecution in preference to that of defence. The relevant observations are as under :-  "It is well-settled that a disciplinary enquiry has to be a quasi- judicial enquiry held according to the principles of natural justice and the Enquiry Officer has a duty to act judicially. The Enquiry Officer did not apply his mind to the evidence. Save setting out the names of the witnesses, he did not discuss the evidence. He merely recorded his apse dixit that the charges are proved. He did not assign a single reason why the evidence produced by the appellant did not appeal to him or was considered not credit- worthy. He did not permit a peep into his mind as to why the evidence produced by the management appealed to him in preference to the evidence produced by the appellant. An enquiry report in a quasi-judicial enquiry must show the reasons for the conclusion. It cannot be an ipse-dixit of the Enquiry Officer. It has to be a speaking order in the sense that the conclusion is supported by reasons. This is too well-settled to be supported by a precedent. In Madhya Pradesh Industries Ltd. v. Union of India, (1966)1 S.C.R. 466 : A.I.R. 1966 S.C. 671, this court observed that a speaking order will at best be a reasonable and at its worst be at least a plausible one. The public should not be deprived of this only safeguard. Similarly in Mahabir Prasad vs. State of Uttar Pradesh, (1970) S.C.R 201 : A.I.R. 1970 S.C. 1302, this court reiterated that satisfactory decision of a disputed claim may be reached only if it be supported by the most cogent reasons that appealed to the authority. It should all the more be so where the quasi- judicial enquiry may result in deprivation of livelihood or attach a stigma to the character." In J.S. Gulati v. Improvement Trust, Ludhiana and others, 1983(2) S.L.R. 100, it has been held by this court that "the Enquiry Officer should have carefully examined and appraised the evidence, documentary as well as oral, adduced by the parties in support of each charge, he was not required to write judgment, still he had to indicate as to what was the evidence on which he was relying. No doubt he could draw his own inferences from oral and documentary evidence and base his conclusions thereon. Strangely in the enquiry report there is no reference to the evidence of any witness or document. After reading the report, one does not come to know if any witness was examined at all. There is not even a whisper of what was stated by the witness what to say of any discussion of the same. A departmental inquiry is a serious and solemn affair. The witnesses are examined and evidence produced to establish the charges. A delinquent is given an opportunity to cross-examine the witnesses and adduce evidence. This process is undergone in order to reach the truth. This is not just a ritual. The evidence has to be examined and analysed and appraised by the Inquiry Officer. He has to base his conclusion on such appraisal. The Inquiry Officer is not an arbitrator." Recently, in B.C. Chaturvedi v. Union of India and others, 1996(1) SCT 617(SC) : J.T. 1995(8) S.C. 65, it has been held by the Apex Court that judicial review is not an appeal from a decision, but a review of the manner in which it is made. The Apex Court held "Power of judicial review is meant to ensure that the individual receives fair treatment and not to ensure that the conclusion which the authority reaches is necessarily correct in the eye of the court. When an inquiry is conducted on charges of misconduct by a public servant, the Court/Tribunal is concerned to determine whether the inquiry was held by a competent officer or whether rules of natural justice are complied with. Whether the findings or conclusions are based on some evidence, the authority entrusted with the power to hold inquiry has jurisdiction, power and authority to reach a finding of fact or conclusion. But that finding must be based on some evidence. Neither the technical rules of Evidence Act nor of proof of fact or evidence as defined therein, apply to disciplinary proceeding. When the authority accepts that evidence and conclusion receives support therefrom, the disciplinary authority is entitled to hold that the delinquent officer is guilty of the charge. The Court/Tribunal in its power of judicial review does not act as appellate authority to re-appreciate the evidence and to arrive at its own independent findings on the evidence. The Court/Tribunal may interfere where the authority held the proceedings against the delinquent officer in a manner inconsistent with the rules of natural justice or in violation of statutory rules prescribing the mode of inquiry or where the conclusion or finding reached by the disciplinary authority is based on no evidence. If the conclusion or finding be such as no reasonable person would have ever reached, the Court/Tribunal may interfere with the conclusion or the finding, and mould the relief so as to make it appropriate to the facts of each case." It, thus, stands settled that in disciplinary enquiry which affects the livelihood of an individual and casts stigma, it is required that the Inquiry Officer after carefully examining, appraising and evaluating the evidence, documentary as well as oral, adduced by the parties in support of each charge, must record finding separately in each charge. Judicial review is permissible only to the extent where the court finds that the proceeding held against the delinquent employee was inconsistent with the rules of natural justice or in violation of statutory rules or the finding reached by the discilplinary authority is based on no evidence. Where the finding is unsupported by any evidence or is based on no evidence or shocks the conscience of the Court, the Court would be empowered to alter or interfere with the finding and the penalty imposed on the delinquent. In cases where the delinquent is aggrieved of the finding of the Inquiry Officer on the ground that relevant evidence on record, may be oral or documentary, has not been considered, the course open is to agitate the matter in an appeal or where the appeal is not provided, to agitate by way of the review and in such circumstances, the appellate/reviewing Authority is to pass a well-reasoned and speaking order.  8. In order to appreciate the third contention of counsel for the petitioner, it would now be appropriate to lay down the charges served on the petitioner before enquiry :  "(1) That during the year 1980, he had been in possession of assets amounting to Rs. 1,94,000/- disproportionate to his known sources of income, which he was not able to satisfactorily account for and thereby he had failed to maintain absolute integrity and had contravened rule 3 (1) of the Government Employees (Conduct) Rules, 1966. (2) (a) That he had acquired by purchase on 4.6.1978 a House at Chandigarh and subsequently had disposed of by sale on 20.10.1980 the said residential site, all without the previous knowledge of the Govt. (b) That he through his wife had borrowed on 10.9.1980 a sum of Rs. 60,000/- from Smt. Daljit Kaur through her husband Sh. Charan Singh, a person within the local limits of his authority with whom he was likely to have official dealings. (c) That he had purchased on 2.6.1980 a new scooter No. DEN-4251 for Rs.7,000/- and sold. on 11.9.1980 his old scooter No. CHG-4923 for Rs. 5,500/- but had failed to report to the Government these transactions concerning his movable property; thereby he had failed to maintain devotion to duty, and had contravened Rule 3(ii) of the Government Employees (Conduct) Rules, 1966". In answer to the charges, petitioner vide his interim reply dated 17.12.1984 submitted that a detailed probe into the matter had already been done by the Vigilance Cell, U.T. Chandigarh and the Administration Department (Health Department) U.T. and on the basis of enquiry, the then Chief Commissioner was satisfied with the sources explained by the petitioner and after completion of enquiry, the then Chief Secretary, Punjab, heard the petitioner in person and decided to close the matter in view of wide difference of opinion between the Administrative Department Officers, i.e. D.S.F.-cum-Deputy Secretary, Health/F.S.-Cum-Health Secretary and the Vigilance Inspector. However, along with the interim reply he furnished the incoming and out-goings received and spent during the year 1980. He also furnished supporting documents in the form of affidavits, confirmatory letters, statement of Accounts, Memorandum of gift-deeds, copies of receipts and copy of assessment order from the Income- Tax Department for financial year 1980-81. In regard to the second charge, petitioner submitted that no purchase was effected of a residential site on 4.6.1978, but a residential site at Mohali was purchased on 4.6.1976 before he joined on the post of Health Officer in Union Territory, Chandigarh and subsequently it was sold on 29.10.1980 to repay the loan after obtaining due clearance from the Income-tax Department. A house was also purchased at Chandigarh on 12.9.1980 and intimation in this regard was sent. Apart from this, he submitted that his wife took loan of Rs. 60,000/- on 10.9.1980 from Smt. Daljit Kaur and a new scooter for Rs. 7,000/- was purchased in 1980 from an authorised dealer, which was booked in the year 1970. This scooter was purchased after selling the old scooter No. CHG-4923 for Rs. 5,500/-. Along with his reply, petitioner sent certificates of distinction which he had earned during his entire service period, and also gave the details of loan which he had received for the purchase of house at Chandigarh. In the enquiry proceedings, the department examined 16 witnesses in support of their case. Petitioner also examined one Daya Chand, besides giving his own statement. The Inquiry Officer in his report dated 28.11.1986 opined that the complaint made by Mohinder Singh (though later on he refiled from his statement) stands fully established regarding purchase of residential plot and its subsequent sale, purchase of built-up house at Chandigarh, and that the said transactions were duly financed by unexplained sources of the petitioner and there was no reason why he should not have obtained permission of the competent authority before entering into such purchase/sale. In the concluding paragraph, he held that as per evidence led by the department and the petitioner and his reply to the questions put by the Inquiry Officer, it is established beyond doubt that various charges against the petitioner being in possession of assets disproportionate to his known sources of income during the year 1980 are fully established. Regarding the purchase and sale of scooter, residential plot, built-up house or his raising loan during the year 1980 itself are subservient to the main charge which stands thoroughly established.  9. Challenge made to the report and conclusions arrived at by the Inquiry Officer are on the ground that though the department examined 16 witnesses but the Inquiry Officer did not discuss the statement of any of the witnesses. Besides this, it has also been submitted that petitioner also produced one person namely Daya Chand but the Inquiry Officer did not care to discuss his evidence. Daya Chand had stated that petitioner wrote letter dated 27.10.1980 to the Director, Health Services. Punjab informing him about his intention to sell a plot which was later on sold on 29.10.1980. He had further stated that the petitioner had written another letter to respondent No. 4 informing him about the purchase of house at Chandigarh. The witness produced the despatch register of the office of Medical Officer of Health, Chandigarh. Challenge is also on the ground that the statement of Kehar Singh, D.S.P. (Vigilance) had not been taken note of. According to the counsel, this witness not only conducted the preliminary enquiry but had also stated that all the persons who advanced loan to the petitioner had admitted before him (Kehar Singh) that they had advanced loan to the petitioner. Counsel further contended that he is not asking this court to analyse and appraise the evidence led before the Inquiry Officer but his effort is to show that the report consists of only surmises and conjectures since the evidence which could have exposed the falsehood of the charges levelled against the petitioner has intentionally not been referred to by the Inquiry Officer.  10. It is true that the evidence, mention of which has been made by counsel for the petitioner, has not been dealt with by the Inquiry Officer, but this by itself is not sufficient enough to exercise the power of judicial review because it cannot be said that the enquiry report is based on no evidence. Regarding the grievance that entire evidence has not been considered by the Inquiry Officer or the disciplinary Authority, the matter could have been agitated in appeal but in this case, since no appeal is provided against the order passed in the name of the President of India, the Disciplinary Authority was requited to deal with the objections of the petitioner, against the report, in review. This has not been done by respondent No. 1 despite the direction given by this court. He has failed to deal with the grounds taken by the petitioner in his review petition and the order passed is not a well- reasoned and speaking one and, therefore, the impugned orders have to be quashed.  11. On quashing of the orders, Annexures P-10 and P-15, the usual course would have been to ask respondent No. 1 to pass a well-reasoned and speaking order afresh, but no useful purpose would be served in doing so since the petitioner has died during the pendency of writ petition. Accordingly, orders dated 11.5.1990 and 10.1.1991 (Annexures P-10 and P-15 respectively) shall stand quashed. Consequent upon quashing of these orders, respondent No. 1 is directed to give, to the legal representatives/heirs of the petitioner, all the consequential benefits to which the petitioner, if alive, would have been entitled to receive. Let the direction be complied with within a period of two months from the date of communication of order from this court.  12. The writ petition stands allowed in the aforesaid terms. No costs.  Petition Allowed.
summary: A. The Punishing Authority in a case involving the dismissal of a Medical Officer Health, acted without independent conclusion by awarding the penalty of reduction in rank to a lower level in the time scale, solely on the advice of Public Service Commission. Although advisory in nature, Punishing Authority failed to exercise its independent thinking resulting in a non-application of an independent mind, thereby justifying the quashing of the Order. [Para 5] B. A case involving the dismissal of an employee reveals absence of natural justice when the concerned individual was not given a copy of Enquiry Report at the time of dismissal. The only provision for review instead of an appeal provided no independent consideration of review, even when reviewing authority was required to do so after thorough reconsideration. The order was declared to be bad in law. [Para 6] C. In order to establish charges against an individual, departmental enquiries are carried out, wherein witnesses are examined, evidence is adduced, and opportunity is given to the delinquent to defend themselves. This is not a mere formality, but rather a serious process intended to reach the truth. The enquiry officer is required to appraise and analyze the evidence and base the report on the file material, and not act as an arbitrator. [Para 7]

text: Viney Mittal, J. - The plaintiff having lost before the learned first appellate court, has approached this Court through the present Regular Second Appeal  2. He filed a suit for declaration that he was entitled to leave encashment of Rs. 12,290/-. He also claimed that some retiral benefits have been paid late to him and, therefore, he was entitled to interest on the same. The suit filed by the plaintiff was decreed by the trial court and he was held entitled to grant of commuted leave for the periods March 05, 1999 to March 19, 1999 and April 22, 1999 to May 10, 1999 and was also held entitled to interest on certain delayed payments.  3. The matter was taken up in appeal by the State of Punjab.  4. The learned first appellate Court re-appraised the evidence on record and on such re-appraisal and on consideration of the proviso attached to Rule 8.119(c), it was held that the plaintiff was working in a vacation department, therefore, he was not entitled to earned leave and since the plaintiff had availed of the aforesaid earned leave, therefore, it was held that the claim made by the plaintiff in the suit was not legally sustainable and the refund of the payment made for leave encashment, had been rightly ordered. However, the learned first appellate court held that the plaintiff would be entitled to interest at the rate of 6% on the delayed payment of death-cum-gratuity and other benefits, as ordered by the trial court.  5. Consequently, the appeal filed by the defendants was partly allowed and the suit of the plaintiff, to that extent, was dismissed.  6. Nothing has been shown that the findings recorded by the learned first appellate court suffer from any infirmity or are contrary to the record.  7. No question of law, much less any substantial question of law, arises in the present appeal.  8. Dismissed.  Appeal dismissed.
summary: In the case of the plaintiff working in a vacation department, the retiral benefit of earned leave is not applicable. As a result, the payment made for leave encashment should be refunded in accordance with the court's order. [Para 4]

text: G.R. Majithia, J. - The plaintiff has dome up in regular second. appeal against the judgment and decree of the Wrist Appellate Court partly modifying the decree of the trial Judge.  2. The facts :  The defendant-respondent appointed, the plaintiff-appellant as a Manager Incharge of the Printing Press with effect from March 1, 1958 at a salary of Rs. 150/- per month; that he was to remain on probation for six months; that after completion of the probation period, the salary a to be raised to Rs. 250/- per month that the plaintiff AM was confirmed with effect from March 1, I with benefits of provident fund etc.; that the plaintiff worked as Branch Manager till May 13, 1962 when the services of the employees of the Press were retrenched, but the plaintiff was allowed to continue; that the services of the plaintiff were terminated with one month's notice with effect from April 8, 1964 without assigning any reason and that since the plaintiff continued to be in the service of the bank, he levied claim of Rs. 9249.79. as arrears of salary etc. In the alternative he also claimed Rs. 4880/- by way of damages for illegal termination of the, service and Rs. 4369.79 on account of gratuity, earned leave, provident fund, allowance etc. He also challenged Rule 17(1) of the Service Rules framed by he Registrar Cooperative Societies, under which the purported action was taken was invalid.  3. The defendant denied the allegations and justified the order of termination.  4 The pleadings of the parties gave rise to the following issues :-  (1) Whether the plaintiff was entitled to the benefit of Provident Fund etc. ? OPP (2) What are the duties of the plaintiff after the retrenchment of the Press staff and with what effect ? OPP (3) Whether the services of the plaintiff were terminated under the circumstances as alleged in para No. 6 of the plaint ? If so, what is its effect ? OPP (4) Whether the termination of the services of the plaintiff is wrongful, illegal, ultra vires and mala fide for the reasons an grounds stated in para No. 7 sub-paras (i) to (iv) and para No. 8 sub-paras (i) to (vi) of the plaint ? OPP (5) Whether the resolution No. 25 dated 8.4.1964 is bad, and illegal, wrongful and mala fide and beyond the powers of the Directors alleged ? OPP (6) Whether the resolution No. 25 dated 8.4.64 referred to above was passed under threat, influence and pressure as alleged in para No. 9 of the plaint ? OPP (7) Whether the plaintiff is entitled to gratuity earned leave wages, overtime-allowance and bonus ? OPP (8) Whether the plaintiff is entitled to declaration that he is still in service of the defendant ?  (9) If issue No. 8 is not proved but issues No. 4, 5 or 6 are proved, to what at amount of damage is the plaintiff entitled ? OPP (10) Whether the defendant is entitled to retain the admitted amount till the audit objections have been completed ? OPD  (11) Whether the claim of bonus and the suit is within time ? (12) Relief. 5. Additional issue was framed after the defendant filed the amended written statement and the same reads thus :  1A. Whether the jurisdiction of Civil Court is barred as alleged in the additional plea of the written statement ? OPD  6. The trial Judge under issue No. 1-A held that the jurisdiction of the Civil Court was not barred and issue No. 1-A was decided in favour of the plaintiff; issue No. 2 was decided in favour of the plaintiff and it was held that the plaintiff had been prosecuting the case on behalf of the defendant against the retrenched employees; issue Nos. 3 and 6 were decided against the plaintiff; issue Nos. 4 and 5 were disposed of together and it was held that termination of the services of the plaintiff was illegal and he was entitled to pay for the unexpired portion of his service; issue No. 7 was partly decided against the plaintiff and it was held that he was not entitled to bonus; issue No. 8 was decided against the plaintiff and it was held that he was not entitled to declaration that he was still in service; issue No. 9 was decided in favour of the plaintiff and it was held that he was entitled to Rs. 4880/- as damages on account of loss of salary; issue No. 10 was decided against the defendant and it was held that it was not entitled to retain the amount due to the plaintiff and issue No. 11 was held to be redundant. In the ultimate analysis, the trial Judge held that the resolution dated April 8, 1964 vide which the service of the plaintiff was terminated was illegal and a decree or recovery of Rs. 7802,50, detailed as under, was passed in favour of the plaintiff and against the defendant.  (a) Damages on account of loss of salary. Rs. 48880.00 (b) Earned leave wages for 4 months. Rs. 700.00 (c) RE with interest Rs. 1418.00 (d) Arrears of salary for 9 days from 1.5.1964 to 9.5,1964 Rs. 54.50 (e) Security deposit with interest. Rs. 750.00 Total Rs. 7802.50. 7. The defendant challenged the decree of the trial Judge in first appeal and the plaintiff filed cross-objections challenging the decree of the trial Judge to the extent the relief claimed by him was denied. The First Appellate Court held that the Civil Court had jurisdiction to entertain the suit and the jurisdiction of the civil Court was not barred by virtue of Section 2-A of the Industrial Disputes Act and also by virtue of Section 55 of the Punjab Co- operative Societies Act. The First Appellate Court further held that procedure for the termination of the services of the permanent employees had not been provided for in the Rules and the bye-laws of the defendant society and the termination from service was not within the scope of the powers of the Board of Directors. It found that the claim for bonus was wrongly denied by the trial Judge and held that the plaintiff was entitled to bonus in the sum of Rs. 875/-. It, however, reversed the decree of the trial Court to the extent to which it has allowed the claim of the plaintiff for Rs. 700/- for his unavailed of four months earned leave. In coming to the conclusion it took note of the fact that there was no provision under the Rules under which the plaintiff was entitled to the benefit of unavailed four months earned leave. On the ultimate analysis, the First Appellate Court allowed the appeal of the defendant and disallowed the claim for the recovery of Rs. 700/- claimed as unavailed of earned leave. It, however, allowed the cross-objection to the extent of Rs. 700/- towards unavailed earned leave.  8. I have gone through the judgment of the First Appellate Court. The First Appellate Court was in error in observing that the termination of the services is not covered by the service rules. The rule has not to be literally construed. If the employer has a right to dismiss, it has also got a right to terminate the services provided it follows the rules of natural justice before passing the order. However, I am not inclined to express any final opinion on this aspect of the matter since the defendant has not challenged the judgment and decree of the First Appellate Court either by way of appeal or by way of cross-objections. Having gone through the judgment of the First Appellate Court, I do not find any ground to differ with the overall conclusion arrived at by it. The appeal is devoid of any merit.  9. For the reasons stated above, the appeal fails and is dismissed, but with no orders as to costs.  Appeal dismissed.
summary: Rules pertaining to employment interpretation - Literal interpretation to be avoided - Employer's right to terminate - Natural justice principles must be followed before issuing orders. [Para 8]

text: G.S. Singhvi, J. (Oral) - This petition has been filed for grant of the following substantive relief :-  "to issue an appropriate writ, order or direction especially in the nature of mandamus directing the respondents to supply the copy of the service book to the petitioners under Rule 12.5 of Punjab Civil Service Rules, Volume-1, Part-1."  We have heard Shri R.C. Chatrath and have perused the averments made in the writ petition.  2. In our opinion, there does not appear to be any plausible reason or justification for non-supply of the copies of the service books of the petitioners in terms of Rule 12.5 of the Punjab Civil Services Rules, Volume I Part I. We are also of the opinion that omission on the part of the competent authorities to accept the request of the petitioners has resulted in denial of various service benefits due to them in terms of revised pay rules etc. Therefore, it just and proper to direct the respondents to make available copies of the service books of the petitioners on payment of the prescribed fee and grant them benefits admissible as per rules.  3. The writ petition is disposed of in the manner indicated above. The petitioners are directed to submit a copy of this order along with the copy of the writ petition before the respondent Nos. 2 and 3 within ten days and these respondents shall carry out the direction of the Court within next two months.  Petition allowed.
summary: Punjab Civil Service Rules, Vol. 1 Part 1, Rule 12.5 - Petitioners not provided with copies of Service books - No grounds given for this breach of Rule 12.5 - Government instructed to supply copies of service books within a two-month period upon payment, and grant petitioners benefits that are admissible under the rules. [Paras 2 and 3]

text: Jasbir Singh, J. - Petitioners have filed this writ petition under Articles 226 of the Constitution of India with a prayer to issue a writ of certiorari, mandamus or suitable writ, direction or order and they be declared entitled to the grant of selection grade as per policy decision Annexure P-1 with effect from December 8, 1981. They have further prayed that arrears be paid to them along with interest.  2. Briefly stated, case of the petitioner is that at the time of filing this writ petition, petitioner No. 1 was working as Addressograph in the Department of Printing and Stationery, Punjab. He joined as a Packer on July 12, 1963 and was confirmed on that post on April 1, 1966. Thereafter, he was promoted to the post of Addressograph on September 15, 1971 and was confirmed on that post on June 1, 1975. Petitioner No. 2 originally joined the Department as a Mazdoor on March 18, 1957. He was then promoted as Packer on September 25, 1961. After his confirmation on that post, he was promoted as Gestetner Operator on February 20, 1969 and was confirmed on that post on June 1, 1975. Petitioners have further stated that in the respondent-Department, there existed only one post of Addressograph and one post of Gestetner Operator and no further promotion was available. Above mentioned posts were in the pay scale of Rs. 400-600. Cadre of Gestetner Operator and Addressographer consists of only one post each. State of Punjab vide letter dated June 7, 1977 issued instructions regarding determination of number of posts for grant of selection grade. Those instructions provided that selection grade was to be sanctioned to 20% of the posts in a particular cadre and that in case 20% of the cadre strength comes to a fraction of 0.5 or more, it was to be treated as one post and where it comes to less than 0.5, it was to be ignored. Thereafter on representations made, matter was reconsidered by the Government and letter dated December 8, 1991 (Annexure P-1) was issued vide which it was decided that the selection grade at the rate of 20% would be admissible subject to the minimum of one post. By referring to above mentioned letter, it was stated that even in a cadre comprising only of one or two posts, selection grade was made admissible to one post. It is averred that in view of subsequent instructions issued in the year 1981, both the petitioners had became entitled to selection grade in the scale of Rs. 510-800 with effect from December, 1981. They made various representations to the respondent to grant them the selection grade. They were informed by the respondent- Department that their matter had been taken up with the Government and was under consideration. When no relief was granted to them, they again made representations to the respondent. They were informed that the matter was under consideration and whatever decision would be taken by the Government, the petitioners would be intimated of the same. After waiting for some time, the petitioners sent a reminder on June 5, 1986 (Annexure P-5). In reply thereto, they were informed vide letter dated July 30, 1986 (Annexure P-6) that the cases regarding grant of selection grade to those individuals working against solitary post have now been recommended to the Third Pay Commission, which had already been set up. Petitioners then filed this writ petition by averring that the action on the part of the Government was totally unreasonable and against instructions issued from time to time, especially Annexures P-1 and P7/A as they are entitled to the grant of selection grade, which was granted by the Government to other similarly situated employees.  3. Upon notice, respondent appeared and filed a written-statement, wherein facts regarding entry of the petitioners in service, their promotions etc. were admitted. However, it has been stated that since the Second Pay Commission had not made any specific recommendation regarding of selection grade to the posts of Addressographer and Gestetner, the petitioners were not automatically entitled to get that benefit on the basis of instructions referred to above. Their case was considered and sent for recommendation/approval and since in the meantime, Third Pay Commission was constituted, it was thought proper to refer the matter for consideration of the Third Pay Commission. This policy decision was made applicable not only to the petitioners but all other posts, similarly situated, in other Departments also.  4. Shri Balram Gupta, learned Senior Advocate appearing for the petitioners, vehemently contended that as per policy decisions (Annexure P-1, P7/A and R1), the petitioners were entitled to the grant of selection grade, which had unjustifiably been declined to them. By referring to orders Annexures P-7 and P7/A, he submitted that in the case of Drivers and Steno-typists, selection grade was awarded even to the incumbents holding isolated post, after completion of eight years of service, in the junior scale. Shri Gupta further contended that the petitioners were entitled to get benefit of selection grade with effect from December 8, 1981, when instructions Annexure P-1 were issued. They had been agitating the matter and making representations to the department and there was no occasion to refer the matter and await the decision of the Third Pay Commission. They were entitled to get benefit on the basis of recommendations of Second Pay Commission and subsequent instructions issued by the Government from time to time. He prayed that Annexure P-6 be quashed and the respondents be declared entitled to the payment of selection grade.  5. This prayer has vehemently been opposed by Shri G.P.S. Nagra, Assistant Advocate General, Punjab. He submitted that as a policy decision, all those cases involving single post cadre were referred to the Third Pay Commission for decision. He contended that since no specific provisions/recommendations were made by the Second Pay Commission for grant of selection grade to the posts of Gestetner Operator and Addressographer, the petitioners were not automatically entitled to the grant of selection grade. However, since in the meantime Third Pay Commission was constituted the matter was referred to it for its opinion/recommendation.  6. After hearing counsel for the parties, this Court is of the opinion that this writ petition deserves to succeed. It is apparent from the records that on the basis of recommendations made by the Second Pay Commission, State of Punjab issued instructions from time to time regarding grant of selection grade to its employees. Initially, it was provided that number of selection grade posts, at each level, should not exceed 20% of the strength of the basic cadre, for which the selection grade posts are to be sanctioned. Vide letter dated June 7, 1977, it was envisaged that where number of selection grade posts comes to 0.5 or more, it should be taken as one post and where the fraction works out to be less than 0.5, it should be ignored. It was further provided that in case of a cadre consisting of two posts, no selection grade post would be admissible. This matter was reconsidered and vide letter dated December 8, 1981 (Annexure P-1), it was decided by the Government that selection grade at the rate of 20% would be admissible subject to the minimum of one post. It ws further clarified that in a cadre comprising even one or two posts, the selection grade would be admissible to one post. Thereafter consolidated instructions regarding grant of selection grade were issued by the Government vide letter dated October 29, 1984 (Annexure R-1). This letter contains summary of all the guide-lines issue earlier regarding grant of selection grade and reads as under :-  "1. No. 8/30/78-FR(5)/1845, dated the 3rd March, 1980. (i) Selection grades will be provided in cases where the number of higher posts (all levels taken together) to which employees in a particular case can seek promotion is less than half the strength of that cadre or where there is no promotion post at all, available to a cadre or service : (ii) The number of selection grade posts at each level should not exceed 20% of the strength of the basic scale for which the selection grade posts are to be sanctioned. For the purpose of calculating the number of selection grade posts, all posts including temporary posts, which have been in existence for three years, should be taken into account; and  (iii) Selection grade will not be admissible to an officer unless he has completed 15 years service. The service should either be in the basic scale where appointment to the basic scale is from the point of fresh entry into service or as the sum total of the employees's service in the basic scale and in the one scale next below. (2) No. 8/30/78-FR(5)3369, dated the 5th April, 1980. The observations of the 2nd Punjab Pay Commission as contained in paragraphs 9.11 to 9.13 of its report (Extract at Appendix-I), particularly the observations relating to levels of `promotions' available in the respective cadres, should be kept in view. (3) No. 8/30/78-FR(5), dated the 19th November, 1980. Specific sanction determining the number of selection grade posts in each case should be issued by the Administrative Department concerned in consultation with the Department of Finance. (4) No. 7/84/81-5FR/10191, dated the 8th December 1981. Selection grade @ 20% would be admissible subject to the minimum of one post. Thus, in a cadre comprising even one or two posts the selection grade would be admissible to one post." 7. Shri Nagra, on getting instructions from Shri Manjeet Singh, Assistant in the Department of Printing and Stationery, Punjab, stated that these are the final instructions regarding grant of selection grade to employees of the Government. After reading above mentioned instructions, this Court feels that there was no necessity to send case of the petitioners for recommendations of the Third Pay Commission. It should have been taken note of and considered on the basis of instructions issued by the Government as referred to above. Admittedly, petitioners claim grant of selection grade on the basis of recommendations made by the Second Pay Commission and also on the ground that similarly situated persons, who were getting the same pay scale/grade, i.e. 400-600 were granted benefit of selection grade in the scale of Rs. 510-800. To strengthen this argument, Shri Gupta, learned Senior Advocate, referred to the documents Annexure P-7 and P7/A, vide which selection grade was granted to Drivers, Clerks and Steno-typist.  8. This Court feels that the case of the petitioners was not dealt with by the competent authority in a proper manner. There was no justification to send their case to the Third Pay Commission. Their case was required to be decided on the basis of existing instructions, which were prevalent at that time. Consequently, this writ petition is allowed and impugned order/letter dated July 30, 1986 (Annexure P-6) is quashed. Keeping in view facts and circumstances of the case, competent authority, i.e., respondent is directed to decide as to whether the petitioners are entitled to the grant of selection grade on the basis of then existing instructions as found mentioned in letter dated October 29, 1984 (Annexure R-1). The respondent is directed to consider case of the petitioners and pass an appropriate order within two months from the date of receipt of a copy of this order. There will, however, be no order as to costs.  Petition allowed.
summary: Selection grade grant - As per policy framed on recommendation of the second pay commission - Respondents referred matter again to the 3rd pay commission - It was held that there was no justification for referring the case for recommendation to the 3rd pay commission. It should have been dealt with based on prevalent instructions, especially when similarly situated individuals were given benefits. The Respondent is directed to decide as per instructions prevalent at the relevant time. [Para 8]

text: Debi Prasad Sircar, J. - All these revisional applications are taken up together as these are between the same parties and over the questions of fact and law and as such governed by this Single Judgment.  2. The petitioner No. 1 is the firm of which the other petitioners are partners. The firm commenced this business in 1949. The case of the petitioners is that till December 1976 the firm did not reach the numeric strength of its employees for coverage of the provisions of Employees' Provident Fund and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952 (hereinafter referred to as the Act). Since December 1976 the petitioner firm came under the coverage of the Act and steps are being taken regularly for complying with the provisions of the Act depositing the contributions to the appropriate authority. Sometimes in 1976 the Opposite Party No. 1 inspected the office of the petitioner and asked for production of the papers for the ten preceding years for determining whether the firm would come within the spell of the Act. The petitioners' case is that it was submitted before him that prior to December 1976 the number of employee of the firm being less than twenty, the petitioners were not liable to make the deposit under the Act. But a notice was served upon the petitioners in November 1976 from the office of the Regional Provident Fund Commissioner claiming that the petitioners were liable for deposits. Summons were served upon the petitioners under Section 7A of the Act for determining the amount payable by the petitioners. Although the petitioners made categorical statement and representation that they were not liable to deposit any amount before December 1976 assessment was made against them for the alleged defaulted amount. The petitioners received further notices and finally the Provident Fund Authorities assessed that an amount of Rs. 1,27,294.74 was due from the petitioners for the period from March 1969 to November 1976. The Provident Fund Authorities filed proceeding under Public Demands Recovery Act for recovery of the amount. But the certificate case was cancelled by the appropriate authority, that is, the Certificate Officer, on 25.2.1983. After even dismissal of that case the Provident Fund Authorities filed ninety-three complaint cases against the petitioners before the learned Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Calcutta as described in Annexure `C' of the petition with prayer for conviction of the petitioners for non-payment of the amounts alleged to have been due from time to time. The petitioners submit that the act on the part of the Provident Fund Authorities was grossly mala fide. The petitioners were not responsible to the firm for the day to day act as there were Managers for looking into that executive function. As the certificate proceeding has been dismissed the claims of the Provident Fund Authorities were proved baseless. Institution and continuation of the said proceedings before the learned Metropolitan Magistrate were illegal and for that all of these should be quashed.  3. The Opposite Parties appeared through the learned Advocate and oppose the prayer for the aforesaid relief.  4. The argument of the learned Advocate for the petitioners in a nut- shell is that under Section 1(3) of the Act the petitioners are not liable to come within the mischief of the Act unless the number of employees engaged in any period was twenty or more and although the Provident Fund Authorities examined all the papers, they did not find anything to show that the petitioners engaged twenty heads of employees or more at any time before December 1976. He further argues that as the certificate case for realizing the alleged defaulted amount was cancelled, evidently the claim of the Provident Fund Authorities that anything was due from the petitioners for the period under demand was not established and, as such petitioners could not have any criminal liability for non-deposit of any amount. The petitioners stoutly raised disputes on these points challenging the jurisdiction of the Provident Fund Authorities to recover any amount as deposit of the contribution etc. before December 1976. Under the Act then prevailing over this arena as embodied in Section 19A, the dispute as to the applicability of the Act could be decided only by the Central Government and not by the Provident Fund Commissioner or anybody under him. The Provident Fund Authorities, in absence of the appropriate order of Central Government, had no jurisdiction to consider whether the Act was applicable to the present petitioners and whether they are liable to make deposit taking into consideration the objection raised by the petitioners. Thus the acts of the Provident Fund Authorities in filing the complaints before the learned Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Calcutta and the proceedings resulting thereon were grossly illegal. The complaint cases having been filed on the ground of non payment of the contributions for recovery of which the certificate case being cancelled on 23.2.1983 and no appeal being preferred against that order the criminal liability of the petitioners was a myth. The learned Advocate for the petitioners relies on the ruling reported in (1) 1981 LIC 1015.  5. Although the petitioners did not take any such plea, the learned Advocate for the O.P. argues that the case cannot fail for delay for seven years. The learned Advocate for the O.P. No. 1 further argues that the order passed against the petitioners were not at all ex parte. After promulgation of the present provisions Section 22 of the Act, Old Section 19A of the Act now substituted, cannot have any effect in favour of the petitioners. The papers were produced from the Provident Fund Authorities which are with them and as such the O.P. is not in a position to show that at any time during the period of dispute, the petitioners engaged twenty employees as claimed by the Provident Fund Authorities.  6. I have considered the arguments diligently. I find that the mischief of this Act cannot be attracted to the petitioners for any period of time, unless it is proved that during the period the firm engaged twenty employees or more. Although the papers were under enquiry by the Provident Fund Authorities there was nothing to show that at any period of dispute, that is, before December 1976 the petitioners engaged twenty employees or more. I agree with the learned Advocates for the petitioners that under Section 19A of the Old Act, now substituted, the authority for ascertaining the applicability of the Act was with the Central Government as is provided under Section 19A(iii). The complaints were filed in 1983 and the assessment was made even before that. The Old Section 19A was deleted and the New Sections 20, 21 and 22 were inserted by the Act 33 of 1988 which came into operation on 1.3.1988. This amendment does not have any retrospective effect. So the position as it stood before 1.3.1988 was that reigning provision was Section 19A of the Act, now deleted. Clearly the Regional Provident Fund Commissioner or anybody under him had no authority at that time to decide the dispute about the applicability of the Act. Hence in the face of the objection raised by the petitioners the Regional Provident Fund Authorities had no jurisdiction to make the assessment without obtaining the order of the Central Government. The petitioner rightly relies on the ruling reported in 1981 LIC 1015.  7. Further in view of cancellation of certificate case which was filed for recovery of the alleged defaulted amount of Rs. 1,27,294.74 for the alleged default in making deposits, and no appeal or revision being preferred thereagainst the claim does not stand. As the civil liability to make the deposit goes unsubstantiated the cases filed before the learned C.M.M., Calcutta for the default attracting any sort of criminal liability are undoubtedly baseless and do not have any leg to stand upon.  8. Hence, the complaints lodging criminal cases against the petitioners as challenged in these revisional applications cannot proceed and are grossly illegal. Those proceedings must be quashed.  The revisional applications as described above are allowed. The proceedings in the complaint cases before the learned C.M.M., Calcutta as described in Annexure `C' of the petition are hereby quashed. Learned Lower Court be informed. Stay orders in respect of those cases are made absolute.  Applications allowed.
summary: Sections 1(3), 7-A, 19-A, 19-A(iii) of the Employees Provident Fund and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952 are discussed in the text. If a firm has less than twenty employees, a certificate case for non-payment of contributions may be cancelled. The Regional Provident Fund Commissioner cannot decide disputes about the Act's applicability, and a criminal case against the petitioner is deemed illegally. [Paras 4, 6 and 8]

text: K. Jagannatha Shetty, J. - St. Stephen's College at New Delhi and Allahabad Agricultural Institute at Naini are two of our premier and renowned institutions. The former has been affiliated to the Delhi University and the latter to the U. P. University. Both are aided educational institutions and getting grant from the State funds. They have their own admission programme which they follow every academic year. The admission programme provides for giving preference in favour of Christian students. It is claimed that they are entitled to have their own admission programme since they are religious minority institutions. The validity of the admission programme and the preference given to Christian students are the issues that need to be resolved in these cases. The questions are of great constitutional importance and consequence to all minority institutions in the country.  THE FACTS IN GENERAL  ST. STEPHEN'S COLLEGE  2. St. Stephen's College was founded on February 1, 1881. It is the oldest College in Delhi. It was first affiliated to Calcutta University and then to Punjab University and thereafter to Delhi University. Upon affiliation to the Delhi University it became one of its three original constituent colleges. The College offers three years' degree course in B.A./B.Sc. (Hons.), B.A. (Pass) and B.Sc. General as well as two years' Post-graduate degree course in M.A. and M.Sc. For the academic year 1980-81, the College published "Admissions Prospectus" on May 25, 1980, inter alia, providing that applications for admission for the first year course must be received in the College office on or before June 20, 1980. In the same prospectus, it was also provided that there would be interview prior to final selection of students for admission to the College. It appears that on May 22, 1980 the Vice-Chancellor of the Delhi University in exercise of his emergency powers under Statute 11-G(4) of the Statutes of the University, constituted an Advisory committee to consider and recommend the dates for admission/registration to various under-graduate/post-graduate courses in the Faculties of Arts and Social Sciences/Mathematics and Science for the academic session 1980-81 and for other related matters concerning admissions. The constitution of the Advisory Committee was approved by the Academic Council in its meeting held on May 29, 1980 and the Academic Council also authorised the Vice-Chancellor to accept the recommendations of the Advisory Committee for implementation. The Advisory Committee, inter alia, laid down as follows :  "(i) Admission to B.A. (Pass)/B.A. Vocational Studies Courses be based on the merit of the percentage of marks secured by students in qualifying examination. (ii) The admission to B.Com (Pass), B.A. (Hons.) and B.Com. (Hons.) Courses be also on the basis of marks. However, the College may give weightage to marks obtained in one or more individual subjects in addition to the aggregate marks of the qualifying examination. But whenever weightage is proposed to be given to individual subject(s) by the College, it should be notified in advance to the students through the College Prospectus/Notice Board so that applicants seeking admission known in advance the basis of admission. 3. These recommendations were accepted by the Central Admission Committee and also by the Vice-Chancellor.  THE CIRCULARS OF THE UNIVERSITY  4. That on June 5, 1980 the University issued circular to all affiliated Colleges prescribing the last date for the receipt of applications as June 30, 1980. The circular also provided phased programme of admission as follows :  "A First phase of admission For Students securing 45% of marks or above. i) Notification of First Admission List by the Colleges Wednesday 2nd July, 1980 Payment of fees (upto) Friday 4th July 1980 up to 4 p.m. General Note :  The number of names in all admission lists shall correspond to the number of seats available in the courses concerned. No student whose name appears in an admission list (or who qualifies on the basis of the percentage indicated in the list) shall be denied admission provided he/she pays the fees by the date and time stipulated.  ii) Notification of Second Admission List by the Colleges Friday 4th July 1980, 6 p.m. Payment of fees Saturday 5th - Monday 7th July 1980 upto 4 p.m. B. Second phase of admission 40% For students securing below 45% but above 40% marks Notification of Third Admission List by the Colleges Tuesday 8th July 1980, 12.00 Noon Payment of fees (up to) Thursday 10th July 1980, 4.00 p.m. 5. On June 9, 1980, the University issued another circular to Principals of all Colleges intimating inter alia, that Admission to B.A. (Pass)/B.A. Vocational study courses be based on the merit of the percentage of marks secured by students in the qualifying examination. The admission to B.Com. (Pass), B.A. (Hons.) and B.Com. (Hons.) courses shall be on the basis of marks. However, the College may give weightage to marks obtained in one or more individual subjects in addition to the aggregate marks of the qualifying examination. But whenever, weightage is proposed to be given to individual subject(s) by the College, it should be notified in advance to the students through the College Prospectus/Notice Board so that applicants seeking admission know in advance the basis of admission. This circular also provides certain guidelines for admission to sportsmen and persons with other distinctions.  6. The Delhi University Students Union had complained to the University authorities that the College was violating the University Statutes and Ordinances by fixing its own time schedule for receipt of applications as well as by stipulating interview before admission. On the basis of this complaint, the Registrar of the University wrote a letter dated June 9, 1980 requesting the Principal of the College to conform to the University schedule communicated to the College by the circular dated June 5, 1980. This was followed by some more correspondence between the College management and the Vice-Chancellor. The College management pointed out that at that late stage, it would not be possible to make any changes in their admission programme. There then the Vice-Chancellor addressed a letter dated 7/9th June 1980 to the Chairman of the Governing Body of the College stating that as per the decision of the Central Admission Committee, the last date for receipt of admission forms for undergraduate courses should be June 30, 1980 and the stipulation of the College as June 20, 1980 for that purpose would be very embar rassine to the University authorities. The Vice-Chancellor again asked the College Management to conform to the dates prescribed by the University.  7.
