In this written statement, it has been inter alia observed that "the licensing authority (Civil Surgeon, Ambala) re-examined the case and decided, vide letter dated 18.1.1993 (Annexure P.1) that the petitioner can be considered as qualified person and his name can be entered in the licence of existing firm and he can also be granted Retail Sale Drugs Licence in case he or (the) firm applies for it. "It is, thus, the writ petitioner is qualified to sell drugs etc. and is eligible for the grant of a licence. Thus, the very basis on which the show cause notice was issued to the petitioner by the Confed is non-existent. Mr. Laler has been at pains to point out that in fact, a licence was granted to the petitioner in 1994. Mr. Gupta appearing for the respondents is not in a position to admit or deny this statement of fact. However, it has been conceded that in view of the factual position as disclosed in the short reply filed by the Assistant State Drugs Controller on behalf of respondent Nos. 1 and 2, the show cause notice given to the petitioner is no longer valid. That being so, it has been submitted on behalf of the Confed that the writ petition has been rendered infructuous as no action shall be taken in pursuance of the show cause notice.  9. Resultantly, it is held that the show cause notice given to the petitioner was not valid and that he shall not be liable to be removed from service on account of the reasons as given in the impugned notice.  10. Lastly, we come to C.M. No. 2825 of 1995 and Review Application No. 21 of 1995 in LPA No. 568 of 1993. Mr. Patwalia submits that the case of Mr. L.C. Verma who was respondent No. 7 in CWP No. 1388 of 1991 is completely at par with that of Mr. R.K. Sehrawat (respondent No. 8 in the said writ petition) insofar as the eligibility for the post of Pharmacist is concerned. Even though, the notice of the writ petition was served on him and he had contested the case but the finding that he was not qualified cannot be sustained as there was no provision in the Common Cadre Rules promulgated on April 23, 1979 by which the prescribed qualifications were to apply retrospectively to the persons who had already been recruited. The qualifications were to be applicable only to the persons to be recruited to the service in future. It was on account of this reason that while making retrenchment, the respondent-Federation had not chosen Mr. L.C. Verma as one of the persons on whom the axe had fallen. Still further, it has also been contended that he possesses the prescribed qualifications. In view of this factual position, learned counsel contends that by virtue of the provisions of Order 41 Rule 33, he should be granted the same relief as is admissible in the case of Mr. R.K. Sehrawat. It is in this situation that he objects to the withdrawal of LPA No. 568 of 1993 which was allowed vide order dated August, 8, 1995 and prays for the review of the order. In the alternative learned counsel submits that the requisite relief can be granted even in LPA No. 649 of 1994 wherein Mr. L.C. Verma has been impleaded as one of the respondents. On the other hand, it has been submitted by Mr. Hemant Gupta, counsel for the respondent- Federation that no post of Pharmacist is available against which Mr. L.C. Verma may be accommodated. After making an enquiry, he has submitted that certain posts of Accountants are available. These posts are in the same scale of pay as the post of a Pharmacist.  11. It is undoubtedly correct that Civil Writ Petition No. 5542 of 1994 filed by Mr. L.C. Verma had been dismissed in limine on May 3, 1994 as his services had been terminated in pursuance of the directions in CWP No. 1388 of 1991. Thereafter, even his application No. 1089 of 1994 for condonation of delay and for entertainment of his appeal viz. LPA No. 689 of 1994 had been dismissed. Then, he had filed an application for being transposed as an appellant in LPA No. 568 of 1993. This was C.M. No. 208 of 1995. This was rejected on May 8, 1995 in view of the fact that he could get the requisite relief in LPA No. 568 of 1993 wherein the Confed was duly protecting his interests. Yet, the fact remains that he had been appointed as a Pharmacist on November 8, 1969. He had been absorbed in the Common Cadre in 1979. He had continued in service till 1994 when his services were suddenly ordered to be terminated. After having served for 25 years, he was not even entitled to any pension. He is still 51 years of age and has a period of about 7 years to serve the Respondent-Federation. In this situation, we think it would be adjust to keep in out of survey especially when he is not likely to get any retiral benefits after a service of 25 years. In the peculiar circumstances and without intending to lay down any precedent, we consider it appropriate to direct the Respondent-Federation to reinstate Mr. L.C. Verma as a Pharmacist. Mr. Verma is present in court. He has instructed Mr. Patwalia to state that he would not make any claim for arrears of salary from the date of the termination of his services, viz., April 19, 1994 to the date on which he is reinstated. However, the benefit of continuity of service should be given to him and his salary may be drawn against the available post of Accountant. It may be clarified that this would not affect the rights of any of the persons who are working on the posts of Pharmacists nor would the services of any of them be terminated on this account. In particular, it may be clarified that Mr. Sukhbir Singh, respondent No. 3 in LPA No. 649 of 1994 is admittedly working on the post of Pharmacist. The directions given by us in respect of Mr. L.C. Verma shall not in any way adversely affect his rights.  12. In view of the above, we allow L.P.A. No. 649 of 1994. We hold that the appellant and respondent No. 10 are entitled to continue on the posts of Pharmacists subject to the conditions mentioned above. It is clarified that Mr. L.C. Verma shall not be entitled to any arrears of salary. C.W.P. No. 7784 of 1992 is allowed. The show cause notice, a copy of which has been produced as Annexure P-2, is set aside. In view of the above, C.W. No. 2825 of 1995 and Review Application No. 21 of 1995 in LPA No. 568 of 1993 are rendered infructuous. These are, accordingly, disposed of. In the circumstances, there will be no order as to costs.  LPA allowed.
summary: Constitution of India, Articles 16 and 14 - Retrenchment from the post of Pharmacist - Petitioners challenged retrenchment orders on the basis that unqualified individuals were allowed to work while they were fully qualified - Learned Single Judge found that Respondents No. 7 and 8 were not qualified for the post - Management issued show cause notice to Mr. Sehrawat - Writ petition allowed and retention of Respondents No. 7 and 8 in service set aside - LPA allowed on grounds that Respondent No. 8 was condemned unheard and not served notice - Show cause notice to petitioner not valid and he was not to be removed from service - Respondent No. 7 directed to be reinstated as Pharmacist. [Paras 5, 7 and 8]

text: A.R. Lakshmanan, J.- The nine petitioners in W.P. No. 16302 of 1995 who are working as Junior Assistants, Assistants, Superintendents and Assistant Revenue Officers and the two petitioners in W.P. No.16913 of 1995 who are working as Junior Assistant and Assistant, in the Madurai Unit of the Tamil Nadu Housing Board, have filed the writ petitions challenging the common order dated 17.11.1995 of the Managing Director of the Tamil Nadu Housing Board, transferring them from Madurai to various places. According to them, the impugned order is illegal and an unfair labour practice and that the same has been passed by way of punishment for their trade union activities. According to the petitioners in W.P. No. 16302 of 1995, they have served only for a short period in the present station in which they were working as detailed below:  1st petitioner-One year and seven months  2nd petitioner-Seven years  3rd petitioner-Five years 4th petitioner-Six months 5th petitioner-Six months 6th petitioner-Two years  7th petitioner-Three years 8th petitioner-Five months 9th petitioner-One year and 11 months. According to the petitioners in W.P. No. 16913 of 1995, they have completed only a short period in the present station.  2. It is stated in the affidavit filed in support of W.P. No. 16302 of 1995 that on 10.10.1995 one Superintendent by name G. Meenakshisundaram was assaulted by the Executive Engineer Mr. Natarajan, Divisional Accountant Mr. K. Palaniappan and the Assistant Mr. Varadharajan. In that assault, the said Meenakshisundaram sustained grievous injuries and he was hospitalised, where he had undergone an operation. Since one of the staff members was brutally attacked by the higher official, condemning this act and to take legal action as against the concerned officials, the Joint Council of all Union Employees of the Housing Board, Madurai submitted a representation to the Managing Director on 17.10.1995 and since no action was taken till 31.10.1995, on 2.11.1995 the Joint Council submitted a representation expressing their intention to go on mass Casual Leave on 10.11.1995 showing their protest for not taking any action against the officials who has assaulted the Superintendent.  3. Subsequent to this, basing on the instructions of the Managing Director, the Superintending Engineer, Madurai, by memo dated 8.11.1995 instructed the Executive Engineer to bring to the notice of the employees that disciplinary action will be taken for taking mass casual leave. Meanwhile, the Joint Council instructed the employees to withdraw the mass Casual Leave on the basis of the discussions it had with the Managing Director in this regard on 6.11.1995, and basing on the assurance given by the Managing Director, the Joint Council had informed the Managing Director that the employees have withdrawn the mass Casual Leave. In addition to this, each individual also submitted a letter on 10.11.1995 withdrawing the casual leave and attended to the work, which fact was also informed by the Joint Council to the Managing Director.  4. According to the petitioners, though First Information Report was filed in the Criminal Case as against the three officials, no action was taken against them. On the other hand, in order to wreak vengeance for their union activities, the petitioners, who are prominent members of the union, were transferred by way of punishment. It is stated that the petitioners were not transferred for any administrative lapses or for any other irregularities but for putting forth a rightful claim for an unjust act. Neither any disciplinary proceedings are pending nor the petitioners are undergoing any punishment so as to warrant the transfer. Mass transfer can be ordered only during general transfer period and during the middle of the academic year, the petitioners cannot be disturbed arbitrarily. The petitioners' children are studying in Madurai and in the present office they have completed only a short period. Besides, the transfer order has been made in order to wreak vengenance against the petitioners for raising their voice as against an unlawful act of higher officials.  5. The same is the contention in W.P. No. 16913 of 1995 filed by the two other employees of the Tamil Nadu Housing Board.  6. The respondents filed a counter affidavit dated 4.12.1995 through the Secretary and Personnel Officer of the Tamil Nadu Housing Board. It is stated that the petitioners who were working in the four offices in Madurai viz., Madurai Circle, Madurai Housing Unit, Madurai Special Division and Tamil Nadu Urban Development Project, Madurai Division, for several years continuously were transferred purely for administrative reasons. As many as 20 persons serving in various categories were transferred from the above mentioned four offices to various other places by six different orders dated 17.11.1995. In the above orders, 20 persons were transferred from Madurai and 20 other persons were posted in the vacancies that arose at Madurai out of the said order of transfer.  7. According to the respondents, apart from the transfer orders relating to Madurai area, some other persons were also ordered to be transferred in the said proceedings from one place to another totally unconnected with the Madurai Area. One N. Ramakrishnan, Superintendent, who was working at Salem Housing Unit was transferred to Special Division 11, Coimbatore; one S. Thirugnanam, Divisional Accountant was transferred from K.K. Nagar Circle, Madras, to Ramanathapuram Housing Unit; one N. Durairaj, Divisional Accountant, Villupuram Housing Unit was transferred to TNUDP, Tiruchirapalli Division; and one G. Gladson, Junior Assistant from Vellore Housing Unit to Tirunelveli Housing Unit and likewise.  8. It is stated in the counter-affidavit that the following categories of persons were transferred from the four offices located at Madurai to various places;  Executive Engineer One Allottee Service Manager One Division Accountant. One Section Officer/Asst. Revenue Officer/Superintendent. Five  Assistant/Junior Assistant Eleven Out of the abovenamed persons, only nine persons alone have approached this Court aggrieved against the said order of transfer. It is also denied in the counter-affidavit that the petitioners have served only for a short period at Madurai. The break up details of total period of service put in by the petitioners at Madurai are found in paragraphs 5 of the counter affidavit, which is reproduced hereunder:  A. Jeevanandam (1st petitioner) 16 years 6 months  R. Pushpavanam, (2nd "), 21", 5"  E. Muruganandam, (3rd"), 19" 10"  V. Eswaran, (4th "), 20 ", 10 "  S. Mohan, (I) (5th "), 12 ", 10-1/2 "  R. Pandy, (6th "), 12 ", 7-1/2 "  P. Periakaruppan, (7th "), 22 ", 8-1/2 "  N. Nageswaran, (8th "), 27 ", 10 "  S. Arulanandam, (9th "), 24 ", 4-1/2 "  9. It is also stated in the counter-affidavit that a case has been registered under Sections 341, 323 and 506, I.P.C., by Tallakulam Hl Police Station in Crime No. 1485 of 1995 against one K. Natarajan, Executive Engineer and Administrative Officer, Madurai Special Division, Palaniappan, Divisional Accountant, Madurai, Special Division, and Varadharajan, Assistant, Madurai Special Division, on the basis of the complaint given by one Meenakshisundaram, Superintendent, Madurai Special Division, on 12.10.1995 and since the said case is pending, the respondents are awaiting the outcome of the said case, reserving liberty to proceed further on the basis of the result of the criminal case. The respondents have also denied that the impugned order has been passed by way of punishment or pursuant to any disciplinary proceedings.  10. The petitioners filed a reply affidavit dated 7.11.1995 to the counter- affidavit filed by the respondents. In the reply affidavit, the petitioners have furnished certain particulars in regard to the names of persons/individuals who are serving at Madurai for more than 15 to 20 years. The respondents filed an additional counter-affidavit dated 8.1.1996 and another additional counter-affidavit dated 22.1.1996.  11. I have heard Mr. K. Alagiriswami, learned Senior counsel for the petitioners and Mr. N. Kannadasan, learned counsel for the respondents.  12. Mr. K. Alagiriswami reiterated the contentions raised in the affidavit and mainly contended that the order of transfer is punitive in nature because of the petitioners' union activities and that the petitioners, who were working for a short period in the present office, were transferred to other places en masse for their union activities. Inviting my attention to the particulars furnished in the reply affidavit, Mr. K. Alagiriswami contended that the petitioners alone have been discriminated and persons who were working for more than 15 to 20 years in the same station (Madurai) were not at all disturbed, which would amount to discrimination. He further said that the persons who are transferred from other stations in the place of the petitioners have not joined and therefore the order of transfer impugned in these writ petitions is liable to be set aside. In support of his contentions, Mr. K. Alagiriswami cited the following decisions reported in P. Pushpakaran v. The Chairman, Coir Board, Cochin, 1979(1) SLR 309; Biman Kumar Roy v. S. Lakhshminarayanan, 1978(2) SLR 139 (Cal); C. Ramanathan v. Acting Zonal Manager, Food Corporation of India, Madras, 1980(1) SLR 309 (Madras); Prakash Chandra Sexana v. State of Madhya Pradesh, 1980(1) SLR 788; Mohammad Thekkethil v. Director of Panchayats, 1982(2) SLR 390 (Kerala); and K.K. Jindal v. General Manager, Northern Railway, 1996(2) CAT 27.  13. Mr. N. Kannadasan, per contra, contended that the order of transfer has been made only on administrative grounds and that the petitioners have been working in Madurai itself for more than 16, 21, 19, 20, 12, 12, 22, 27 and 24 years respectively as per the particulars furnished in paragraph 5 of the counter-affidavit. It is contended that the petitioners cannot claim, as a matter of right, to stick on at Madurai itself for the entire length of their service and that the break up details furnished in paragraph 5 of the counter-affidavit would disclose that in their entire tenure of office the petitioners were allowed to work at Madurai itself for a very long period and that all of them have served in stations other than Madurai only for a short period and as such, no motive could be attributed to the impugned orders of transfer. Since the impugned orders of transfer were passed purely for administrative reasons, no motive could be alleged as if the impugned order has been passed by way of punishment. This apart it is contended that several orders of transfer were passed on the same day viz., 17.11.1995, which involve nearly 45 persons in the entire State but only the petitioners alone have come forward to this Court alleging mala fides against the said orders of transfer. In support of his contentions, Mr. N. Kannadasan cited the following decisions reported in Union of India v. S.L. Abbas, AIR 1993 SC 2444 : 1995(4) SCT 455(SC); Rajendran Roy v. Union of India, AIR 1993 SC 1236 : 1993(2) SCT 65(SC); Union of India v. N.P. Thomas, 1994(1) SCT 46 (SC) : 1993 Supp. (1) SCC 704 and State of Madhya Pradesh v. S.S. Kourav, 1995(1) SLJ 350 : 1995(2) SCT 195(SC). 14. I have carefully considered the arguments of the learned counsel appearing on either side. I have also gone through the decisions cited on either side. I do not propose to individually refer to decisions cited by both sides in view of the settled position of law as discussed infra.  15. A cursory perusal of the particulars furnished in paragraph 5 of the counter-affidavit would disclose that the petitioners have served in Madurai Region itself for several years as extracted in paragraph 8 above. A perusal of the break up details would disclose that the petitioners have worked in Madurai itself for a very long period and have served in other stations only for a very short period.  16. It is true that criminal prosecution has been launched against three of the officers and the matter is pending before the Criminal Court and that the Board was awaiting the outcome of the said case, reserving liberty to proceed further on the basis of the result of the criminal case. A complaint has been registered under Sections 341, 323 and 506. I.P.C., by Tallakulam Hl Police Station in Crime No. 1485 of 1995 against K. Natarajan, Palaniappan and Varadharajan.  17. The motive alleged for transfer is the demonstration made by the petitioners against the management for not taking action against the aforementioned three officials for assaulting one G. Meenakshisundaram, a member of the petitioners' union. It is now represented that a complaint has already been lodged and the matter is taken on file by the competent Criminal Court. It is also stated that they are waiting for the outcome of the Criminal case for proceeding against the officers who are involved in the assault case. Therefore, no motive can be alleged for transfer of the petitioners to other stations.  18. The further averment of the petitioners that the impugned order of transfer has been passed by mass order is also incorrect and the same has been denied specifically by the Housing Board. As stated already, several orders of transfer have been passed on the same day, i.e., 17.11.1995 involving about 45 persons in the entire State. It is not in dispute that only nine persons have come forward before this Court alleging mala fide against the order of transfer. The mala fide alleged, in my opinion, has no basis at all. The petitioners, as a matter of right cannot claim to stick on at Madurai itself for the entire length of their service. It is also pointed out to me that one N. Ramakrishnan, Superintendent, who was working at Salem Housing Unit was transferred to Special Division II, Coimbatore; one S. Thirugnanam, Divisional Accountant was transferred from K.K. Nagar, Madras, to Ramanathapuram Housing Unit, one N. Durairaj, Divisional Accountant, Villupuram Housing Unit TNUDP, Tiruchirapalli Division; and one G. Gladson, Junior Assistant from Vellore Housing Unit to Tirunelveli Housing Unit. The above facts would amply demonstrate that the orders of transfer were issued purely for administrative reasons and not confined to the petitioners alone. It is also pertinent to notice that all the posts which have fallen vacant because of the transfer of the petitioners were already filled up by persons who were also ordered to be transferred from other offices. It is further contented by the respondents that excluding the last grade servants such as Officer Assistants, there are about 391 or more persons working in Madurai as officers out of which only 20 persons were transferred. Therefore, in my opinion, it cannot be termed that the petitioners alone were transferred by virtue of a mass transfer order. As rightly contended by Mr. N. Kannadasan, the impugned orders of transfer were passed purely for the purpose of stream-lining, re-organising and toning up the quality of administration in various offices throughout the State and therefore, there is no mala fide or motivation on the part of the administration in effecting the said orders of transfer. I see much force in the above contention of the learned counsel for the respondents.  19. In the course of argument it is contended by the petitioners that the substitutes who were posted in the posts that were occupied by the petitioners were forced to join duty for the sake of record and none of them was working as on the said date after joining their respective posts at Madurai Division. It is also contended that the substitutes immediately after reporting for duty have gone on leave and not working there continuously. This Court directed the respondents to ascertain and inform this Court about the veracity of the statement made by the petitioners. In this connection, an additional counter-affidavit was filed by the respondents stating that the statement made on the side of the petitioners is absolutely false and not correct. It is stated in the additional counter-affidavit that for the 11 posts from which the petitioners were transferred, all the 11 substitutes have joined immediately after availing joining time and ten persons are continuously working from the date of their joining duty at Madurai Office and that only one individual by name R. Santhanam, who has joined duty on 27.11.1995, is on leave on medical ground and all the remaining persons except two individuals who have gone on leave for a short while are working continuously from the date of their joining duty. The two individuals who have availed leave for a short while have also subsequently joined duty and are working there continuously.  20. In the course of arguments Mr. K. Alagiriswami, made a further plea to the effect that the petitioners can be retained at Madurai till the end of the academic year. The matter was adjourned for the said purpose. Mr. N. Kannadasan, after consulting the respondents, submitted that this request of the petitioners will create certain administrative problems as detailed in the additional counter-affidavit filed on 8.1.1996. They are :  a. The sanctioned strength of the Board/Circle/Unit/Division would increase in the event of reposting the petitioners once again in the same office,  b. Two persons cannot be appointed or posted to a single vacancy. Further, there is no extra work load in the Madurai Office which can be entrusted to the petitioners since the work has already been allocated among the existing staff and the persons who were posted as substitutes have already joined duty.  c. The work relating to the offices wherein the petitioners were posted would be affected and dislocated if the said posts are kept vacant and the same would adversely affect the administration in other offices.  d. Frequent shifting of personnel will cause dislocation to both the offices i.e., the office at Maduari as well as the offices where the substitutes were posted in the place of the petitioners leading to let up in service to the general public and allottees.  e. As per the Service Regulations of the Tamil Nadu Housing Board, the posts in which the incumbents have been working are transferable within the offices of the Board which are located throughout the State including in the middle of the academic year for administrative reasons.  f. All the petitioners were transferred purely on administrative grounds and to streamline the functioning of the officers for which no mala fide could be attributed. In view of the explanation offered by the respondents, as stated above, I am of the view that it is not for this Court to interfere with the orders of transfer which have been made on administrative grounds.  21. Another additional counter-affidavit was filed on 22.1.1996 to clarify the plea raised by Mr. K. Alagiriswami, on the previous hearing date with regard to the memorandum dated 27.12.1995 issued by the Executive Engineer and Administrative Officer, Madurai, Housing Unit to some of the writ petitioners. It is submitted that the Executive Engineer has issued the said memo to the individuals concerned when he came to know that they are in the habit of availing casual leave/earned leave without obtaining any prior permission resulting in dislocation of routine work of office. The Executive Engineer and Administrative Officer have, therefore, issued the said memo in order to point out the lapses on the part of the individuals concerned and even though they were directed to submit a reply within a period of three days, no action was initiated against any of the individuals consequent on the memo dated 27.12.1995.  22. The allegation of victiminisation alleged by the petitioners, in my opinion, has to be rejected as the petitioners cannot claim any immunity from transfer merely by reason of their being office-bearers of the union. The fact that they had organised protests and agitations is not a ground from which intention to victimise the petitioners can be inferred. Apart from the general allegation that their trade union activities have led to their transfer, there is no other material from which it could be inferred that the transfers were effected with a view to victimise the petitioners. Therefore, I reject the contention of Mr. Alagiriswami, that the transfers were made by way of punishment and also for the trade union activities of the petitioners.  23. Transfer of employees has been considered by this Court in numerous decisions and it has been held by this Court that transfer is a general condition of service of the employees, that such transfers are to be effected for the administrative convenience and that the Court does not sit in appeal nor call for details of administrative exigencies. It is not alleged by the petitioners that because of the transfer order there is any loss of emoluments or any loss to their status. Therefore in my view, it cannot be characterised as an amount of punishment. In fact, l myself have held in a number of cases that the Housing Board or the Electricity Board is entitled to transfer any of its employees if the transfer is necessitated by administrative exigencies. It is worthwhile to remember that no employee has a right to work in a particular place. As already seen, the petitioners have worked in Madurai itself ranging from 10 to 20 years. As pointed out by Mr. N. Kannadasan, the order of transfer need not necessarily be passed on the balance of convenience and an order of transfer is passed purely on administrative exigencies. It is also settled law that Courts do not exercise supervisory control over orders of transfer. It is a necessary concomitant of every service. This is what the various High Courts including this Court and the Supreme Court have consistently laid down.  24. The allegations of mala fide were not made out on the facts of this case. Only in cases where the order of transfer is found to be mala fide or in cases where such orders are in colourable exercise of power, the orders would become wholly illegal and void. In this case, it has not been made out by any acceptable material that the order of transfer has been made with any mala fide intention. In a recent decision in N.K. Singh v. Union of India, 1994(5) JT (SC) 298 : 1995(1) SCT 269(SC) the Supreme Court has observed as follows :  ``No roving enquiry into the matter is called for or justified within the scope of judicial review of a transfer scrutinised with reference to the private rights of an individual.... Transfer of a Government servant in a transferable service is a necessary incident of the service career."  25. In my opinion, there are no compelling or strong circumstances to cancel the order of transfer. In my considered opinion, the order of transfer is not vitiated by any mala fides or extraneous considerations as contended by Mr. K. Alagiriswami. The transfer of the petitioners is in accordance with the Regulations of the Housing Board and it is not for this Court to enter into a roving enquiry into the matter to ascertain the precise nature of the administrative exigency and judicially review the same. This apart, as a matter of fact, all the persons who were transferred to the posts of the petitioners have already joined and they are working in the said posts.  26. For the foregoing reasons, I hold that there are no merits in any of the contentions raised by the petitioners. Accordingly, both the writ petitions are dismissed. However, there will be no order as to costs.  Petitions dismissed.
summary: The Constitution of India, Articles 14, 16, and 226 - Transfer - Petitioners who are office bearers of the Trade Union - Their post is transferable throughout the State - Transfer is made because of administrative reasons and convenience, not by way of punishment -The transfer order does not necessarily have to be based on convenience - Courts do not have supervisory control over transfer orders - in writ jurisdiction, no interference is allowed - The order of transfer is not affected by any mala fide or extraneous consideration. [Paras 23 & 24]

text: Eswara Prasad, J. (Oral) - The petitioner is the President of Andhra Pradesh Urdu Academy, Hyderabad. He was nominated as the President of the Board of Governors of the Urdu Academy by the Government of Andhra Pradesh, the first respondent, in G.O.M.s. No. 294, Education (SAM) Department, dated 16.11.1990. Orders regarding the term, remuneration and other perks to the President were to be issued separately. Subsequently, by G.O. Rt. No. 1915, Edn., dated 19.12.1990, the perks of the President were fixed. With regard to the term of Office of the petitioner, it was stated that orders of the Government will be issued separately. By the impugned order dated 31.3.1992 in G.O.Ms. No. 117, the term of Office of the petitioner was fixed as one year and the petitioner was directed to hand over the charge of the Office of President, as one year had already elapsed since he assumed Office as President.  2. The petitioner impugns G.O.Ms. No. 117, dated 31.3.1992 as a arbitrary and illegal and prays for consequential directions to the first respondent to continue the petitioner as President, till the expiry of three years from the date of his appointment on 16.11.1990.  3. The learned Counsel for the petitioner submitted that the term of office of Board of Governors of the Urdu Academy, of which the petitioner is the President, is three years as per clause 4(2) of the Rules of Urdu Academy. He contends that the term of the petitioner cannot be fixed as one year and that the Government is bound to continue the petitioner for a period of three years from the date of his nomination. He further contended that the petitioner had a reasonable expectation of being continued in Office for the full term of three years and that the reduction of the period to one year is arbitrary, illegal and mala fide.  4. The A.P. Urdu Academy is a society, registered under the Public Societies Registration Act. It is managed by Board of Governors consisting of seven Officers of Government, who are ex officio Members and donors who donated Rs. 10,00,000/- or more and the President and Vice-President and thirty six others, to be nominated by the Government. As per the constitution of the Board, it may be reconstituted once in every three years. The Memorandum of Articles or the Rules and Bye-laws do not prescribe any term for such nominated persons. On 12.8.1985 by G.O.Ms. No. 381, the Board of Governors was nominated for a period of three years. After the expiry of three years, the Board was not to be constituted. The petitioner alone was nominated as the President of the Board by the order dated 16.11.1990.  5. The learned Advocate-General appearing for the first respondent contended that the Chief Minister of the State is the President of the Academy and he nominated the petitioner as his Nominee. No term is fixed so far as the President is concerned. As such the petitioner was nominated without fixing any term by the order dated 16.11.1990. There can be no claim for fixing three years term, as contended by the petitioner. No material to show any mala fides on the part of the Government is placed before the Court. The Government was within its rights in fixing the term of Office of the President as one year. The rules and Bye-laws are not statutory and are not enforceable and that no principles of natural justice are violated.  6. The first submission of Sri V. Rajagopal Reddy is that the term of Office of the President is three years, as envisaged by Clause 4(2) of the Rules of Urdu Academy, cannot be accepted. The relevant rules are as follows :  "Constitution of the Board of Governors :  (1) The First Board of Governors shall be as specified in the Memorandum of Association. The First President, Vice-President, Member and nominated member of the Academy shall hold Office until the Board of Governors is reconstituted under Sub-Rule (2).  (2) At the expiration of three years from the date of registration of the Academy and thereafter at the expiration of every three years, the Board of Governors shall be reconstituted".  From a reading of the above rules, it is seen that under Sub-Rule 2, the Board of Governors has to be reconstituted after the expiration of every three years. It only shows that the term of Office of the Board of Governors has to be reconstituted with the new Board of Governors, after the expiry of three years. In the present case, the petitioner alone was appointed as President and no Board of Governors was reconstituted in the year 1988. Clause 4(2) is not applicable in the case where the President alone is nominated. The petitioner cannot claim any right to be nominated for a period of three years. As rightly contended by the learned Advocate General, the Rules and Bye-laws of the Urdu Academy are not statutory and are not enforceable.  It is also not pertinent to note that the petitioner accepted nomination on 16.11.1990 without the term of the Office being fixed. He did not raise any contention that the term should have been fixed as three years. The petitioner has full knowledge that the Government may fix any term it chooses by a subsequent order. Even by the order dated 19.12.1990, the petitioner was informed that an order fixing his term of Office will be issued separately. Therefore the question of a reasonable expectation to be continued in Office for a period of three years, as contended by the learned Counsel, does not arise.  7. Sir V. Rajagopal Reddy referred to several decisions of the Supreme Court in S.L. Kapoor v. Jagmohan, AIR 1981 SC 136., Cantonment Board, dinapore v. Taramani Devi, AIR 1992 SC 61 Sumati p. Shere v. Union of India, 1989(2) SLP 422 (SC); Shrilekha Vidyarthi v. State of U.P., 1990(6) SLR 1 (SC); Central Inland Water Transport Corpn. v. Brojo Nath, 1986(2) SLR 345 (SC); Union of India v. Tulsiram Patel, 1985(2) SLR 576 (SC); Delhi Transport Corpn. v. DTC Mazdoor Congress, 1990(5) SLR 311 : 1991(1) S.C.T. 675(SC); M/s R.B.S.D. Pd. & P.N. Das v. Settlement Commn., (IT & WT), AIR 1989 SC 1038; R. Jeevaratnam v. State of Madras, 1967 SLR 57 (SC) and contended that the order terminating the Office of the petitioner without notice is illegal. The decisions in all the aforesaid cases were in respect of service matters. The Office of the petitioner cannot be said to be an ordinary service under the State. The Urdu Academy is a public body registered under the Public Societies Registration Act. The petitioner is not an employee of the Academy. The ratio of the said decision is not applicable in the case of the petitioner.  The learned Counsel also relied on a decision in Vice-Chancellor, O.U. v. Chancellor, AIR 1967 SC 1305 and contended that the term of Office of the petitioner cannot be reduced. That was a case where an enactment was made reducing the term of Office of Vice-Chancellor. The enactment was struck down as it was made for the purpose of unseating Dr. D.S. Reddy, whose term was earlier fixed. In the present case the term of Office of the petitioner was not fixed by an order by which he was appointed. The petitioner was informed that the term will be fixed later and the Government thought it fit to fix only one year as the term of Office. As rightly contended by the learned Advocate-General, the Government reserved its right to fix the term of Office. The petitioner accepted his nomination without reservation and cannot now be permitted to complain that the term should have been fixed at three years. Petitioner's right to Office flows only from the order of nomination. The fixing up of a term of Office is not a penalty. There is no legal right for the petitioner to continue for a larger time than fixed by the impugned order. The impugned order is not arbitrary and needs no interference. No grounds attributing mala fides to the first respondent are made out. The Writ Petition is liable to be dismissed.  8. Under the impugned G.O., the term of the Office of the petitioner was fixed as one year from 16.11.1990, which expired on 15.11.1991. The impugned order was dated 31.3.1992. The petitioner continued to be the President after the expiration of one year and he is in Office till today by virtue of interim orders of this Court dated 3.4.1992. The learned Advocate-General fairly stated that the petitioner will not be asked to refund the honorarium paid to him and to pay back the amounts covered by the other perks, enjoyed by the petitioner after the expiry of one year and the said statement is recorded.  9. The Writ Petition is accordingly, dismissed. No order as to costs.  Petition dismissed.
summary: Constitution of India, Articles 311 - Termination - The petitioner was appointed as President of the Board of Governors of Urdu Academy by the Government of Andhra Pradesh. The term of office was not fixed by the order of appointment. The Government fixed the term of office for one year and reserved its right to fix the term of office. The petitioner accepted the nomination without reservation and cannot complain that the term should have been fixed at three years. The petitioner's right to office flows only from the order of nomination. Fixing up of a term of office is not a penalty and there is no legal right for the petitioner to continue for a longer time that fixed by impugned order. The impugned order is not arbitrary, and therefore does not need any interference. [Para 7]

text: D.P. Mohapatra, J. - This appeal filed by the State of Haryana, represented by the Chief Secretary and the Secretary to Government of Haryana, Department of Finance, is directed against the judgment of the Punjab & Haryana High Court dated 13.8.1986 in CWP No. 4206/95 filed by the Haryana Civil Secretariat Personal Staff Association through its General Secretary Shri Ram Mehar Sharma. In the writ petition the petitioner prayed for a writ in the nature of mandamus directing the respondents to grant the Personal Assistants (for short `P.A.s') the pay scale of Rs. 2,000-3500 plus Rs. 150/- as special pay which have been given to the P.A.s working in the Central Secretariat for the reason that the State of Haryana had accepted the recommendations made by the Fourth Central Pay Commission with regard to revision of pay scales with effect from 1.1.1986 with all consequential benefits like fixation of pay, arrears and other benefits.  2. The case of the writ petitioner sans unnecessary details was that prior to 1986 the P.As in the Civil Secretariat, Haryana were enjoying higher scale of pay than the P.A.s of the Central Secretariat. On receipt of the Fourth Central Pay Commission Report the Central Government revised the pay scale of P.A.s to Rs. 2000-3500 with effect from 1.1.1986. Though the Government of Haryana accepted the recommendations of the Fourth Central Pay Commission and implemented the same in respect of certain categories of employees but in respect of P.A.s in the Civil Secretariat the revised scale of pay was fixed at Rs. 1640-2900 + Rs. 150/- as special pay, instead of Rs. 2000-3500. The further case of the petitioner was that in respect of certain categories of employees of different departments of State of Haryana like Education, Police, Transport, Health and Engineering and Technical staff, the State Government revised the scale of pay exactly according to the recommendation of the Fourth Central Pay Commission and granted them the scale of Rs. 2000-3500 but in case of he P.A.s. the State Government fixed the lower revised scale of pay denying them parity of pay scale with their counterparts in the Central Government. The petitioner alleged that the post of P.A. in Civil Secretariat of the State of Haryana is comparable with the post of P.A. in Central Secretariat; they discharge similar duties and responsibilities as those of their counterparts in the Central Secretariat. The petitioner contended that employees like Police Inspectors and some others who were borne on the same scale of pay as P.A.s prior to implementation of the Fourth Central Pay Commissioner Report i.e. Rs. 700-1250, were granted the pay scale of Rs. 2000-3200 whereas the P.A.s were placed in the scale of Rs. 1640-2900 only. Such action on the part of the State Government, the petitioner contended, was arbitrary, discriminatory and irrational. The further case of the petitioner was that on receipt of several representations from the petitioner-association and its members, the State Government referred the matter to the Pay Anomalies Commission headed by the Chief Secretary, which did not accept the claim of the petitioner but only recommended the Selection Grade of Rs. 2000-3200 to the 20% of the posts of P.As. with the condition of 12 years of service. It was asserted by the petitioner that the P.A.s working in the Civil Secretariat were entitled to get the pay scale of Rs. 2000-3500 with effect from 1.1.1986 and the decision taken by the State Government granting the Selection Grade of Rs. 2000-3200 and that too only to those P.As. who have completed 12 years of services and maximum up to 20% of the posts in cadre is wholly illegal and unjust.  3. Refuting the allegations made in the writ petition the respondents in their counter affidavit questioned the very basis of the claim laid by the petitioner which was based on the assumption that P.A.s in the State Civil Secretariat were entitled to the same scale of pay granted by the Central Government to P.A.s working in the Central Secretariat. Such comparison for the purpose of claim of parity of pay, the respondents contended, was misconceived and was of no avail to the petitioner in the case. According to the respondents, though the State Government on principle accepted the report of the Fourth Central Pay Commission it did not entitle the members of the petitioner to claim post to post and scale to scale parity of pay. The respondents asserted that considering various relevant aspects which were required to be taken into account for fixation of pay scale the State Government decided to fix the revised scale of Rs. 1640-2900 for P.As. working in the Civil Secretariat and subsequently on recommendation of Pay Anomalies Commission the State Government decided to grant the Selection Grade pay of Rs. 2000-3200 plus Rs. 150/- special pay to P.A.s with 12 years of service and up to 20% of the posts in the cadre. Such administrative decision, the respondents contended, was within the power of the State Government; therefore the decision cannot be said to be arbitrary or irrational.  4. The High Court in the judgment dated 13.8.1996 allowed the writ petition, declared that the P.A.s were entitled to the scale of Rs. 2000-3500 from 1.1.1986 and directed that arrears would be restricted to 38 months from the date of filing of the writ petition i.e. 21st March, 1995 but after fixing the pay notionally from 1.1.1986. The High Court further directed that the selection grade would merge with the revised scale of Rs. 2000-3500 and the State may consider if it would like to grant the special pay to the P.A.s or not. The State Government, feeling aggrieved by the judgment rendered by the High Court, has filed this appeal assailing the judgment.  5. In the judgment the High Court placed reliance on the principle of `equal pay for work'. It also took note of the principle of law that ordinarily the matter of fixation of pay should be left to be determined by the executive authorities and court would only interfere when it finds that classification is improper or discriminatory. Then the High Court proceeded to consider facts of the case particularly taking note of the position that in case of certain other category of employees the State Government had granted exactly the revised scale of pay, Rs. 2000-3500 sanctioned by the Central Government whereas in the case of P.A.s a lower scale was fixed. The High Court appears to have proceeded on the assumption that P.A.s serving in the Civil Secretariat are discharging the duties and responsibilities similar to those of P.A.s in the Central Secretariat for the simple reason that the averment to the effect in the writ petition was not rebutted by the respondents. The High Court observed : "it is true hat it is for the government to fix the scales but the same cannot be done by ignoring the equities and the principles of equality". Referring to certain decisions of this Court like State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar, 1952 SCR 284, Randhir Singh v. Union of India & Ors., 1982(1) SCC 618, P. Savita & Ors. v. Union of India & Ors., 1985(3) SLR 29, State of Madhya Pradesh & Anr. v. Pramod Bhartiya & Ors., 1993(1) Recent Services Judgments 618 : 1993(1) SCT 138 (SC), Purushottam Lal & Ors. v. Union of India & Anr., AIR 1973 SC 1988, Haryana State Biologists Association v. The State of Haryana, 1994(4) Recent Services Judgments 444 : 1994(3) SCT 198 (P&H)(DB), the High Court accepted the case of the writ petitioner, allowed the writ petition and issued the directions as noted earlier.  6. Shri P.C. Jain, learned senior counsel appearing for the appellants contended that the High Court has ignored the settled principles of law in a claim relating to party of pay and fixation of revised scale of pay; the judgment of the High Court is patently erroneous and should be set aside.  7. On the other hand, Shri Anup G. Choudhary, learned senior counsel appearing for the respondent supporting the judgment urged that in the context of facts and circumstances of the case the High Court rightly accepted the claim of parity of scale of pay pleaded by the respondent and no interference with the judgment is called for.  8. From the discussions in the impugned judgment it is clear to us that the High Court has ignored certain settled principles of law for determination of the claim on parity of pay scale by a section of government employees. While making copious reference to the principle of equal pay for equal work and equality in the matter of pay, the High Court overlooked the position that the parity sought by the petitioner in the case was with employees having only the same designation under the Central Government. Such comparison by a section of employees of State Government with employees of Central Government based merely on designation of the posts was misconceived. The High Court also fell in error in assuming hat the averment regarding similarity of duties and responsibilities made in the writ petition was unrebutted. The appellants in their counter affidavit have taken the specific stand that no comparison between the two sections of employees is possible since the qualifications prescribed for the P.As. in the Central Secretariat are different from the P.A.s in the State Civil Secretariat. Even assuming that there was no specific rebuttal of the averment in the writ petition that could not form the basis for grant of parity of scale of pay as claimed by the respondent. The High Court has not made any comparison of the nature of duties and responsibilities, the qualifications for recruitment to the posts of P.A.s. in the State Civil Secretariat with those of P.A.s of the Central Secretariat.  9. This Court in the case of Secretary, Finance Department & Ors. v. West Bengal Registration Service Association & Ors., 1993 Supp. (1) SCC 153 : 1992(2) SCT 301 (SC), dealing with the question of equation of posts and equation of salaries of government employees, made the following observations :  "We do not consider it necessary to reverse the case law on which reliance has been placed by counsel for the appellants as it is well settled that equation of posts and determination of pay scales is the primary function of the executive and not the judiciary and, therefore, ordinarily courts will not enter upon the task of job evaluation which is generally left to expert bodies like the Pay Commissions, etc. But that is not to say that the Court has no jurisdiction and the aggrieved employees have no remedy if they are unjustly treated by arbitrary State action or inaction. Courts must, however, realize that job evaluation is both a difficult and time consuming task which even expert bodies having the assistance of staff with requisite expertise have found difficult to undertake sometimes on account of want of relevant data and scales for evaluating performances of different groups of employees. This would call for a constant study of the external comparisons and internal relativities on account of the changing nature of job requirements. The factors which may have to be kept in view for job evaluation may include (i) the work programme of his department (ii) the nature of contribution expected of him (iii) the extent of his responsibility and accountability of the discharge of his diverse duties and functions (iv) the extent and nature of freedoms/limitations available or imposed on him in the discharge of his duties (v) the extent of powers vested in him (vi) the extent of his dependence on superiors for the exercise of his powers (vii) the need to co- ordinate with other departments, etc. We have also referred to the history of service and the effort of various bodies to reduce the total number of pay scales to a reasonable number. Such reduction in the number of pay scales has to be achieved by resorting to broadbanding of posts by placing different posts having comparable job charts in a common scale. Substantial reduction in the number of pay scales must inevitably lead to clubbing of posts and grades which were earlier different and unequal. While doing so care must be taken to ensure that such rationalization of the pay structure does not throw up anomalies. Ordinarily a pay structure is evolved keeping in mind several factors e.g., (i) method of recruitment, (ii) level at which recruitment is made, (iii) the hierarchy of service in a given cadre, (iv) minimum educational/technical qualifications required, (v) avenues of promotion (vi) the nature of duties and responsibilities, (vii) the horizontal and vertical relativities with similar jobs, (viii) public dealings, (ix) satisfaction level (x) employer's capacity to pay, etc. We have referred to these matters in some detail only to emphasise that several factors have to be kept in view while evolving a pay structure and the horizontal and vertical relatives have to be carefully balanced keeping in mind the hierarchical arrangements, avenues for promotion, etc. Such a carefully evolved pay structure ought not to be ordinarily disturbed as it may upset the balance and cause avoidable ripples in other cadres as well. It is presumably for this reason that the Judicial Secretary who had strongly recommended a substantial hike in the salary of the Sub-Registrars to the Second (State) Pay Commission found in difficult to concede the demand made by the Registration Service before him in his capacity as the Chairman of the Third (State) Pay Commission. There can, therefore, be no doubt that equation of posts and equation of salaries is a complex matter which is best left to an expert body unless there is cogent material on record to come to a firm conclusion that a grave error had crept in while fixing the pay scale for a given post and Court's interference is absolutely necessary to undo the injustice". (emphasis supplied)  10. It is to be kept in mind that the claim of equal pay for equal work is not a fundamental right vested in any employee though it is a constitutional goal to be achieved by the Government. Fixation of pay and determination of parity in duties and responsibilities is a complex matter which is for the executive to discharge. While taking a decision in the matter several relevant factors, some of which have been noted by this Court in the decided case, are to be considered keeping in view the prevailing financial position and capacity of the State Government to bear the additional liability of a revised scale of pay. It is also to be kept in mind that the priority given to different types of posts under the prevailing policies of the State Government is also a relevant factor for consideration by the State Government. In the content of complex nature of issues involved, the far reaching consequences of a decision in the matter and its impact on the administration of the State Government courts have taken the view that ordinarily courts should not try to delve deep into administrative decisions pertaining to pay fixation and pay parity. That is not to say that the matter is not justifiable or that the courts cannot entertain any proceeding against such administrative decision taken by the government. The courts should approach such matters with restraint and interfere only when they are satisfied that the decision of the government is patently irrational, unjust and prejudicial to the section of employees and the government while taking the decision has ignored factors which are material and relevant for a decision in the matter. Even in a case where the court holds that order passed by the government to be unsustainable then ordinarily a direction should be given to the State Government or the authority taking the decision to reconsider the matter and pass a proper order. The court should avoid giving a declaration granting a particular scale of pay and compelling the government to implement the same. As noted earlier, in the present case the High Court has not even made any attempt to compare the nature of duties and responsibilities of the two sections of employees, one in the State Secretariat and the other in the Central Secretariat. It has also ignored the basic principle that there are certain rules, regulations and executive instructions issued by the employers which govern the administration of the cadre.  11. On the discussions in the foregoing paragraphs, we have no hesitation to hold the High Court was in error in allowing the writ petition and directing the appellants to grant the scale of Rs. 2000-3500 to the P.A.s of the State Civil Secretariat with effect from 1.1.1986. The judgment of the High Court is unsustainable. Therefore, the appeal is allowed and the judgment under challenge is set aside. The writ petition filed by the respondent herein is dismissed. There will, however, be no order for costs.  12. We make it clear that if any of the Personal Assistant(s) serving in the Haryana State Civil Secretariat has/have received any additional emoluments in pursuance of the judgment of the High Court under challenge such amount will not be recovered from him/them.  Appeal allowed.
summary: Constitution of India, Articles 14, 16 and 226 - Equal pay for equal work - Court jurisdiction to evaluate - Equal pay for equal work is a constitutional goal rather than a fundamental right - Fixation of pay and determination of parity in duties and responsibilities is complex and falls under the responsibilities of the executive, considering several relevant factors - The State's prevailing policies establish the priority given to various posts, which is a relevant factor - Courts should generally refrain from interfering in administrative decisions regarding pay parity - However, there is no absolute bar for taking legal action against such decisions - When deciding on such matters, the court should exercise caution and only interfere when the executive decision is patently irrational, unjust, and prejudices relevant factors - A court should avoid granting a declaration granting a particular scale of pay and compelling the government to implement it. [Para 10]

text: S.B. Sinha, J. - Leave granted.  Respondent was appointed as a Driver by Appellants herein. On 07.12.1986, he was driving a bus on Aligarh-Agra route. A barrier was installed at Sasani Bus Stand by the public. The barrier was not installed by Appellant-Corporation or by any other statutory authority. Respondent allegedly dashed into the barrier intentionally and caused injuries to one Bhoodev. He was placed under suspension. A domestic inquiry was held. He was found to be guilty of the charges levelled against him. He was directed to be removed from services. An industrial dispute was raised whereupon the State referred the following dispute for adjudication to the Labour Court, Agra :  "Whether the termination of services of Shri Shivaji, S/o Shri Sundarlal, Driver, by the employees vide order dated 07.09.1987 is legal and valid ? If not, then to what relief/benefit the workman is entitled ? And with what details ? 2. A preliminary issue was raised as to whether the domestic inquiry was legal and valid. It was held not to be so; whereupon Appellants were granted opportunity to adduce evidence to prove the charges against Respondent. Evidence was led before the Labour Court. On analysis of the evidence brought on records, the Labour Court held :  "...Shri Bhoodev Singh, S/o Mulayam Singh has been produced on behalf of employers who stated that on 07.12.1986 the witness was posted as Sasani. A barrier was installed in front of bus stand to stop the bus which was used to be opened by the witness. On the said date the concerned workman came along with bus from the side of Aligarh. The witness has lowered the barrier to stop the bus but concerned workman did not stop the bus. The bus went ahead by breaking the barrier due to which the witness fell down and got injuries in his hands and legs. In cross examination also no contrary fact has been emerged from this witness and he has supported his original statement. 7. The concerned workman has not produced any evidence in his defence. From consideration of all the evidence and documents available on record the conclusion is arrived that the workman has intentionally hit the barrier due to which one employee got injured. In this accident there could be serious loss of life and property. Therefore my opinion is that concerned workman is guilty of serious misconduct and has no right to remain in service. The termination of workman's services w.e.f. 07.09.1987 is legal and valid and he is not entitled for any benefit/relief. Both parties will bear their own costs." 3. A writ petition was filed questioning the correctness of the said Award by Respondent before the High Court which by reason of the impugned judgment was allowed, stating :  "Statement of aforementioned sole witness has been brought on record along with supplementary affidavit. In the statement of aforementioned witness it has been mentioned that he has received minor injury. It has been admitted by him that while bus was proceeding from Aligarh to Sasni then he asked to get bus stopped when the Bus was near to barrier and by that time he was putting barrier down bus caused injuries to him. It has been admitted that said barrier was not belonging to Roadways and it was totally private barrier. No injuries has been caused by bus rather on account of barrier falling, the rope was loosened on account of which he fell down. It has been admitted that bus could have passed even without putting barrier down. No justification has come on record as to why said bus was being stopped at that private barrier. No First Information Report has been lodged, no medical examination was done at Government Hospital. It is true that High Court has got no authority to appreciate evidence, but the case in hand, taking the sequence of events clearly establish that it is practically case of no evidence. Tested on the touchstone of reasonableness and fairness, no reasonable or prudent man would construe, this case to be a case of misconduct as has been alleged. Even the sentence, which has been awarded, same is shockingly disproportionate to the charge which had been levelled i.e. non-stopping of bus at barrier. Injuries alleged to be received by Bhoodev Singh are attributable to his own conduct as Bus in question could have passed even putting barrier down." 4. The learned counsel appearing on behalf of Appellants urged that Respondent having been found guilty of a serious charge of misconduct by the Labour Court, the findings of fact arrived at by the Labour Court should not have been interfered with by the High Court.  5. Ms. Sharda Devi, the learned counsel appearing on behalf of Respondent, on the other hand, supported the judgment.  6. The Labour Court exercised its jurisdiction under Section 11-A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (for short, `the Act'). It was categorically held that the domestic inquiry was not fair or valid and Respondent in the domestic inquiry had not been granted adequate opportunity to defend his case. Appellant was, therefore, granted opportunity to adduce evidence afresh. The opinion of the Labour Court in the matter has, therefore, to be judged on the basis of the evidence adduced before it. The Labour Court did not analyze the evidence adduced by the parties at all. It adopted a wrong approach. It did not consider as to whether `Bhoodev' who was examined on behalf of the Corporation, being its employee could have operated the said barrier particularly when his job was only to serve water to its employees. The barrier, according to him, had not been put up by the Corporation. He was not on duty to operate the said barrier. As noticed hereinbefore, the public allegedly installed the said barrier for which no authority existed.  7. The fact as to why the said barrier was put up and whether the same was within the knowledge of all the drivers of the Corporation had not been disclosed. Even according to the said witness, no First Information Report was lodged. He did not receive any serious injury. The statement of `Bhoodev' before the disciplinary authority was marked as an exhibit. In his statement before the domestic inquiry he stated :  "Q. When you had closed the barrier, how far was the bus standing ? A. As soon as the bus came, I had pulled down the barrier but as soon as the driver of the bus lowered down speed of the bus and asked to raise the barrier, I tried to open the barrier, but even then it was hit by the corners of the portion of the bus above the glass. Q. When you raise the barrier, how far were you dragged along with rope behind the bus ? A. I was dragged for about the distance of five hands."  8. The charge levelled against Respondent was noticed by the Labour Court in the following terms :  "...On 18.12.1986 information has been received against the Driver that on 07.12.1986 when he was driving bus No. UTR 4007 on Aligarh-Agra route, he intentionally broken the barrier installed near Sasani bus stand. He had negligently driven the bus towards Agra due to which an employee Bhoodev received injuries in the accident. On this basis a charge-sheet was issued to concerned workman on 20.01.1987 and domestic enquiry got made in accordance with law..." 9. The offence to cause any intentional injury, thus, cannot be said to have been proved. The High Court was, therefore, not wholly incorrect in opining that there was no evidence to prove the charges levelled against him.  10. In fact, the Presiding Officer, Labour Court, did not assign any reason as to how the charges could be said to have been proved. He had not taken into consideration his power under Section 11-A of the Act in regard to quantum of punishment. Why he had opined that the workman was guilty of serious misconduct and had no right to remain in service has not been explained.  11. The matter in ordinary course should have been remitted to the Labour Court for passing an appropriate award, but keeping in view the fact that the matter is pending for a long time, we ourselves considered the evidence on records.  12. We, therefore, are of the opinion that the impugned judgment cannot be faulted in its entirety. The High Court has granted reinstatement of Respondent with only 50% back wages. The said order has been stayed by this Court. Respondent was out of service for a long time. He, as noticed hereinbefore, even during the pendency of the domestic inquiry had been kept under suspension. He, however, was driving rashly and negligently.  13. In a case of this nature, doctrine of proportionality would also be applicable. Doctrine of irrationality is now giving way to doctrine of proportionality. [See Commissioner of Police and Others v. Syed Hussain, 2006(2) SCT 219 (SC) : (2006)3 SCC 173]. The Labour Court also did not consider this aspect of the matter. If only a charge of negligence had been proved against him, we are of the opinion that the interest of justice would be subserved if he is directed to be reinstated in service with 25% back wages.  The appeal is disposed of with the aforementioned directions. No costs.  Appeal disposed of.
summary: Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, Section 11A - Workman - Disciplinary proceedings - Termination of service - The Labour Court's findings of fact cannot be reversed by the High Court - High Court found serious flaws in the charge of intentional injury - No FIR lodged, barrier not put up by corporation, and no medical examination conducted - The Labour Court did not assign a reason as to how the charges are proved nor did he take into consideration his power under Section 11A - The doctrine of proportionality applies in a case of this nature - Reinstatement of workman with 25% backwages is in the interest of justice instead of 50% as granted by High Court.  [Paras 6, 7, 9, 10, 12, and 13]

text: Jawahar Lal Gupta, J. - Dr. Hardeep Kaur, the respondent, who belongs to the category of Scheduled Castes, was a candidate for admission to the M.D. Course in Obstretics ad Gynaecology. She was not admitted. Aggrieved by this action, she approached this Court through Civil Writ Petition No. 12525 of 1992. The learned Single Judge following the decision in an earlier case, viz., C.W.P. No. 11052 of 1992 (Avtar Singh v. The State of Punjab, 1993(2) S.C.T. 628) decided on December 11, 1992, allowed the writ petition. Aggrieved by the decisions in both the cases, the State of Punjab has come up in these two Letters Patent Appeals Nos. 462 and 359 of 1993. Learned counsel for the parties are agreed that these can be disposed of by one order. The facts as appearing in L.P.A. No. 462 of 1993 may be briefly noticed.  2. On January 24, 1992, the State Government issued a notification ordering that selection of students for admission to 'Three Years Post Graduate Degree Course' at the Government Medical Colleges, Patiala and Amritsar shall be made by holding an entrance test. It was further provided that 25% of the total seats will be filled on All India basis through competitive Entrance Test. Of the remaining seats, 60 per cent will be filled from amongst the eligible P.C.M.S. in service Doctors while 40 per cent will be filled from fresh graduates who are not in service through Post-Graduate Entrance Test." The conditions of eligibility were prescribed. It was further provided that 25% seats in each course shall be filled up from amongst the members of Scheduled Castes/Scheduled Tribes. The respondent, who was eligible, claims that she appeared in the entrance test and was placed at No. 11 in the merit list of the persons belonging to the reserved categories. On her qualifying the examination, she was eligible to be admitted to the Post-Graduate, Course in Obstretics and Gynaecology. Having not been admitted, she approached this Court. The appellants controverted the claim made by the candidate.  3. The learned Single Judge after consideration of the matter found that "out of total twelve number of seats in this speciality, roster points, 1, 5 and 9 had to be reserved for Scheduled Castes/Scheduled Tribes category, and one of these three seats had to go to the fresh graduates while the other two in service candidates as per relevant instructions of the State Government. Dr. Navdeep Singh and Dr. Beant Singh only in service category and belonging to scheduled castes have been given admission but strangely enough roster `9' meant for fresh graduates from this reserved category has not been filled up." It was further observed that the department had not "alleged in the return that any candidate higher in merit to the Petitioner in this reserved category had applied for admission on this speciality." In view of this position, the writ petition was allowed.  4. Challenging the judgment, the only contention raised by Mr. Ashok Aggarwal, learned counsel for the Appellants, is that in accordance with the prescribed procedure, 60% of the total seats had to be filled up from amongst the members of the Punjab from amongst the members of Scheduled Castes, who were already in the employment of the State Government. According to the counsel, this was substantial compliance with the instructions of the department and no relief could have been granted to the respondent. This claim was controverted by Mr. G.S. Sandhu, the learned counsel for the respondent.  5. It was admitted position that there were a total of 12 seats which had to be filled up by the State Government. It is also admitted that 25% seats were reserved for members of Scheduled Castes. It is, thus, clear that three seats, had to be filled up from amongst the members of the Scheduled Castes. Factually, only two have been given. There was thus one more seat falling to the share of the members of the Scheduled Castes which was wrongly not given to them. Resultantly, in the circumstances of this case, the seat ought to have been given to the present respondent.  6. Mr. Aggarwal, however, contended that the 12 seats had to be divided amongst the in service candidates and the fresh graduates in the ratio of 60:40. He is undoubtedly right. However, this also makes no difference to the position regarding the reservation. On this basis, 8 seats will have to be filled up from amongst the members of the Punjab Civil Medical Service and four from amongst the fresh graduates. Even if the provision regarding reservation is applied to these categories separately, two out of eight falling to the share of in-service candidates and one out of four seats which had to be filled from amongst the fresh graduates had to be given to the members of Scheduled Castes. While two seats out of eight filled up from amongst the in-service candidates were given to the members of Scheduled Castes, none was given out of the four filled up from amongst the fresh graduates. Thus, viewed from any angle, the result is that one seat which should have been filled up from amongst the members of Scheduled Castes was not given to the eligible category.  7. Similar is the position in the case of Avtar Singh. It is the admitted position that there were a total of 11 seats in the speciality of Orthopaedics and only two were filled up from amongst the members of Scheduled Castes. One more seat which fell to their share at roster point No. 9 was not given to them.  8. Accordingly, we find no merit in these appeals which are dismissed. It is directed that the appellants shall admit the two candidates to their respective courses forthwith. In fact, Mr. P.S. Patwalia, learned counsel for Mr. Avtar Singh has pointed out that after the judgment of the learned Single Judge, the Principal, Medical College, Amritsar had vide order dated March 2, 1993 granted admission to him, which was, however, cancelled on June 18, 1993, in view of the interim order passed by a Bench of this Court. Since we have dismissed both the appeals, the interim order shall stand vacated. As a result, the order admitting Dr. Avtar Singh shall stand restored. The appellants shall also admit the other candidate Dr. Hardeep Kaur immediately. In the circumstances, the parties are left to bear their own costs.
summary: Petitioner, Ashok Aggarwal, and Respondent, Mr. G.S. Sandhu, Advocate, were present. The case discussed two issues. Firstly, a Scheduled Caste candidate was not admitted to the M.D. course even though there were 25% reserved seats for members of the Scheduled Castes and only two out of three seats were filled by them. The Single Judge was right in ruling that the remaining seat should have been given to the respondent and he must be admitted for the M.D. course as directed. Secondly, in the specialty of Orthopaedics, only two out of eleven seats were filled by members of Scheduled Castes and they were due an additional seat at roster point no. 9, which was not given to them. The order admitting another candidate in an earlier case was restored. [Paras 5-8]

text: A.L. Bahri, J. - This second appeal has been filed by Bhagat Singh, plaintiff against the judgment and decree of Additional District, Judge, Chandigarh dated August 12, 1985, whereby the appeal filed by him was dismissed and judgment and decree of the trial Court was affirmed. The trial Court had dismissed the suit filed by him for declaration and for the grant of permanent injunction, on August 29, 1983. The appeal was transferred to the Central Administrative Tribunal in view of the provisions of the Administrative Tribunal Act. Subsequently, the Tribunal returned the same inter alia holding that Tribunal had no jurisdiction to entertain the appeal. In the meantime, Regular First Appeal No. 469 of 1986 had been admitted to D.B. and this appeal was ordered to be heard along with the aforesaid first appeal. That is how the appeal is before this Bench.  2. Bhagat Singh, plaintiff, joined the Ordnance Cable Factory at Chandigarh as a Driver in the factory. In the service-book prepared, his date of birth was recorded as 14.8.1923. Subsequently, when he came to know that his actual date of birth was 10.1.1929 he moved General Manager of the factory for correction of his date of birth. Vide order dated 16.7.1981, the said request was turned down by the General Manager. Bhagat Singh has studied upto 7th Class in a School in his village, Shah, District Fatehpur (U.P.) in the year 1944. Thereafter he started helping his father who was running a tailor shop. When he joined service in the factory, no effort was made to obtain School Leaving Certificate to give the correct date of birth. Subsequently, when such a certificate was obtained, the defendant was moved for correction. No opportunity was given to the plaintiff before his request was turned down. If his correct date of birth had been recorded, he would have served in the factory for a period of six more years. Thus, he claimed declaration that order dated 16.7.1981 was illegal, arbitrary and against the principles of natural justice. He also sought decree for permanent injunction that he should not be retired before the due date of his superannuation and the defendant be directed to correct his date of birth.  3. The suit was contested by the defendant Union and another inter alia allege that correct date of birth of the plaintiff was recorded on his own statement in the service-book as 14.8.1923. There was no reason to change it to January 10, 1929. The suit was alleged to be barred by time. The plaintiff was estopped from filing the suit.  The following issues were framed in the suit.  1) Whether the suit is within limitation ? OPP 2) Whether the plaintiff is estopped by his acts and conduct to file the present suit ? OPP 3) Whether the impugned order dated 16.7.1981 is illegal, arbitrary ? OPP 4) Whether the plaintiff is entitled to the declaration prayed for ? OPP The trial Court held under issue No. 1 that the suit was within time. Under issue Nos. 2 to 4, the correct date of birth of the plaintiff was heard to be as recorded in the service-book i.e. 14.8.1923 and the plaintiff was estopped from filing the suit. He was not entitled to the declaration prayed for. The order dated 16.7.1981 was held to be valid. This judgment of the trial Court was affirmed by the lower Appellate Court.  4. Chapter V of the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1985 deals with the question of jurisdiction of the Tribunal and other Courts to entertain or dispose of cases relating to the employees either by the ordinary Courts or by the Tribunal constituted therein. Section 29 provides for transfer of suits or other provisions before any court or authority pending immediately before the date of establishment of the Tribunal under the Act, to such Tribunal for disposal. However, this provision is not applicable to any appeal pending before the High Court. Section 29-A was inserted by Act No. 19 of 1986 with effect from 22.1.1986.
