It appears that by an order dated 18.6.1992, a learned single Judge of this Court permitted the petitioner to join the said school, inter alia, on the ground that after dismissal the petitioner has to seek some employment for survival of himself and his family. The learned Judge, therefore, granted leave to the petitioner to join the said Dumdum Sree Arbinda Vidyamandir without prejudice to his rights and contentions in that matter. It was, however, made clear that Barasat Satyabharati Vidyamandir shall also be not adversely affected in any way by his joining Dumdum Sree Arabinda Vidyamandir on the strength of the said order. Pursuant thereto, the petitioner joined the latter school on 26.6.1992. The petitioner was drawing a scale of pay of Rs. 3,600/- as basic pay and other allowances as per revised scale of pay. The petitioner claimed his additional increment, but the Secretary of the school informed the District Inspector of Schools that he is entitled to the revised scale of pay. Moreover, by an order dated 31.10.1994, the scale of pay of the petitioner was reduced.  4. The pay scale of the petitioner was again revised. However, in the meantime, the petitioner attained his age of superannuation on 30.11.1996. Curiously enough, the Managing Committee informed the petitioner that they had taken a resolution terminating his service with effect from 23.11.1996 and allegedly the Board had approved the proposal by its letter dated 5.5.1997. Questioning the aforementioned order reducing his scale of pay, the petitioner filed C.O. No. 7-83(W) of 1995. Despite direction, no affidavit in opposition has been filed in any of these matters. The petitioner has also filed an application for bringing on record subsequent events, namely, the order of dismissal passed against him by the Managing Committee dated 19.5.1997. In his aforementioned application bringing on record subsequent events the petitioner raised various contentions that the matter being sub judice, neither any order of suspension or dismissal could have been passed. The said order dated 19.5.1997 as contained in Annexure `Y' to the application for bringing on record subsequent events reads thus :  "This is to inform you that the Managing Committee of the School by resolution dated 17.5.1997 resolved to terminate your services with effect from 23.11.1996 on various grounds as intimated to you in the charge sheet and show cause served. Subsequently the West Bengal Board of Secondary Education by a letter No. 24/22721/G dated 5.5.1997 informed us of the approval of the Managing Committee's proposal taken in the meeting No. 12/96 dated 23.11.1996 to terminate your services from school A xerox copy of such letter is enclosed herewith. In view of the above you are hereby informed that your service in the post of Headmaster stands terminated from 23.11.1996." 5. A bare perusal of the said order would show that the same is ex facie illegal, as the Managing Committee could not have passed a resolution on 17.5.1997 for terminating the service with effect from 23.11.1996. Assuming that the petitioner has committed misconduct and, therefore, a disciplinary proceeding had been initiated against him, from the said letter dated 19.5.1997 it appears that the services of the petitioner had been terminated with retrospective effect from 23.11.1996. An order of termination of service, as is well known, takes effect from the date of communication of the said order. Reference in this connection may be made to a decision reported in AIR 1966 SC 1313 in the view of the matter, service of the petitioner could not have been terminated even by Dumdum Sree Arabinda Vidyamandir with retrospective effect from 23.11.1996. Even, nothing has been shown that requirement of Rule 28(8) of 1969 Rules as has been explained by a Division Bench of this court in Sujit Das v. West Bengal Board of Secondary Education reported in 1997(2) CLJ 497, had been followed. Although, this appears to be a peculiar case, as the petitioner despite an order of removal was allowed to join another school by leave of this court, and no attempt had been made by the authorities of the school or the State to clarify the position, this court has no other option but to hold in view of the decision of this court, in Sujit Das (supra) that the order of removal dated 4.12.1991 as contained in annexure `G' to the writ application, being C.O. No. 18800(W) of 1992 is illegal. For the self-same reason also on the ground that the petitioner's services could not have been terminated after he had superannuated from his service, the order of termination dated 19.5.1997 cannot also be sustained. The question, therefore, which remains is what relief should be granted to the petitioner. The petitioner had filed several applications. This court, without any material on record, is not in a position to arrive at a conclusion, as has been submitted by Ms. Nandini Mitra, learned counsel appearing for Dumdum Sree Arabinda Vidyamandir, that the petitioner obtained his service by suppression of fact. It is really a matter of regret that if the petitioner was appointed by committing fraud, the same should have been brought to the notice of this court, as the petitioner had joined the school with the leave of this court in terms of this court's order dated 18.6.1992. However, there cannot be any doubt that on the principle of no work no pay, the petitioner would not be entitled to salary for the period he had not worked. In the peculiar facts and circumstances of this case, it is directed that the petitioner shall not be paid his full salary during the period for which he was under suspension, but there cannot be any doubt that for the period he has actually worked he will be entitled to salary in terms of the scale of pay to which he is entitled to. From the impugned order as contained in annexure `B' to the writ application, it does not appear that any reason has been assigned for non-payment of the petitioner's remuneration on any justifiable ground. The said order has been passed only because he has failed to produce his last pay certificate. From annexure `P' itself, it appears that as far back on 31.10.1991, the District Inspector of Schools was aware that the petitioner had been removed from service, and the matter is pending in this court and thus, it was obligatory on his part in the aforementioned situation, to take steps to move this court for variation and/or vacation of the order and/or bring to the notice of this court the circumstances under which the order of approval had been wrongly given in favour of the petitioner. The said authority having granted approval of the appointment cannot be heard to say that the petitioner would be entitled to a salary of Rs. 2440/- only and not the salary to which he is entitled to under law. The petitioner may be paid his arrears to which he would have been entitled to had he continued in his former school, namely Satyabharati Vidyapith upon deduction of the salary which he had received from Dumdum Sree Aarbinda Vidyamandir. No order of dismissal could have been passed after the petitioner reached his age of superannuation without extending his service or in the absence of any rule to the contrary. No order for extending his service for continuing the departmental proceeding has been produced before this court, nor any extant rule has been shown. In the opinion of this court, the aforementioned order shall meet ends of justice as the petitioner had worked in the latter school with knowledge of his order of removal passed against him. Furthermore, as the order of removal passed by the former school as contained in annexure `J' in C.O. No. 18800(W) of 1992 is set aside, he will be deemed to be continuing in service in that school, but as the petitioner cannot get double benefit, all the salary he has drawn from Dumdum Sree Arabinda Vidyamandir be deducted from his arrear salary. The respondents shall, however, be at liberty to initiate any appropriate proceedings against him if permissible under the law. The Director of School Education shall be entitled to take such action against the erring officer as he may deem fit and proper.  6. These two writ applications are disposed of with the aforementioned directions.  7. Xerox certified copy be supplied on priority basis.  Petition allowed.
summary: Constitution of India, Articles 226 and 311 - Termination of services - Effective date - Petitioner was terminated from service with retrospective effect while working as Headmaster and while in suspension - Order of termination takes effect from the date of communication of order - Petitioner's service also could not be terminated after he had superannuated - Relief - Salary cannot be claimed for period during which no work was done - He will be treated as still in service. [Para 5]

text: Swatanter Kumar, J. - Ex-Constable Ravinder Singh was discharged from the service of Punjab Police under Rule 12.21 of the Punjab Police Rules (hereinafter referred to as `the Rules') vide order dated 7.11.1992. Against this order of discharge, he preferred an appeal by way of representation before the Inspector General of Police, Border Range, Amritsar, who vide his order Annexure P-2 to the writ petition, dismissed the appeal by giving detailed reasons. Aggrieved from the said order, the petitioner approached this Court praying for quashing of these two orders and his reinstatement into service with all consequential benefits.  2. The facts relevant for determination of the controversy raised before us are that petitioner joined as a Constable in the Punjab Police on 30th November, 1989. He states that he fell sick and remained ill and admitted to Primary Health Centre, Verka, from 9.9.1992 to 23.9.1992. He, thus, was absent for 13 days 4 hours and 25 minutes. This resulted in the passing of order of discharge as afore-referred.  3. Challenge to the notice of discharge by the petitioner, inter alia, is on the following grounds :  (i) the impugned order is not an order of discharge simplicitor within the scope of Rule 12.21 but is punitive in its content; (b) the impugned order of discharge has been passed in violation to the provisions of Rule 19.5 of the said Rules and, as such, is vitiated; and lastly, the order of discharge is arbitrary.  4. Upon notice, the respondent-State filed the detailed reply wherein it was stated that the writ petition is not maintainable. Under Rule 12.21 a Constable can be discharged within a period of three years of his enrolment as member of the Punjab Police.  5. According to the averments made in the written statement, he has been absenting himself continuously in an unauthorised manner and as such passing of the order of discharge was imperative and was in the interest of the organisation.  6. In the order dated 7.11.1992 the Senior Superintendent of Police, Majitha has referred that the petitioner had been absent earlier on different occasions and even orders were passed with the direction that no salary be paid to him and, resultantly, discharged him from service. It is a settled principle of law that the order of discharge simplicitor does not postulate responsibility on the part of the respondents to hold a departmental enquiry and to strictly adhere to the principles of nature justice. The said rule undoubtedly vests a power in the competent authority to discharge a police constable within the prescribed period on the ground that he is unlikely to prove an efficient police officer. The conclusion of the authority obviously must be based upon some facts and record. It cannot be an order without any basis. An order simplicitor certainly does not mean an order passed without reference to any record and material before the concerned authorities. If it would be so, it ex facie would be an arbitrary order. Reference to more facts which are even undisputed would not vitiate the order for non-compliance of the provisions.  7. In support of the impugned order the respondents in their written statement while replying to paragraph 5 of the writ petition, have stated as under :  "That the contents of para No. 5 of the petition are denied. The ruling mentioned in this para is not applicable. The petitioner remained absent from duty during short period of service as mentioned below. From To Total days 20.6.90 2.8.90, 44 days, leave without pay 11.8.90 16.8.90, 06 days, leave without pay 19.11.90 22.11.90, 03 days, leave without pay 11.12.90 18.12.90, 07 days, leave without pay 8.10.91 14.10.91, 07 days, leave without pay 9.9.92 23.9.92, 14 days leave without pay In view of above record it cannot be said that the petitioner worked diligently and honestly. His service was less than 3 years when the impugned order dated 7.11.92 was passed by the competent authority. From this, it is proved that the petitioner was not taking interest in his service and duty and is not likely to become an efficient police officer. The order dated 7.11.92 is legal, valid, operative and according to rules." 8. No rejoinder to the counter was filed before us and, in fact, even during the course of arguments it was not disputed that averments made in the written statement are not correct. Another feature of his case which we must notice is that though no appeal is permissible under Rule 12.21, still the Inspector General of Police, Amritsar entertained the representation of the petitioner Annexure P-4 to the writ petition and passed an order Annexure P-2 rejecting the appeal. Even in the memorandum of appeal it has not been disputed that he was unauthorisedly absent earlier and that he was not paid salary and appropriate order had been passed even on earlier occasion. All that was stated in the appeal was that he was ill from 9.9.1992 to 23.9.1992 suffering from typhoid and as such he could not have attended to his duties. In the order, the Inspector General of Police has specifically noticed that no medical treatment or appropriate medical record/certificate was produced from the Medical officer in support of his contention. From the facts afore- noticed, it is clear that the petitioner was absent repeatedly from service that too without sanction of the competent authority. In view of the undisputed facts, reliance by the learned counsel for the petitioner upon the judgment of the Supreme Court in the case of State of Haryana v. Jagdish Chander, 1995(2) SCT 42 (SC) : JT 1995(2) SC 108 is not of much help to the petitioner.  9. Coming to the second argument raised on behalf of the petitioner that the respondents have not complied with the provisions of Rule 19.5 and as such the order is vitiated, again is a contention without any merit. Provisions of Rule 19.5 are regulatory in nature and require the supervising authority to keep an effective control and report on the conduct of the trainee constables at intervals of six months and send it to the higher authorities. The provision is primarily meant for internal management and supervisory control of the superior police officials over the trainee constables. In the present case, the records of the petitioner speak volumes about his conduct as a trainee constable. The concerned authorities were satisfied that the petitioner would not prove to be a good police officer and thus, discharged him. This opinion of the concerned authorities, cannot be stated to be without any basis or foundation, much less that it could be called an arbitrary order.  10. For the reasons afore-stated, we find no merit in this petition and the same is dismissed, however, leaving the parties to bear their own costs.  Petition dismissed.
summary:
A. Punjab Police Rules, 1934, Rule 12.21 - Discharge from service - Petitioner was absent from duty on multiple occasions and was found to be a habitual absentee. The authorities stopped his pay in earlier occasions and dismissed his appeal when he provided no proof for medical treatment. He was discharged from service considering that he would not prove to be a good police officer. The order of discharge was not illegally passed. [Paras 6, 7 & 8]

B. Constitution of India, Articles 14 & 16 - Punjab Police Rules, 1934, Rule 19.5 - Natural justice - The authority can discharge a police constable within the specified period if they believe that the constable would not prove to be an efficient police officer. The record of the petitioner's inefficiency and conduct indicated that he would not be effective as a police officer. The authorities were not satisfied with his conduct and found that the discharge was justified as he was unlikely to prove to be a good police officer. The order of discharge did not require an enquiry or strict adherence to the principles of natural justice. [Paras 6, 7 & 9]

text: S.K. Jain, J. - The facts :  The petitioner was appointed as a Clerk in the office of District Red Cross Society, Hissar in the year 1959. Under orders of the President, he was promoted to the post of Accountant and again to the post of Assistant Secretary. After the formation of new District Sirsa (carved out of old district Hissar), District Red Cross Society, Sirsa came into being. The petitioner was transferred as Assistant Secretary to that society in the month of September, 1979. With effect from 16.4.1986 he was promoted to the post of Secretary. He remained on probation till 15.4.1987.  2. On the grounds that he was initially appointed as a clerk in the office of District Red Cross Society, Hissar; that he was promoted from time to time in that office; that he was transferred by order of the President, Red Cross Society, Hissar and that he retained his lien on the said post there, the petitioner instituted Civil Suit No. 792-C of 1981 on 6.1.1981 Radha Kishan Rajpal Vs. (i) District Red Cross Society, Sirsa (ii) District Red Cross Society, Hissar, and (iii) Indian Red Cross Society, Haryana State Branch, Chandigarh, for a decree of declaration to the effect that he was entitled to service in the District Red Cross Society, Hissar, where he had retained his lien as Accountant and the order dated 4.2.1986 passed by the President, District Red Cross Society, Hissar, was erroneous, illegal and was liable to be set aside.  3. That suit was decreed for declaration to the effect that the plaintiff was entitled to serve with the defendant No. 2 District Red Cross Society, Hissar, as Accountant till he was confirmed as Assistant Secretary with District Red Cross Society, Sirsa, by Sub-Judge, 2nd Class, Sirsa, vide his judgment and decree dated 11.3.1983.  4. That judgment and decree was challenged by one Kanwaljit Singh, Accountant, District Red Cross Society, Hissar on the ground that the said judgment and decree would adversely affect him. Neither District Red Cross Society, Hissar, nor District Red Cross Society, Sirsa had challenged the said judgment and decree.  5. Civil Appeal No. 51 instituted on 18.4.1983 was dismissed by Shri C.R. Goel, Additional District Judge, Sirsa vide his judgment and decree dated 3.10.1985. Kanwaljit Singh, Accountant, District Red Cross Society, Hissar, brought RSA No. 3092 of 1985 against the said judgment and decree of the lower appellate Court. It was dismissed as withdrawn vide order dated 23.8.1993 of this Court.  6. The case of the petitioner is that on account of differences between him and Shri B. B. Kaushil, City Magistrate, he was falsely implicated in a case for misappropriation etc. Charge sheet dated 18.12.1987 was served on the petitioner which was replied to by him whereafter no further steps were taken in the matter nor the said charge-sheet was withdrawn. However, a fresh charge sheet containing some of the previous charges and new charges was served on the petitioner on 10.2.1988. He was not allowed to inspect relevant documents for submitting effective reply to the charges. He, however, denied the charges vide his reply dated 2.3.1988. An enquiry Officer who was a friend of Mr. B.B. Kaushik was appointed to hold a departmental enquiry. Two applications of the petitioner for transferring the enquiry to some other Officer were declined. Enquiry was completed and report submitted to the disciplinary authority thereby holding the petitioner guilty for some of the charges which were in the nature of the irregularities. The President, District Red Cross Society, Sirsa forwarded the said enquiry report along with the show cause notice to the petitioner asking him as to why his services should not be terminated. The petitioner submitted reply which did not find favour with the Enquiry Officer. For a period of 10 months' no action was taken but suddenly on 17.10.1979 the petitioner was dismissed from service of the society. His representation to the Govenoror-cum-President, Indian Red Cross Society, Haryana State Branch, Chandigarh was still pending. Vide this writ petition, the petitioner has challenged order dated 17.10.1989 Annexure P-6 vide which he was dismissed from service by respondent No. 2 'inter-alia' on the following grounds that :-  (i) since the petitioner had a lien on the post of Assistant in the office of District Red Cross Society, Hissar as held by Civil Court, respondent No. 2 was neither his appointing nor punishing authority and, therefore, the impugned order was without jurisdiction;  (ii) no action on the first charge-sheet was taken nor the same was withdrawn, therefore, the issuance of the second-charge sheet was illegal;  (iii) the petitioner having not been allowed to inspect all the relevant documents, he would not submit effective reply to the charge sheet and, therefore, had been gravely prejudiced. The enquiry, therefore, stood vitiated;  (iv) that since no Presenting Officer had been appointed, the Enquiry Officer himself was acting as such which prejudiced the case of the petitioner;  (v) the evidence led by the petitioner in defence had not been taken into consideration by respondent No. 2 while passing the impugned order;  (vi) that the impugned order was a non-speaking order inasmuch as the evidence produced in defence had not been discussed nor the reasons as to why the same was discarded have been assigned; and  (vii) that the impugned order was passed in flagrant disregard of the provisions of clause 20(ii) of the Model Draft Constitution because the petitioner who was the Secretary of the District branch could not be dismissed from service by the President without obtained concurrence of the State branch.  7. Written statement was filed on behalf of respondent No. 2. The case is that the matter regarding lien had not been finally decided so far. Charge- sheet dated 10.2.1988 was issued by the then President, Red Cross Society and Mr. Kaushik, the City Magistrate had nothing to do with the charge-sheet. The request of the petitioner was never turned down. It was the petitioner who failed to turn up to inspect the relevant record. The Enquiry Officer was an impartial person. The petitioner had been afforded full opportunity at all stages to defend himself. The Enquiry Report was perfectly valid and legal and the show cause notice was issued to the petitioner on the basis of said report. Reply of the petitioner to the show cause notice was considered and then it was proposed to impose the punishment of removal from service upon him. Vide resolution No. 5 passed by the Executive Committee in its meeting held on 16.11.1988, the Punjab Civil Services (Punishment & Appeal) Rules were made fully applicable to the employees of the District Red Cross Society, Sirsa. The President was competent to appoint an employee. He was also competent to terminate his services, but it has to be in accordance with Model Draft Constitution of the Society. All the allegations levelled by the petitioner were denied.  8. Learned counsel for the appellant has argued that while transferring the petitioner from District Red Cross Society, Hissar to District Red Cross, Society, Sirsa, his consent was not taken. The petitioner, therefore, had lien on his substantive post at Hissar. A decree to that effect had been passed by the Civil Court and was affirmed by the lower appellant Court. Red Cross Society did not file any regular second appeal. The RSA filed by Kamaljit Singh bearing No. 3092 of 1985 was dismissed as withdrawn on 23.9.1993. Therefore, it stands finally decided that the petitioner had a lien on his substantive post with District Red Cross Society, Hissar. Besides this, the District Red Cross Society, Sirsa vide its letters dated 27.9.1977, 3.1.1978, 14.7.1980 and 16.9.1980 had admitted that the petitioner had no lien at Sirsa.  9. Relying on the various judgments, he was submitted that an employee had a lien on such a post upon which he is confirmed even after his allocation to other District/State and that such a lien cannot be suspended or terminated without passing a specific orders to that effect and that too if he is confirmed on the post of his new assignment. He has further argued that lien on the post cannot be terminated even with the consent of the employee concerned if the result of such termination is to leave him without a lien or a suspended lien upon a permanent post and the lien is not automatically suspended on appointment in substantive capacity to a permanent post out side the cadre and the competent authority was bound to pass order for suspending his lien. The aggrieved employee could not be made to suffer because of the inaction or ommission of the competent authority. In the absence of written request by an employee, lien on the post permanently held by him cannot be terminated.  Learned counsel for the respondents has argued supporting the impugned order.  10. I have carefully considered the above arguments.  In Civil Suit No. 792-C of 1981, "Radha Kishan Rajpal v. District Red Cross Society, Sirsa and two others" it was held under issue No. 1 as under :-  "The lien of the plaintiff having not been proved to be terminated at any stage, much less on 6.10.1975, I am of the view that the plaintiff is entitled to serve with the defendant No. 2 - Society as Accountant and he retains his lien with that society till he is confirmed by the defendant No.1 - Society.  This finding of the Subordinate Court was affirmed by the lower appellate Court in the following terms :-  "Furthermore, as discussed above, the defendants themselves have admitted that the plaintiff-respondent had a lien on the said permanent post of accountant, at Hissar, but on his transfer to Sirsa, the same was terminated, whereas it is not so. For that reason also, now it does not lie in their mouth to defeat the claim of the plaintiff-respondent on the assertion that he has no lien on the said permanent post of accountant at Hissar. Consequently, findings recorded by the learned trial Court, on issue No. 1, are hereby affirmed, as there is no ground to reverse the same."  The above facts have been taken from the file of Regular Second Appeal No. 3092 of 1985 which was being heard along with this writ petition.  11. Regular Second Appeal against the judgment and decree dated 3.10.1985 of the lower appellate Court having been dismissed as withdrawn, the above findings became final between the parties and, therefore, there is no escape from the conclusion that the petitioner herein, had his lien with the District Red Cross Society, Hissar against the permanent post of Accountant. In Dharam Pal v. State of Haryana and others, 1991(3) S.L.R. 648 : 1993(1) SCT 361 (P&H), a Single Bench of this court has held that when an employee of District Level Service is transferred in public interest, his seniority will be kept in parent District and he will be considered for next higher promotion in his parent District.  12. In Ramnarayan Chand v. State of Rajasthan and Collector Jaisalmer, 1981(1) SLR 85, it has been held by a Division Bench of Rajasthan High Court that lien on a post cannot be terminated even with the consent of the official concerned if the result of such termination is to leave him without a lien or a suspended lien upon a permanent post.  13. In view of the above discussion, I find that the petitioner retained his lien against the permanent post of Assistant in the District Red Cross Society, Hissar.  14. Now the next question to be answered is as to whether the President, District Red Cross Society, Sirsa had an authority to suspend, charge-sheet, hold an enquiry into charges and terminate the services of the petitioner.  15. Learned counsel for the petitioner has submitted that the subordinate judge in his judgment dated 11.3.1983 had held as under :-  "...... It is proved on the file that no rules have been adopted by the defendant/society so as to govern the services of its employees under Civil Services Rules but the rules of natural justice are to be followed by every organisation. In view of the statement of the plaintiff, it is proved on the file that he is still unconfirmed Assistant Secretary and in case his services are terminated, then he would be rolling on the road.....".  In para No. 10 of his judgment, the lower appellate Court has discussed this point as under :-  "In this regard it is further note-worthy that defendant No. 1 has admitted that the services of the plaintiff-respondent were governed the service rules of local bodies, as Red Cross Society is a corporate (Statutory) body, established under the Act. In such circumstances, even if the concerned civil service rules are not applicable to its employees, at least the basic principles of the same are very much applicable to them as even held right by the learned court below."  Then the learned counsel for the petitioner has drawn my attention towards the provisions of Clause 20 of the Model Draft Constitution under which the appointment of the Secretary at the District Branch of the Red Cross Society is made by the President with the approval of the State Branch. Such an appointment could not be annulled except with the previous concurrence of the State Branch.  16. In para No. 14 of the writ petition a specific ground to this effect has been taken. Corresponding para of the written statement filed on behalf of the respondent No.2 reads as under :-  "14. In reply to para 14, it is submitted that the petitioner was placed under suspension vide orders No. 20 dated 2.1.1988. A copy of the order of suspension was also sent to the Secretary Indian Red Cross Society, Haryana State Branch, Chandigarh presently respondent No. 1. The same duly translated in English is appended as Annexure R-2/1. A true copy in Hindi is also enclosed. Thereafter the respondent No. 2 received the letter dated 15.1.1988 from the office of the respondent No. 1 requesting therein to send a copy of the charge sheet served on the petitioner for their information. A true copy of the same is reproduced/appended as Annexure R-2/2. In response to this, the respondent No. 2 vide letter dated 10.2.1988 forwarded the charge sheet to respondent No. 1. A true copy of this letter is appended as Annexure R-2/3 duly translated in English. A copy of letter is also enclosed."  17. Before proceeding further, it is also necessary to note that in para Nos. 11 and 12 of the written statement, the answering respondent has taken following stands :-  "It is further submitted that the Punjab Civil Services (Punishment & Appeal) Rules are fully applicable to the employees of the District Red Cross Society, Sirsa. This decision was taken vide resolution No. 5 passed by the Executive Committee in its meeting held on 16.11.1988. The contents of the same are produced below :-  "it is decided that to all employees of all the branches of Red Cross, the Haryana Government's Service & Conduct Rules, 1966 will be applicable."  However, the President is competent to appoint and terminate the terms of employment of the employees working in the District Red Cross Society. But this has to be in accordance with the Model Draft Constitution of the Society. The contents of rest of para are denied. The departmental inquiry was conducted in accordance with the rules. The petitioner was given full opportunity to defend himself."  18. From the above, it is evident that the case of the respondents is two- fold. Firstly, their stand is that the President District Red Cross Society was competent to appoint and terminate the services of an employee of the society strictly in accordance with the Model Draft Constitution of the Society and Secondly, that vide resolution No. 5 dated 16.11.1988 the Punjab Civil Services (Punishment & Appeal) Rules, 1966 were made applicable to the employee of the society.  19. In order to find out as to whether the services of the petitioner had been terminated in accordance with clause 20(ii) of the Model Draft Constitution which is produced in para No. 14 of their written statement, it is evident that no concurrence of the State Branch had been taken. Therefore, inescapable conclusion is that the impugned order vide which the services of the petitioner had been terminated by the President, District Red Cross Society, Sirsa, without obtaining previous concurrence of the State Branch was without jurisdiction.  20. Learned counsel for the appellant has then argued that the departmental enquiry is quasi-judicial in nature and where the principles of natural justice have not been observed, it stands vitiated. Further eloborating his argument, he has submitted that no Presenting Officer was appointed by the Department. The Enquiry Officer has acted as a prosecutor as well as a Judge which could not be allowed to be done.  21. I find force in the argument of the learned counsel for the petitioner. In para No. 16(iv) of the writ petition this ground has been taken. In the corresponding para of the written statement it is stated as under :-  "(iii), (iv) & (v); In reply to these paras it is submitted that full opportunity was given to the petitioner to defend his case."  22. It is thus clear that no Presenting Officer was appointed and the Enquiry Officer had acted both as Prosecutor as well as the Judge. It cannot be allowed to be done. The principles of natural justice have been violated.  23. The next submission of the learned counsel for the petitioner is that since the petitioner was not allowed to inspect the relevant documents, he could not submit effective reply to the charge sheet and, therefore, the inquiry proceedings stood vitiated. This ground had been taken in para No. 16(iii) of the writ petition. In the corresponding para of the written statement it is submitted that full opportunity was given to the petitioner to defend his case. Thus it is evident that the plea of the petitioner that he was not allowed to inspect the documents has not been denied.  24. In Kashinath Dikshita v. Union of India and others, AIR 1986 Supreme Court 2118, it has been held by the Apex Court that where the Government refused to its employee who was dismissed, the copies of the statements of the witnesses examined at the stage of preliminary inquiry proceeding the commencement of the inquiry and copies of the documents said to have been relied upon by the disciplinary authority in order to establish the charge against the employees and even in this connection the reasonable request of the employee to have the relevant portions of the documents extracted with the help of his stenographer was refused and he was told to himself make such notes as he could, and the Government failed to show that no prejudice was occasioned to the employee on account of non-supply of copies of documents, the order of dismissal rendered by the disciplinary authority against the employee was violative of Article 311(2) inasmuch as the employee has been denied reasonable opportunity of defending himself. In para No. 16(3) of the writ petition, the petitioner has taken a specific plea in this regard but in the correspondent para of the written statement, it has not been denied on behalf of the respondents. As mentioned earlier, it has been contended on their part that full opportunity was given to the petitioner to defend his case. Otherwise also, the respondents have not shown that no prejudice was occasioned to the petitioner on account of denial of inspection of the relevant record. Therefore, the case in hand is fully covered by the ratio laid down in above mentioned Supreme Court case.  25. It is next submitted on behalf of the petitioner that the enquiry report was submitted by the Enquiry Officer more than five months after the submission of the written arguments. This inordinate delay was not explained by the Enquiry Officer. Further the impugned order was passed about 10 months after the reply to show cause notice was submitted. This delay also remained unexplained and, therefore, the whole of the proceedings including the impugned order stood vitiated.  26. This argument also has force. In Smt. Manjit Kaur v. State of Punjab and others, 1991(6) SLR 762, a Single Bench of this Court has held that where inordinate delay in finalising the proceedings has not been explained satisfactorily, disciplinary proceedings were liable to be quashed.  27. Now on to the arguments of the learned counsel for the respondents.  28. First submission of the learned counsel for the respondent is that the writ petition was not maintainable against the respondent-society. In reply, learned counsel for the petitioner, however, contended that the petitioner is not seeking to enforce his Fundamental Rights. He, on the other hand, complains that there has been infraction of the Punjab Civil Service Rules applicable to the petitioner and his services have been terminated in violation of the Rules of natural justice. He contends that for redress of this grievance of the petitioner, his writ petition is maintainable and the society is amendable to the writ jurisdiction of this Court. In support of this contention he has relied upon the following judgments :-  (i) Ajay Hasia etc. v. Khalid Majib Sehravardi, AIR 1981 S.C. 487 wherein it has been held as under :-  "It is immaterial for determining whether the corporation is an authority, whether the Corporation is created by a statute or under a statute. The test is whether it is an instrumentality or agency of the Government and not as to how it is created. The inquiry has to be not as to how the juristic person is born bue why it has been brought into existence. The Corporation may be a statutory corporation created by a statute or it may be a Government company or a company formed under the Companies Act or it may be a society registered under the Societies Registration Act or any other similar statute. Whatever be its general originality would be an 'authority' within the meaning of Article 12 if it is an instrumentality or agency of the Government and that would have to be decided on a proper assessment of the facts in the light of the relevant factors."  (ii) Sarmukh Singh v. Indian Red Cross Society, 1985 Lab. & Indl. Cases 1972, wherein it has been observed that the society was incorporated for humanitarian purpose only. The aim was to continue in peace time on a wider basis the work which was being done by the Indian Branch of the British Red Cross Society and the Joint War Committee of the order of St. John of Jerusalem. The predominant object is to give relief to the disabled, sick or wounded soldiers during the war time and also to provide relief from sickness, suffering or distress in India, whether due to the operation of war or otherwise.  29 (iii) Indian Red Cross Society v. R.N. Kaul, D. B. Special Appeal No. 65 of 1978 (Raj. High Court) followed in 1987 (1) PLR 69. In this judgment it has been held as under :-  "Keeping in view of the raio decidendi laid down in Ramana v. I.A. Authority of India (Supra), we have no hesitation in holding that the Rajasthan Branch of the Indian Red Cross Society is not an authority within the meaning of Article 12 of the Constitution of India. The Society has been created by a statute. If the statute is not there, the society cannot exist. The statute given an exclusive domain and monopoly to the Society to act in a particular sphere. The assets which fell to the share of Pakistan were transferred under Section 13 of the said Act. The share which fell to the share of Burma was allocated by the Red Cross Society (Allocation of Property) Act, 1936. As stated earlier, the Constitution provides that the Governor shall be the patron-in-Chief, Chief Minister would be the President, Health Minister would be the Chairman and Director of Medical and Health Services would be Vice-Chairman, Clause 44 of Annexure R-2/2 clearly states that the services of all the employees shall be governed by the rules which are in force for the employees of the State of Rajasthan. All these factors lead to the irresistible inference that though the Indian Red Cross Society is not an authority as envisaged under Article 12 of the Constitution of India, yet it is amenable to the jurisdiction of the Court under Article 226 of the Constitution."  (iii) Manmohan Singh Jaitla v. Commissioner Union Territory, Chandigarh, AIR 1985 S.C. 364; and  (iv) Pant Raj Sachdev v. The Indian Red Cross Society, through the Secretary General and others, 1987(1) PLR 69, wherein it has been held that the writ petition on the ground of infraction of the Service Rules and the rules of natural justice can be maintained against the society.  30. Next submission of the learned counsel for the respondent is that on new district of Sirsa having been carved out of Old District of Hissar, District Red Cross Society, Sirsa came into being and the services of the petitioner were allocated to the new society. Therefore, his lien stood automatically terminated. Since the petitioner did not challenge the initial order of his allocation dated 6.10.1975, it became final and, therefore, he could not now turn round and say that he still had lien against a permanent post of Assistant in the District Red Cross society, Hissar. This argument is without any force. As mentioned in the earlier part of this judgment, the lien of the petitioner having not been terminated at any stage, he was entitled to serve with the Red Cross Society, Hissar as he retained his lien with that society against the permanent post of the Accountant. The respondents have failed to produce any order terminating his lien or even suspension of such lien. Rather, they have themselves admitted vide letters dated 22.9.1977, 3.1.1978, 14.7.1980 and 16.9.1980 that the petitioner had a lien against the permanent post of Accountant at Hissar.  31. Last submission of the learned counsel for the respondents is that till the order dated 4.2.1980 passed by the President, District Red Cross Society, Sirsa, to the effect that he could not be sent back to the post where he retains his line is finally set aside in the Regular Second Appeal the petitioner continued to be an employee of the District Red Cross Society, Sirsa and, therefore, the President of the said society could suspend, charge sheet and after holding a departmental enquiry against him, could punish him and, therefore, the impugned order of termination of his service was valid. This argument is without any force. As mentioned herein before, the petitioner had filed Civil Suit No. 792-C of 1981 "Radha Kishan Rajpal v. District Red Cross Society, Sirsa and two others". After contest that suit was decreed and the order dated 4.2.1980 was declared illegal. That judgment of the Subordinate Court was confirmed by Additional District Judge, Sirsa vide his judgment and decree dated 3.10.1985 in Civil Appeal No. 51 instituted on 18.4.1983. Regular Second Appeal No. 3092 of 1985 against the above said judgment and decree of the first appellate Court was dismissed as withdrawn vide judgment of this Court dated 23.8.1983. Therefore, the order dated 4.2.1980 stood declared illegal and invalid finally.  32. In view of the above discussion, it is held :-  (i) that the order dated 4.2.1980 having been declared illegal and invalid finally, the petitioner Radha Kishan had a lien upon a permanent post of Assistant in District Red Cross Society, Hissar;  (ii) that the inquiry proceedings and the report of the Inquiry officer and the impugned order of dismissal stood vitiated on the grounds mentioned in the earlier part of this judgment i.e. on account of the authorities having committed infraction of the Punjab Civil Service Rules which were adopted vide resolution No. 5 dated 16.12.1988 by the respondents and  (iii) that no prior concurrence of the State Branch having been taken, the impugned order of termination of services of the respondent was illegal.  33. In the result, this writ petition is allowed. However, the parties are left to bear their own costs.  Petition allowed.
summary:
A. Petitioner, initially appointed as a clerk in the office of District Red Cross Society, was promoted but later transferred from one District Red Cross Society to another without their consent. An employee has a lien on the post they are confirmed on, even after they are allocated to a different district or state. Without a specific order, such a lien cannot be terminated or suspended. As such, the petitioner's lien with the District Red Cross Society, Hissar, against a permanent post as an Accountant would be maintained, and their seniority would be kept in the parent district to be considered for the next higher promotion in their parent district. [Paras 11, 12 and 13]

B. The President of District Red Cross Society, Sirsa, lacked the authority to suspend, charge sheet, and terminate the services of the petitioner since they had a lien on a permanent post as an Assistant in District Red Cross Society, Hissar. The impugned order of termination was passed without obtaining prior concurrence from the State Branch, making it without jurisdiction, and set aside. [Paras 18 and 19]

C. The Enquiry Officer had acted as both prosecutor and judge during the enquiry, and since no presiding officer was appointed, the principles of natural justice were violated. [Para 22]

D. The Enquiry Officer submitted the enquiry report more than five months after written arguments were submitted, and the order of termination was passed ten months after the reply to the show cause notice was submitted. No explanation was given for the inordinate delay, which rendered the disciplinary proceedings, including the impugned order, vitiated. [Paras 25 and 26]

E. The District Red Cross Society is amenable to writ jurisdiction under Article 226. A writ petition challenging the infraction of service rules and the rules of natural justice can be maintained against it. [Paras 29 and 30]

F. The inquiry proceedings, report of the inquiry officer, and impugned order of dismissal stood vitiated due to the infraction of rules adopted vide regulation No. 5 dated 16.12.1988 by respondents. [Para 32]

text: A.K. Shrivastava, J. - By this petition under Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution of India, the petitioner is challenging the validity of impugned orders Annexure P-5, dated 1-3-2000 passed by respondent No. 5, Annnexure P-7, dated 25-10-2001 passed by respondent No. 4 in departmental appeal and Annexure P-9, dated 7-3-2003 passed by respondent No. 3 dismissing the revision petition of the petitioner.  2. No exhaustive statement of facts is necessary for the disposal of this petition. Suffice it to state that at the relevant point of time the petitioner was serving on the post of Constable/Bugler. He remained absent w.e.f. 3-8-1999 to 2-9-1999 and his past record was also found to be bad as he remained unauthorizedly absent for 274 days on two earlier occasions. Therefore, he was subjected to a departmental inquiry and two charges were framed against him which read thus :  ARTICLE-I That, the said No. 920990014 Ct/Bug. N. Hanumantha of HQ/107 Bn. RAF/CRPF while functioning as Ct/Bug. committed disobedience of orders/neglect of duty/remissness in discharge of his duty in his capacity as a member of Force in that he deserted from HQ/107 Coy lines on 3-8-99 without sanction of leave or prior permission from competent authority. Thus he acted in a manner unbecoming of a Government Servant which is prejudicial to good order and discipline of the Force and punishable under Section 11(1) of CRPF Act, 1949. ARTICLE-II That, the said No. 920990014 Ct/Bug. Hanumantha of HQ/107 Bn. while functioning in the aforesaid capacity during the aforesaid period, repeated his acts of misconduct in his capacity as a member of Force by deserting from lines on 3-8-99 of which he had become habitual. Thus he acted in a manner unbecoming of a Government Servant which is prejudicial to good order and discipline of Force and punishable under Section 11(1) of CRPF Act, 1949." The imputation in regard to the charges is also the part of Annexure P-1, which is entire charge-sheet.  3. Needless to emphasise, the petitioner refuted the charges as a result of which the departmental witnesses were examined. According to the petitioner, opportunity to lead evidence and to cross-examine the departmental witnesses was not provided to him. However, learned Assistant Solicitor General, appearing for the respondents submits that the department gave opportunity to cross-examine departmental witnesses as well as allowed opportunity to petitioner to examine himself. On completion of the departmental enquiry since both the charges were found to be proved against the petitioner, the disciplinary authority passed the impugned order Annexure P-5 of removal of the petitioner from the service which was ultimately affirmed in appeal and revision. Hence this petition has been filed.  4. Shri Ghildiyal, learned counsel for the petitioner has raised two submissions. First submission of his is that the charge No. 1 is in respect to desertion and it cannot be framed in view of Section 10(m) of the Central Reserve Police Act, 1949 (for brevity, 'the Act'). By inviting my attention to Rule 31 of the Central Reserve Police Rules, 1955 (in short 'the Rules'), it has been put forth by the learned counsel that the term "desertion" as emphasized in Section 9(f) would mean only that an employee if he does not return of his own free will or is not apprehended within sixty days of the commencement of the desertion, absence or overstay of leave. By inviting my attention to Clause (c) of Rule 31, it has been contended that if the employee remains absent more than sixty days, then the Commandant shall publish in the Force Order the findings of the Court of Enquiry and the absentee shall be declared a deserter from the Force from the date of his illegal absence. The contention of learned counsel is that if the imputation regarding charges against Article-I is read in proper perspective, it is gathered that the petitioner appeared in the Unit on 3-9-1999 which would mean that he remained absent w.e.f. 3-8-1999 to 2-9-1999 and if that would be the position as per Rule 31(a) and (c), the petitioner cannot be said to be deserter. By inviting my attention to the decision of the Supreme Court in Capt. Virendra Kumar v. The Chief of the Army Staff, New Delhi, 1986(1) Services Law Reporter 422 : (AIR 1986 SC 1060), it has been contended that provisions of Sections 38 and 39 of Army Act are akin to that of Sections 9 and 10 of the present Act. In this decision the Supreme Court has clarified the word "desertion" and has explained that it would mean that the employee who had not come to join his service. According to the learned counsel since the petitioner himself appeared in the Unit on 3-9-99, therefore, he cannot be said to be a deserter.  5. So far as second charge is concerned, the contention of learned counsel is that the past conduct and misconduct of the petitioner may be taken into account in regard to inflict the punishment, but, it cannot be made the foundation stone in regard to framing of a charge. In support of his contention, learned counsel has placed reliance on the decision of Single Bench of Punjab and Haryana High Court, Satpal Singh v. State of Haryana, 1999(2) SCT 231 (P&H) : 1999(2) SLR 320. On these premised submissions, it has been contended by learned counsel for the petitioner that both the charges are bad in law and if that is the position, punishment order passed by the disciplinary authority and affirmed by the appellate and revisional authorities cannot be allowed to remain stand.  6. Lastly, it has been contended by learned counsel for the petitioner that even if the entire case of the department is accepted in toto, the punishment of removal from service is shockingly disproportionate and in that regard he has placed reliance on a latest pronouncement of the Supreme Court Bhagwan Lal Arya v. Commissioner of Police, Delhi, 2004(2) SCT 253 (SC) : 2004 SCSR 632 : (2004 Lab IC 1748).  7. Per contra, Shri Dharmendra Sharma, learned Assistant Solicitor General by inviting my attention to the averments made in paras 5.1 to 5.5 of the return has submitted that the disciplinary authority as well as the appellate and revisional authorities found the charges to be proved, as a result of which the petitioner was rightly punished by removing him from service. The said order was inflicted on account of incorrigible attitude of the petitioner. It has also been put-forth by the learned Assistant Solicitor General that lenient view has been adopted by the authorities and, therefore, this petition is sans substance and deserves to be dismissed.  8. After having heard learned counsel for the parties, I am of the view that this petition deserves to be allowed.  9. So far as first charge is concerned, it is in regard to desertion. How the term "desertion" would constitute under the Act, the provisions of Section 9(f) is required to be read. This section, pertains to more heinous offences and in Clause (f) desertion is there which reads as -  "(f) deserts the Force." At this juncture it would be apposite to read Section 10 which pertains to "Less heinous offences" and Clause (m) speaks about an employee absent himself without leave, or without sufficient cause overstays leave granted to him. It would be profitable to read Rule 31(a) at this juncture only. This rule deals about "Desertion and Absence without leave" which reads thus : "31. Desertion and Absence without leave. - (a) If a member of the force who becomes liable for trial under Clause (f) of Section 9, or Clause (m) of Section 10 or for deserting the Force while not on active duty under Clause (p) of Section 10 read with Clause (f) of Section 9, does not return of his own free will or is not apprehended within sixty days of the commencement of the desertion, absence or overstayal of leave, then the Commandant shall assemble a Court of Inquiry consisting of at least one Gazetted Officer and two other members who shall be either superior or subordinate officers to inquire into the desertion, absence or overstayal of leave of the offender and such other matters as may be brought before them." Thus it is clear that for the purpose of Clause (f) of Section 9 if a member of the Force who becomes liable for trial under this clause of Section 9, or Clause (m) of Section 10 or for deserting the Force while not on active duty under Clause (p) of Section 10 read with Clause (f) Section 9, does not return of his own free will or is not apprehended within sixty days of the commencement of the desertion, absence or overstayal of leave, then the Commandant shall assemble a Court of Inquiry against him. Clause (c) of Rule 31 reads thus :  "(c) The Commandant shall then publish in the Force Order the findings of the Court of Enquiry and the absentee shall be declared deserter from the Force from the date of his illegal absence, but he shall not thereby cease to belong to the Force. This shall, however, be no bar to enlisting another man in the place of a deserter." On bare perusal of the imputation of misconduct, it is gathered that the petitioner remained absent w.e.f. 3-8-1999 to 2-9-1999. As per case of department the petitioner appeared on 3-9-1999 and if that would be the position, the view of this Court is that the petitioner cannot be said to be a deserter as envisaged in Section 9(f) of the Act. Thus the charge against the petitioner is bad in law on bare perusal of Sections 9(f), 10(m) and Rule 31 (1)(c). In this context I may profitably rely on the decision Capt. Virendra Kumar (AIR 1986 SC 1060) (supra) wherein the similar provisions of Army Act were there and the Supreme Court has clarified that who will be said to be a deserter.  10. So far as Charge No. II is concerned there is sufficient force in the contention of learned counsel for the petitioner that past misconduct can be taken into consideration in order to inflict punishment. But, that itself cannot be made subject-matter of a charge. In the case of Satpal Singh (supra) it has been held that once the employee has been awarded punishment for his absence for the earlier period, the same cannot be made the subject-matter of the enquiry and he cannot be dismissed from service taking into consideration the earlier absence. I too do agree with the submission of learned counsel for the petitioner as well as decision of Satpal Singh (supra) and for this reason also the second charge is bad in law. Since both the charges are found to be bad in law, the punishment inflicted on the said charges cannot be allowed to remain stand.  11. For the reasons stated hereinabove, this petition succeeds and is hereby allowed. The impugned orders Annexure P-5, dated 1-3-1990 passed by respondent No. 5, Annexure P-7, dated 25-10-2001 passed by respondent No. 4 in departmental appeal and Annexure P-9, dated 7-3-2003, passed by respondent No. 3 dismissing the revision petition of the petitioner are hereby set aside. The respondents are directed to take petitioner back in service. However, looking to the facts the petitioner will not be entitled for any back wages. Looking to the facts and circumstances, the parties are directed to bear their own costs.  Petition allowed.
summary: A. Central Reserve Police Force Act, 1949, Sections 9(f) and 10(m) - Central Reserve Police Force Rules, 1955, Rule 31(c) - Removal from service - Unauthorized absence for sixty days constitute desertion - Petitioner's absence of one month cannot be considered as desertion - Hence, removal on this ground is not justified. [Para 9]  B. Constitution of India, Article 311 - Dismissal from service - Past misconduct can be considered for punishment - But framing charges on past misconduct is not permissible - Therefore, the punishment inflicted on the petitioner on those charges is unjustifiable. [Para 10]

text: G.S. Sistani, J. - In this writ petition, under Articles 226/227 of the Constitution of India, the petitioner has prayed that orders in the nature of writ of mandamus be passed directing the respondent to reinstate the petitioner with retrospective effect with consequential benefits. The brief facts of the case are that the petitioner joined the respondents on 29.03.1982. During the period 02.04.1982 to 26.09.1985 he carried out his duties with honesty and sincerity. During the aforesaid period the petitioner has submitted that he was granted leave and he overstayed for which he was given 7 days imprisonment. Various other punishments were also given to the petitioner during the aforesaid period which include 14 days imprisonment on 02.12.1986, 28 days imprisonment on 14.03.1988, 7 days imprisonment on 30.08.1989 and 7 days imprisonment on 30.03.1990. It has been submitted that all these punishments were awarded to the petitioner without any fault on his part and without issuing him any show cause notices or any explanation from him.  2. It is pleaded that vide Order dated 28.05.2001, the petitioner was wrongly and illegally terminated from his service by the respondents w.e.f. from 12.05.2001 without any fault or negligence on the part of the petitioner. The service benefits have also not been paid to him. The respondents have not complied with the provisions of natural justice. Neither any notice was issued to the petitioner nor he was afforded any opportunity to explain the position. The grounds for termination of his service were false and baseless.  3. The respondents have filed their counter-affidavit. It has been contended by the respondents that the present writ petition is liable to be dismissed on the grounds of delay and laches, as the petitioner has approached this Court after more than 13 years of his discharge. The petitioner has failed to give any explanation for the delay in approaching this Hon'ble Court. The petitioner has also not exhausted the remedies which were available to him. It would be useful to reproduce Paras 'A' to 'F' of Para 7 of the Counter Affidavit :-  A. That the petitioner No. 6376715 Ex. Sep. Rishimuni Rai, was enrolled in the Army on 20th March, 1982 and discharged from service under Item III (v) annexed to Army Rule 13(3) as "service no longer required" with effect from 17th May, 1990 (FN).  B. That the petitioner during his 8 years 49 days of service was awarded six punishments on different occasions which are enumerated hereunder :-  a) 7 days RI in Military custody on 27th September, 1983 for an offence under Army Act Section 63 by the Officer Commanding 501 ASC Bn.  b) 14 days detention on 19th December, 1985 for an offence under Army Act Section 39 (b) for Overstay of leave for 27 days by CO 528 ASC Bn.  c) 14 days RI in military custody on 02 December, 1986 for an offence under Army Act Section 39 (b) for overstay of leave for 73 days by Officer Commanding, HQ Wing, ASC Centre (South).  d) 28 days RI in Military custody on 14th March, 1988 for offence under Army Act 39 (b) for overstay of leave for 73 days by OC HQ Wing, ASC Centre (South).  e) 7 days RI in Military custody on 30th August, 1989 for an offence under Army Act 39 (b) for overstay of leave for 13 days by CO 536 ASC Bn.  f) 7 days RI in Military custody on 30th March, 1990 for offence under Army Act Section 63 by OC 536 ASC Bn.  C. That in order to curb indiscipline in the army, Army Headquarters vide letter No. A/13216/159/AG/PS(D) dated 28th December, 1988 had delegated the discretionary power to the OC Unit either to retain the individual having incurred four or more red ink entries or to discharge them being undesirable soldiers. The petitioner, on having incurred four red ink entries, his case was referred to 536 ASC Bn. vide ASC Records (Supply) letter No. 6376715/T8/536/Doc-IV dated 11th May, 1989. Accordingly, a show cause notice was served on the petitioner vide 536 ASC Bn. Letter No. 632638/Sup/ST-12 dated 06 June, 1989. The petitioner vide petition dated 17th June, 1989 requested that he be given an opportunity and he be retained in service. A sympathetic view was taken by CO 536 ASC Bn. and the petitioner was considered for retention.  D. That on 30th August, 1989, the petitioner was again awarded punishment under Army Act Section 39(b) and thereby he incurred another red ink entry, making five red entries. Accordingly, the petitioner was served with show cause notice vide 536 ASC Bn. letter No. 632638/6376715-N/ST-12, dated 10th September, 1989. Again on his request and on an assurance given by him that he would show improvement, another opportunity was given to him.  E. That thereafter, however, the petitioner showed no signs of improvement. He again committed an offence on 21st March, 1990 and was punished under Army Act Section 63. On 28th March, 1990, again a show cause notice was served upon the petitioner vide 536 ASC Bn. letter No. 632638/Sup/ST-12 dated 28th March, 1990. Considering it detrimental to discipline, his case for discharge from service as "service no longer required" was recommended by CO 536 ASC Bn. in IAFY-1948 and sanctioned by General Officer Commanding 36 Infantry Division on 10th April, 1990 and finally SOS with effect from 17th May, 1990.  F. That the petitioner's accounts has been closed as under :-  a) Service gratuity after deduction of debit balance of Rs. 2320/-  Rs. 5000/-  b) AFPP Fund balance  Rs. 4842/-  c) AGI maturity benefits contributed alongwith interest.  Amount  4. Learned counsel for the respondents submitted that Rule 13(3)III(v) clearly empowers the authorities to pass an order of discharge simplicitor. The order of discharge is intended to relieve a person from service without casting any stigma on the service of the person. It is not by way of punishment but is a power vested in the competent authority to discharge a person from army service and is quite distinct from dismissal from service. The Rules have provided an inbuilt procedure before a person can be discharged. Show cause notice should be served upon the person and after receiving his reply, if any, the competent authority has to examine the matter in all seriousness and then pass an order of discharge, if necessary. This power is obviously not a punitive power but is normally exercised after taking the service record of a person in mind and examining his utility in the service in the years to come. At this stage we may refer to a recent judgment of a Division Bench of this Court in the case of Capt. Raj Kumar Singhal v. Union of India and another, (WP(C) No. 1450/2001 decided on 27th July, 2006) where the Court has held as under :-  "15. Learned counsel for the respondents further contended that in spite of repeated warnings and counselling by the commanding officer, the petitioner continued with his acts of indiscipline which included absence from duty or found in state of intoxication while on duty. Due to the behaviour under the Policy of habitual offenders circulated on 14.8.1984 the services of the petitioner warranted the action of his discharge. The respondents have filed along with a counter affidavit, a copy of the conduct-sheet of the petitioner which shows that the petitioner has been awarded 4 red entries and 6 black entries. Mr. Dilip Mehra, learned counsel for the respondents contended that although the policy dated 14.8.1984 are only guidelines and the petitioner has been discharged under Rule 15(2)(g)(ii) of the Air Force Rules, 1969, which reads as under :  "15. Authorities empowered to authorise discharge. - (1) and 2.  TABLE  Class  Cause of discharge  Competent Special authority to authorise discharge  Instructions  1.  2.  3.  4.  Person enrolled (a) to under the Act who have attested.  xxxxxx (F) xxxxxx  xxxxxxxx  (g) His services no longer required :  (i) xxxx  (ii) Unsuitable for retention in the Air Force  Air Officer i/c Administration" 10. Learned counsel for the respondents further submitted that at no point of time the petitioner ever contested the punishment so awarded from time to time. It was argued that the case of the petitioner is squarely covered, as per the policy letter dated 14.8.1984; and even assuming without admitting that Rule 74 has been violated, still the petitioner has been awarded total nine punishments, red and black combined.  11. We have heard learned counsel for the parties and have given our thoughtful consideration as well as perused the record. The counsel for the respondents has taken us through the policy. The entire aim and object of the policy is to deal firmly with the habitual offenders. The policy is based on a study conducted by the Institute of Defence Management regarding the existence of habitual offenders among airmen. As per the study the effect of repetitive indiscipline has a serious adverse effect on the general morale and discipline, especially on the young airman joining various Units from the training centres.  12. The first contention of the petitioner, that as per the show cause notice only three red ink entries have been shown, is factually incorrect.  13. Para 2 of the show cause notice mentions that in the total service of six years and eleven months the petitioner was tried and punished on as many as seven occasions, out of which four are red ink entries. A copy of the conduct-sheet was annexed to the show cause notice. The show cause notice goes on to state further that in spite of written warning the petitioner again indulged in acts of indiscipline which included absence from duty on two occasions and was found in the state of intoxication while on duty. In the writ petition the petitioner has nowhere mentioned whether he had replied to the show cause notice or not. The petitioner in terms of the communication dated 27.9.1991 addressed to the Chief of Air Staff had requested the respondents for supply of four documents on the ground that he had misplaced all his documents; and even in that list he never requested for reply to the show cause notice. The only inference that can be drawn is that no reply to the show cause notice was given. The court cannot lose track of the fact that the main ethos of the policy letter dated 14.8.1984 was to weed out habitual offenders among the airmen, as they had an adverse effect on the general discipline and administration in the Air Force. The conduct-sheet which has been filed by the respondents, as Annexure R-1, clearly shows that the petitioner was completely indisciplined and despite warning letter dated 22.12.1987 he refused to make any amends. The acts of indiscipline of the petitioner are totally unbecoming of a member of the Armed Force. The respondents have followed the procedure which is required to be implemented, as per the policy of discharge. Petitioner was duly warned vide letter dated 22.12.1987 about the implications of his persisting in the acts of indiscipline and even one additional punishment would result in discharge from the Air Force under the provisions of Rule 15(2)(g)(ii) of the Air Force Rules, 1969. The petitioner was thereafter issued a show cause notice and was discharged from service. Having perused the conduct-sheet of the petitioner, the warning letter dated 22.12.1987 and show cause notice dated 4.10.1989, we find that the respondents completely followed the procedure, as per the policy dated 14.8.1984 for discharge of the petitioner. The Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in the case of Union of India v. Corporal A.K. Bakshi and Anr., 1996(2) SCT 287 : JT 1996(3) SC 310 has held that the basic idea underlying the Policy for Discharge is that recurring nature of punishments for misconduct imposed on an airman renders him unsuitable for further retention in the Air Force. Suitability for retention in the Air Force has to be determined on the basis of record of service. Relevant portion of the same reads as under :  "The punishments referred to in the Policy for Discharge are punishments that have been imposed for misconduct under the relevant provisions of the Act and the Rules. The Policy for Discharge envisages that in cases where an airman has been awarded such punishments six times, he is to be treated as a habitual offender and action for his discharge from service should be taken against him under Rule 15(2)(g)(ii) of the Rules. This action for discharge is not by way of punishment for the misconducts for which he has already been punished. The basic idea underlying the Policy for Discharge is that recurring nature of punishments for misconduct imposed on an airman renders him unsuitable for further retention in the Air Force. Suitability for retention in the Air Force has to be determined on the basis of record of service. The punishments that have been imposed earlier being part of the record of service have to be taken into consideration for the purpose of deciding whether such person is suitable for retention in the Air Force. The discharge in such circumstances is, therefore, discharge falling under Rule 15(2)(g)(ii) and it cannot be held to be termination of service by way of punishment for misconduct falling under Rule 18 of the Rules."  14. The plea raised by the learned counsel for the petitioner that there is violation of Rule 74 of the Air Force Rules, 1969 as two separate punishments have been awarded for separate offences in a common trial held on 8.3.1989 is of no help to the petitioner as in all ten punishments have been awarded to the petitioner as per the conduct sheet annexed as Annexure-R.1.  15. The plea taken by the respondents, thus is not without merit. The petitioner himself has been responsible for his acts of misconduct, has been awarded punishments and found to be unsuitable for retention in the Indian Air Force. We find no infirmity in the order of discharge dated 21.10.1993."  5. In the present case since the petitioner had incurred 4 red ink entries, his case was referred to 536 ASC Bn vide ASC Records (Supply) letter No. 6376715/T8/536/Doc-IV dated 11 May 1989, and accordingly a show cause notice dated 6.6.1989 was served on the petitioner. In reply to the aforesaid show cause notice the petitioner in terms of his petition dated 17.6.1989 requested that he be given an opportunity and be retained in service. A sympathetic view was taken and the petitioner was retained in service. That thereafter on 30.8.1989 the petitioner was again awarded a punishment under Section 39(B) of the Army Act and thereby he incurred another red ink entry making a total of 5 red ink entries. The petitioner was once again served with a show cause notice dated 10.9.1989 and in reply thereto he assured that he would improve himself and thus another opportunity be given to him. The petitioner showed absolutely no sign of improvement, and another offence was committed by him on 21.3.1990 as a result thereof he was punished under Section 63 of the Army Act. The respondents were forced to issue another show cause notice dated 28.3.1990, and thereafter orders for discharge were passed against the petitioner. Despite the show cause notices the petitioner made no effort to improve himself. By no stretch of imagination it can be stated that the respondents have not followed the due process of law or have not complied with the provisions of natural justice.  6. We find no infirmity in the order of discharge, as it does not suffer from element of bias or arbitrariness nor it offends the principles of natural justice. For the reasons aforesaid the present petition is dismissed, while leaving the parties to bear their own costs.  Petition dismissed.
summary: Constitution of India, Articles 14 and 16 - Army Act, 1950, Sections 39 and 191 - Army Rules, 1954, Rule 13(3) - Discharge from service - Military personnel who overstay leave after receiving multiple warnings, reprimands and negative entries in service record are retained to provide an opportunity for improvement. However, if the individual does not improve despite receiving show cause notices, their discharge will not violate principles of natural justice or contain any bias or arbitrariness. [Para 5]

text: Thottathil B. Radhakrishnan, J. - Petitioner entered service of the M.G. University as a Lecturer on 4-12-1987 in the faculty of School of Chemical Sciences. The third respondent joined the service of the University as Lecturer in the Department of Basic Medical Sciences on 20-2-1988.  2. On the basis of the notification No. 1726/89/A11(1) Admn. dated 4-1-1990, the University, through its Registrar, invited application for appointment to, among other posts, one post of Reader in Bio-chemistry in the School of Basic Medical Sciences. The Selection Committee found Dr. P. Harikumar as the one entitled to be selected and recommended his name for appointment. He was the only person who was selected in the selection by interview held on 27-2-1991. That selection of Dr. P. Harikumar was challenged by the third respondent by filing O.P. No. 3080 of 1991. Though there was an interlocutory order in that case on C.M.P. No. 5385 of 1991 directing that Dr. P. Harikumar is not to be admitted to the post of Reader in Bio-Chemistry, the selected candidate Dr. P. Harikumar ultimately reported that he is not willing to join the service as Reader in Bio-chemistry in the M.G. University. On record, by that time, was the counter affidavit of the University asserting its stand that the selection of Dr. P. Harikumar was in order. However, in view of the submission made before this Court on 1-6-1994 on behalf of Dr. P. Harikumar, who was the second respondent in O.P. No. 3080 of 1991 that he is not willing to join the service as Reader, the original petition was treated as not surviving and was hence disposed of by judgment dated 1-6-1994, obviously, without entering into merits. The aforesaid facts relating to O.P. No. 3080 of 1991 have been noticed from the file of that case forming part of the records of this Court.  3. The aforesaid would show that the selection of Dr. P. Harikumar in the interview held on 27-2-1991 was not interfered with by this court and it therefore stood, however that, Dr. P. Harikumar did not join. This resulted in the occurrence of the situation where that vacancy remained unfilled. As already noticed, there was no select list of more candidates and Dr. P. Harikumar was the sole candidate selected for the post. This means that, there was no select list available to make any alternate appointment in the event of Dr. P. Harikumar's failure to join duty. The vacancy thus not having been filled following the interview on 27-2-1991, the selection and appointment to that vacancy required to be done de novo. There can be no doubt about this, formidable support to which can be found in the judgments of the Apex Court in State of Punjab v. Raghubir Chand Sharma, 2002(2) SCT 234 : (JT 2001(9) SC 266) and Thrissur District Co-operative Bank Limited v. Delsom Davis P. 2002(2) SCT 998 : (JT 2002(2) SC 329).  4. Thereafter, the University conducted a selection on 21-6-1994 and the third respondent was selected and Ext.P3 appointment order dated 27-8-1994 was issued to him appointing him as Reader in Bio-Chemistry in the School of Bio- Science with effect from the forenoon of 28-7-1994, that is, the date on which he had assumed office of the Reader following letter dated 28-7-1994 issued immediately after the Syndicate had considered and resolved on the recommendations of the Selection Committee. By Ext.P3 order, he was also put on probation for a period of one year in terms of the University laws. Thus, for all intends and purposes, the third respondent became a Reader only with effect from 27-8-1994.  5. It appears that, thereafter the third respondent made representations and the University, by different orders, granted him service benefits retrospectively from the date on which Dr. P. Harikumar was selected and appointed following the Syndicate decision dated 18-3-1991. The net result of the action of the University is that, though selected and appointed as Reader and put on probation only with effect from 27-8-1994, as per Ext.P3, the third respondent started enjoying certain benefits retrospectively from 18-3-1991, that is, the date on which Dr. P. Harikumar was appointed. It has to be immediately noticed that even if this Court had set aside Dr. P. Harikumar's selection in O.P. No. 3080 of 1991, that could not have resulted in the consequence of the petitioner being appointed as against that vacancy without any further selection process. This is because, the petitioner did not find himself in the select list prepared by the Selection Committee which recommended Dr. P. Harikumar for appointment as Reader. Therefore, in terms of the Constitution of India and the laws, in particular, the University laws, there was no room, rhyme or reason to extend any benefits to the third respondent by retrospectively giving him benefits from 18-3-1991 in a matter relating to public appointment.  6.
