However, in the facts and circumstances of the case, we do not think that the petitioner would be entitled to receive interest as claimed in the writ petition.  10. The writ petition is disposed of and the respondents are directed to pay to the petitioner his benefits in terms of this judgment within a period of six months from today. The parties are left to bear their own costs.  Petition allowed.
summary: Pension Regulations for Army 1961, Appendix II, Regulation 173 - Disability Pension - Petitioner discharged from military service with 40% disability - In addition to normal pension, petitioner entitled to receive disability pension - Petitioner's disability increased to 50% due to further deterioration - Resurvey Medical Board assessed petitioner's disability as 50% - CDA(P) has no right to challenge medical findings - Circular/policy decision states that disability under 50% will be read as 50% - Petitioner should receive disability pension with 50% disability element. [Paras 7, 8 and 9]

text: K. Balakrishnan Nair, J.  O.P. No. 11925 of 1998  The petitioner who got employment under the Government as a member of the Scheduled Tribe is now told by the competent authority by Ext. P50 order that he is not a member of the Scheduled Tribe and therefore he should quit the post and refund the salary received by him. Aggrieved by the same, the petitioner has filed this Original Petition. The brief facts necessary for the disposal of the case are the following.  2. The Public Service Commission by Ext. P1 notification dated 30.8.1983 invited applications for appointment to the post of Under Secretary in the Finance Department in the Government Secretariat. It was a special recruitment for the members of the Scheduled Caste/Scheduled Tribe. The petitioner was duly qualified for appointment to the post and he applied for the post as a member of the Scheduled Tribe. He was selected and advised by the Public Service Commission as per Ext. P2 advice memo dated 29.3.1985 and the Government as per Ext. P3 order dated 29.4.1985 appointed him as Under Secretary in the Finance Department. Ext. P22 dated 11.4.1984 is the caste certificate issued by the Tahsildar, Ranni, certifying that the petitioner belongs to Hindu Uraly which is a, Scheduled Tribe. At the relevant time the Tahsildar was one of the competent authorities authorised to issue community certificates. The petitioner completed his probation in the post of Under Secretary and in due course he has been further promoted, and from 1993 he is working as Additional Secretary in the Finance Department.  3. While so, in the year 1995, the petitioner was served with Ext. P4 notice dated 30.10.1995 by the Vigilance Officer of the KIRTADS, calling upon him to attend an enquiry on 15.11.1995. The enquiry related to the caste status of the petitioner. After one or two adjournments, the petitioner appeared for the enquiry held on 5.1.1996. He gave the information sought from him and also filled up and submitted Ext. P5 questionnaire. Later, the petitioner was served with Ext. P6 notice dated 31.1.1997 issued by the Chairman of the Scrutiny Committee for verification of SC/ST claims, constituted under Ext. P51 Government Order dated 8.5.1995. The allegation in Ext. P6 was that the petitioner has made false claim that he is a member of Uraly (Scheduled Tribe) community. The proposed action in the notice was to cancel the Scheduled Tribe certificate wrongfully secured by the petitioner and to take consequential action. Along with Ext. P6 notice Ext. P7 report of the Vigilance Officer of the KIRTADS dated 11.9.1996 was also served on the petitioner.  4. The petitioner submitted Ext. P8 reply to the show-cause notice. He also submitted documents to substantiate his claim that he is a member of the Uraly (Scheduled Tribe) community. Thereafter, the Scrutiny Committee heard the petitioner. At the time of hearing he submitted Ext. P15 explanation and further documents to substantiate his claim. The petitioner was given the hearing on 14.10.1997. He appeared along with his counsel and explained his contentions. It was emphasised that Ext. P7 was prepared on the basis of hearsay and the same should not be relied upon without giving him a chance to challenge the statements of the persons relied on by the Vigilance Officer in Ext. P7.  5. Overruling the objections of the petitioner, the 2nd respondent-Chairman of the Scrutiny Committee passed Ext. P50 order dated 7.3.1998, rejecting the Scheduled Tribe claim of the petitioner and declaring that he is a member of Kuravan (Scheduled Caste) community. The report was submitted before the Government for further follow-up action. The petitioner challenges Exts. P7 and P50 on various grounds.  6. A detailed counter-affidavit has been filed on behalf of the 2nd respondent, supporting the impugned orders. I heard both sides. The learned counsel for the petitioner relied on the decisions of the Apex Court in Goyatrilaxmi Bapurao Nagpore v. State of Maharashtra (AIR 1996 SC 1338) and Gulzar Singh v. Sub Divisional Magistrate, (1999(3) SCC 107) and of the Bombay High Court in Arpit son of Prakash Nimie v. The Scheduled Tribe Caste Certificate Scrutiny Committee, Nagpur (AIR 2001 Bombay 59). The Learned Government Pleader relied on the decisions of the Supreme Court in Kumari Madhuri Patil v. Addl. Commr, Tribal Development, 1995(1) SCT 261 (SC) : (1994(6) SCC 241), Director of Tribal Welfare, Govt. of A.P. v.. Laveti Giri and Anr. 1995(3) SCT 118 : (1995(4) SCC 32) and State of T.N. v. A. Guruswamy (1997(3) SCC 542). I also heard the counsel for the additional 5th respondent. The said respondent was an applicant for the post of Under Secretary notified as per Ext. P1. He is a member of the Scheduled Tribe community.  7. The learned counsel for the petitioner challenged the very jurisdiction of the Scrutiny Committee to go into the caste status of the petitioner. The proceedings against the petitioner admittedly have been initiated under Ext. P51 G.O. dated 8.5.1995. That is manifest from the recitals in Ext. P6 dated 31.1.1997. The Kerala (Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes) Regulation of Issue of Community Certificates Act, 1996 (Act 11 of 1996) was enforced in the State of Kerala with effect from 1.12.1996. The said Act was issued in the place of Ext. P51 G.O. which governed the very same subject-matter till the enforcement of Act 11 of 1996. Since the matters dealt with by Ext. P51 order and Ext. P52 Act were the same, after the enforcement of the Act, the provision of the executive order no longer survive. Therefore, the issuance of Ext. P6 purportedly under Ext. P51 is without jurisdiction. Apart from that, S. 30 of the Act saves Ext. P22 caste certificate issued in favour of the petitioner by the Tahsildar and other similar certificates issued by the competent authorities. S. 30 reads as follows:  "30. Transitional Provision :- A community certificate issued by any authority competent to issue the same under the relevant rules or orders before the commencement of this Act, shall unless it is cancelled under the provisions of this Act, be valid and shall be deemed to have been issued under the provisions of this Act."  In view of this provision, after 1.12.1996 the caste certificate Ext. P22 certifying that the petitioner is a member of the Scheduled Tribe is valid and binding on all including the Government. It can be cancelled only under the provisions of the Act. So, Ext. P6 issued admittedly under Ext. P51 after the enforcement of Ext. P52 is plainly without jurisdiction. It is ultra vires and unauthorised. It is declared so.  8. The petitioner has a case that Ext. P7 has been prepared in violation of the principles of natural justice and Ext. P50 has been issued relying on the findings in Ext. P7, in violation of the principles of natural justice. A reading of Ext. P7 will show that it has been prepared following the inquisitory procedure. The Vigilance Officer went around and collected information from various sources. He also recorded the statements of a number of persons. Everything was done behind the back of the petitioner. The petitioner was also questioned and his statement and explanation were also recorded. Even assuming the Vigilance Officer is entitled to gather information from any source the Scrutiny Committee can act upon the same only after affording a reasonable opportunity to the petitioner to rebut the conclusions in Ext. P7. For that the Scrutiny Committee was bound to follow the adversary procedure. The Supreme Court itself envisaged an adversary procedure where evidence is tendered by the claimant and opposing evidence is to be taken in his presence. This will be evident from the directions of the Supreme Court in Kumari Madhuri Patil v. Addl. Commissioner, (1994) 6 SCC 241, basing on which the Government have issued Ext. P51. In the said decision, the Supreme Court stated :  "6. The Director concerned, on receipt of the report from the Vigilance Officer if he found the claim for special status to be "not genuine" or `doubtful' or spurious or falsely or wrongly claimed, the Director concerned should issue show-cause notice supplying a copy of the report of the Vigilance Officer to the candidate by registered post with acknowledgement due or through the head of the educational institution concerned in which the candidate is studying or employed. The notice should indicate that the representation or reply, if any, would be made within two weeks from the date of the receipt of the notice and in no case on request not more than 30 days from the date of receipt of the notice. In case, the candidate seeks for an opportunity of hearing and claims an inquiry to be made in that behalf, the Director on receipt of such representation/reply shall convene the committee and the Joint/Additional Secretary as Chairperson who shall give reasonable opportunity to the candidate/parent/guardian to adduce all evidence in support of their claim. A public notice by beat of drum or any other convenient mode may be published in the village or locality and if any person or association opposes such a claim, an opportunity to adduce evidence may be given to him/it. After giving such opportunity either in person or through counsel the Committee may make such inquiry as it deems expedient and consider the claims vis-a-vis the objections raised by the candidate or opponent and pass an appropriate order with brief reasons in support thereof." (emphasis supplied)  9. The Apex Court speaks of opportunity to both sides to adduce evidence, either in person or through counsel. In the case at hand, what was done was, the petitioner and his counsel were heard and the petitioner was given an opportunity to produce documents from his side. But overruling his objections to Ext. P7 report, the same was accepted by the Scrutiny Committee. As stated earlier, the conclusions in Ext. P7 were based on discrete enquiries and on statements recorded behind the back of the petitioner. Unless the petitioner is given a chance to challenge the statements of those persons relied on by the Vigilance Officer, the conclusions cannot be pressed into service against the petitioner. The reliance placed by the Scrutiny Committee on the conclusion in Ext. P7, therefore violates the principles of natural justice.  10. Lord Denning in Kanda v. Government of Malaya, (1962 AC 322) stated:  "If the right to be heard is to be real right which is worth anything, it must carry with it a right in the accused man to know the case which is made against him. He must know what evidence has been given and what statements have been made affecting him and then he must be given a fair opportunity to correct or contradict them".  De Smith in Judicial Review of Administrative Action (5th Edition) comments on the right to cross-examine in the following words:  "Refusal to permit cross-examination of witnesses may amount to procedural unfairness, especially if a witness has testified orally and a party requests leave to confront and cross-examine him. The fact that the proceedings may be inquisitorial and informal is inconclusive. As with the question of entitlement to legal representation, the matter is one for the discretion of the tribunal. However, where a "judicialised" procedure has been adopted and witnesses are called to give evidence, then the courts will be very ready in the absence of strong reasons to the contrary to find unfairness where a tribunal declines to allow those witnesses to be tested in cross-examination. As Lord Edmund-Davies has pointed out, "there is a massive body of accepted decisions establishing that natural justice requires that a party be given an opportunity of challenging by cross-examination witnesses called by other parties on relevant issues".  Professor H.W.R. Wade in his Administrative Law (Eighth Edition) states:  "Where an oral hearing is given, it has been laid down that a tribunal must (a) consider all relevant evidence which a party wishes to submit; (b) inform every party of all the evidence to be taken into account, whether derived from another party or independently; (c) allow witnesses to be questioned; (d) allow comment on the evidence and argument on the whole case. Failure to allow the last two rights, which include the right of cross-examination, has led to the quashing of punishments awarded by prison visitors in a series of cases".  Professor P.P. Craig in his Administrative Law (Third Edition) comments:  "The overriding obligation is to provide the applicant with a fair hearing and a fair opportunity to controvert the charge. This may in certain cases require not only that the applicant be informed of the evidence, but that the individual should be given a sufficient opportunity to deal with it. This may involve the cross-examination of the witnesses whose evidence is before the hearing authority in the form of hearsay. Where there are insuperable difficulties in arranging for that evidence to be questioned it should not be admitted in evidence, or the hearing authority should exclude it from their consideration".  Mr. Justice Felix Frankfurter in Joint Anti-Fascist Refugee Committee v. Mc Grath, (1951) 341 US 123 at page 162) has held:  "That a conclusion satisfies one's private conscience does not attest its reliability. The validity and moral authority of a conclusion largely depends on the mode by which it was reached. Secrecy is not congenial to truth-seeking and self-righteousness gives too slender an assurance of rightness. No better instrument has been devised for arriving at truth than to give a person in jeopardy of serious loss, notice of the case against him and opportunity to meet it. Nor has a better way been found for generating the feeling, so important to a popular Government, that justice has been done."  Our Supreme Court in Gulzar Singh v. Sub Divisional Magistrate, 1999(3) SCC 107, which is a case concerning the cancellation of a caste certificate held:  "If there were statements of other persons which were recorded, as seem to have been done in the present case, on the basis of which the Department came to the conclusion that the appellant was not a Majhbi Sikh by caste but was a Christian, then fairness would require that the said statements should be put to the appellant before a final decision is taken."  11. Ext. P7 has been admittedly prepared in gross violation of the above stated principles of law. The Scrutiny Committee did not give a fair opportunity to the petitioner to challenge the statements relied on by the Vigilance Officer. But the learned Special Government Pleader, relying on the decision of the Apex Court in State of Tamil Nadu v. A. Gurusamy, (1997) 3 SCC 542, submitted that the enquiry need not be in the form of trial of a suit. While dealing with the decision of the District Collector regarding caste status, the Apex Court said: "The District Collector does not decide it like a suit". But the said observation cannot be pressed into service in the light of the express words of the Supreme Court in "Kumari Madhuri Patil" (1994(6) SCC 241). The directions therein, as stated earlier, speak of an opportunity to adduce evidence by both sides. It is also directed in the said decision: "The inquiry should be completed as expeditiously as possible preferably by day-to-day proceedings within such period not exceeding two months." If the enquiry is to be over by a single hearing, as was done in this case, there need not be any direction to hold the enquiry on a day-to-day basis, for a period of two months. Therefore, it cannot be said that the examination of witnesses by the Scrutiny Committee was not contemplated by the Supreme Court while issuing the directions in the abovesaid case. Therefore, the contention of the learned Special Government Pleader in this regard cannot be accepted. Therefore, I find that the Scrutiny Committee did not follow a fair procedure in accordance with the principles of natural justice. For this reason also Ext. P50 is vitiated.  12. The petitioner has a case that the assessment of the impact of various documents made by the Scrutiny Committee was one-sided. It is emphasised that the Committee has failed to take into account various valid documents produced by him, or they were rejected on irrelevant grounds. Several other grounds taken in the Original Petition were also urged against the impugned orders. But I am not going into those grounds, in view of my finding that the impugned orders have been issued without jurisdiction and in violation of the principles of natural justice.  13. Another aspect to be considered in this case is whether any action could be initiated against the petitioner to cancel his appointment at this distance of time. The advice of a candidate can be cancelled by the Public Service Commission within one year of the date of advice, in the light of R. 3(c) of Part II of the Kerala State and Subordinate Services Rules. There may be cases where a candidate may be advised out of turn by mistake while applying the communal rotation. Such wrong advice can be cancelled or corrected only within one year from the date of advice. In the case at hand, the case of the respondents is that the petitioner is a member of the Scheduled Caste. So he has been wrongly advised in the turn of Scheduled Tribe. But normally an advice, even if it is found to be wrong, cannot be modified or withdrawn after the lapse of one year, on the strength of any executive order. But in view of Ext. P52 Act, the Government have got ample powers to take appropriate action to cancel the appointment, provided the jurisdictional preconditions stated therein are present. S. 11 of Act 11 of 1996 is the enabling provision by virtue of which the Government can cancel any caste certificate. S. 11(1) reads as follows:  "1. Cancellation of false community certificate - (1) Where, before or after the commencement of this Act, a person not belonging to any of the Scheduled Castes or the Scheduled Tribes has obtained a false community certificate to the effect that either himself or his children belongs or belong to such Caste or the Tribe, the Scrutiny Committee may either suo motu or on a written complaint or report by any person or authority, call for the records and enquire into the correctness of such certificate and if it is of the opinion that the certificate was obtained fraudulently, it shall, by order, cancel the certificate after giving the person concerned an opportunity of making a representation, if any."  The jurisdictional precondition for taking action under S. 11(1) is that a person not belonging to any of the Scheduled Castes or Scheduled Tribes has obtained a false community certificate fraudulently. So, the action is contemplated not against the members of the Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe but against strangers who claim fraudulently that they belong to the Scheduled Caste or the Scheduled Tribe. In the case at hand, even according to the respondents, the petitioner is a member of the Scheduled Caste. It appears that the provisions of the Act are not meant for dealing with the case of a member of the Scheduled Caste claiming S.T. status or vice versa (See the provisions employing similar words in S. 3 of the Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989. The atrocities committed by third parties on the members of the SC/ST alone are covered by this Act. In other words, a member of the SC/ST cannot be accused of an offence under this Act).  14. Further, no-one has a case that the petitioner has acted fraudulently. The worst allegation against him in Ext. P7 is that he has made a false claim. The dictionary meaning of "false" is, wrong, incorrect, not genuine, artificial, sham, pretended etc. But the dictionary meaning of "fraud" is, deceiving somebody illegally in order to make money or obtain goods, and that of "fraudulent" is, deceitful or dishonest. "Fraudulent" is the adjective and "fraudulently" is the adverb. `Deceit' involves deliberate misleading.  15. In the case at hand, the petitioner has been admitted in Standard I by his parents in Kattachira Tribal School with his caste as Malay Uraly. The petitioners' parents were residing in the Tribal colony. Both of them underwent training in a Craft Training Centre for Tribals and they were admitted in the Centre as persons belonging to Uraly (Scheduled Tribe) community. This will be evident from Ext. P9. So, the petitioners' parents even at their young age were claiming that they belong to Uraly (Scheduled Tribe) community. The petitioner was admitted by them in the school when he was a minor aged about 5 years. According to the official respondents, the petitioner's grandfather was a headman of Kuravas, locally known as `Uraly' and he started making the alleged false claim of being a member of the Uraly Scheduled Tribe. It is also alleged that he used his residence in the tribal settlement as a ground for putting forward his claim. The alleged sin dates back to the days of petitioner's grandfather. So, admittedly, the petitioner's claim was not something invented by him. The religion or caste of a child is what he is told by his parents. He has no free choice in that. Since his school records including the SSLC book showed that he is Malay Uraly, he applied for the post of Tinder Secretary as one belonging to the Scheduled Tribe. Since Malay Uraly was treated as Uraly, the competent authority (the Tahsildar) issued Ext. P22 certificate. A person like the petitioner who applies for a post in the public service cannot go to the KIRTADS and request them to make a genealogical study and tell him the correctness of his caste claim and thereafter submit an application for employment relying on such a certificate. The petitioner has done what any other candidate would do, i.e., he relied on the caste status mentioned in the school records and in the certificate issued by the competent authority. So, he cannot be accused of having done anything "fraudulently". Ext. P52 Act, it appears, is not meant to deal with every mistaken claim of caste, especially made by a member of the SC/ST.  16. Anyway, I am not finally pronouncing on the jurisdiction of the Scrutiny Committee or the Government to take action under Act 11 of 1996 because so far as the concerned authorities have not initiated any proceedings under the said Act. The petitioner has prayed, for a declaration that respondents 2 to 4 have no authority or jurisdiction to determine the caste status of the petition under Ext. P52 Act. The contentions of the petitioner in this regard are kept open and he may urge them, in case the Government or any other competent authority proceeds against him under Ext. P52. So it is not necessary to finally decide whether the provisions of the Act are attracted in the case of the petitioner.  17. The Original Petition is allowed quashing Ext. P50. It is declared that the findings in Ext. P7 will not bind the petitioner. But, this will not stand in the way of the Government using the materials contained in Ext. P7 in accordance with law to launch any fresh action against the petitioner, if the same is legally permissible under Ext. P52. The Government are restrained from taking any action against the petitioner based on Ext. P50 or Ext. P51. O.P. No. 16129 of 1999.  18. This Original Petition is filed seeking to implement Ext. P1 order which is Ext. P50 in O.P. No. 11925 of 1998. Since I have already quashed that order, this prayer is liable to be rejected and I do so. The other reliefs sought in the Original Petition are highly stale and belated. Even otherwise, since Ext. P.1 is quashed, the petitioner is not entitled to any of the reliefs prayed for in the Original Petition and it is accordingly dismissed.  Petition allowed.
summary: The Kerela Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes Regulation of Issue of Community Certificates Act, 1996, Sections 11 and 30 stipulate that a member of SC/ST cannot be accused of an offence under the Act. The Petitioner was appointed as a Scheduled Tribe and given a Community Certificate by a competent authority. However, the authorities deemed the Petitioner a Scheduled Caste and ordered them to resign. The court holds that the caste certificate is valid and binding on all, including the government, and can only be revoked as per the provisions of the Act. [Paras 7 and 13]

text: Dr. (Mrs.) Sarojnei Saksena, J. - The petitioner has claimed appointment on compassionate grounds in the Haryana State Electricity Board in accordance with the instructions of the Haryana Government dated November 23, 1992 (Annexure P-1) as adopted by the respondent-Board on April 26, 1993.  2. The facts of the case as stated in the petition, briefly, are that the petitioner's father, Chetan Singh, aged about 55 years, was working as an Assistant Foreman in East Sub Division, Haryana State Electricity Board, Ambala City. On July 1, 1993, he fell down from an electric pole as a result of breakage of rope and suffered serious injuries. He was medically treated in General Hospital, Ambala City and after long treatment of his illness, he developed cancer. He remained on long leave because of his illness. He was referred to P.G.I., Chandigarh for treatment. Vide application dated August 20, 1994 (Annexure P-2) addressed to respondent-2, Chief Engineer, `OP' Z-1, Haryana State Electricity Board, Panchkula, he sought his retirement on medical grounds. Vide order dated March 20, 1995 Annexure P-3, passed by respondent No. 2 he was retired with effect from August 5, 1994, on the basis of the certificate issued by the Medical Board on August 5, 1994 (Annexure P- 4).  3. Petitioner's father expired on April 24, 1995. During his life-time, he made a request to the respondents vide his application dated April 20, 1994 (Annexure P-5) that his son-Gurdeep Singh (petitioner), who is a Matriculate, be given employment on compassionate ground in view of the Haryana Government's instructions dated 23.11.1992 as adopted by the respondent-Board on 26.4.1993. Executive Engineer, Operation Division, HSEB, Ambala City, recommended this application vide his letter dated July 7, 1994 (Annexure P-6) to the Chief Medical Officer, Ambala, for getting the petitioner's father examined from Medical Board so that his prayer for appointment of his son on compassionate grounds may be considered in view of the Haryana Government's policy dated 23.11.1992 (Annexure P-1). Accordingly, petitioner's father was examined by the Medical Board on August 5, 1994. The Medical Board vide Annexure P-4 opined that Chetan Singh was completely and permanently incapacitated for further service of any kind in the Department to which he belonged. On this, Chief Engineer, `OP' Z-1, HSEB, Panckhula (respondent No. 2) wrote to the Additional Secretary, HSEB, Panchkula, vide letter dated 5.10.1995 (Annexure P-7) to consider the application of Chetan Singh, who retired on August 5, 1994 and expired on April 24, 1995, for appointment of his son on compassionate grounds, but this prayer was declined by the respondent-Board vide letter dated 12.7.1996 (Annexure P-8) without assigning any reasons.  4. Haryana Government revised its ex gratia employment scheme, Annexure P-1, by issuing another policy, Annexure P-9, dated August 31, 1995, which was adopted by the respondent-Board on November 13, 1995 vide Annexure P-10.  5. Petitioner's mother sent another application on August 2, 1996, Annexure P-11, for giving appointment to her son (petitioner) on compassionate grounds. The petitioner also submitted such an application dated October 2, 1996, Annexure P-12, but no order was passed by the respondent thereon.  6. The petitioner's contention is that in the revised ex gratia appointment policy, Annexure P-9, there is a clause that if any Government employee is declared medically unfit/blind/incapacitated by a special medical board and retired on or before attaining the age of 55 years in the case of Class I, II, III officers/officials and 57 years in case of Class IV employees, the facility of compassionate employment would be available; but if he is declared incapacitated/blind after 55 years of age in the case of group A, B, C, employees and after 57 years in the case of group D employees, he will not be entitled to this facility.  Petitioner's contention is that this condition of age prescribed in the new ex gratia appointment policy has no nexus with the object sought to be achieved; hence, paragraph 5 of the impugned instructions, Annexure P-9, is contrary to the Punjab Civil Services Rules as applicable to Haryana State and is liable to be quashed being contrary to the mandatory provisions of these Rules. Under Rule 326 of these Rules, a Government employee other than a Class IV Government employee attains the age of superannuation at the age of 58 years and a Government employee in Class-IV attains the age of superannuation at the age of 60 years. Hence the petitioner prays that the respondents be directed to appoint him under the ex gratia employment scheme, Annexure P-1, being son of disabled Chetan Singh. It is also submitted that the fresh instructions, Annexure P-9, cannot be made applicable retrospectively and clause 5 thereof has no nexus with the object sought to be achieved except the blatant discrimination amongst such claimants. Petitioner also averred that other persons similarly situated were granted the relief of compassionate employment under the old ex gratia employment policy, Annexure P-1, while this relief was not granted to the petitioner discriminately.  7. Respondent No. 2 in its written statement admitted that Chetan Singh was an employee of the Haryana State Electricity Board; he met with an accident and suffered injuries; his medical board was held, which declared him incapacitated to render any service to the respondent-Board and on that basis, he was retired prematurely. Later on, he died. But, according to respondent No. 1, the petitioner's father attained the age of 55 years on July 1, 1993, but he was retired from service on March 20, 1995 with effect from August 5, 1994, Respondent No. 2 has further averred that the petitioner's claim for compassionate employment was rightly declined by the respondent-Board as by the time his application came for consideration, the new policy Annexure P-9, was made applicable and since the petitioner's case was not squarely covered under this new policy, his prayer was declined.  8. Petitioner's learned counsel relying on Rajesh Chander Sharma v. The State of Punjab, 1992(2) R.S.J. 737 : 1992(3) SCT 264, Tarun Chakraborty v. State of West Bengal, 1996(2) Services Cases Today 799, Smt. Sushma Gosain and others v. Union of India and others, A.I.R. 1989 S.C. 1979, Surinder Singh v. State of Haryana, 1996(1) SCT 767 : 1996(2) S.L.R. 230, and judgment given in Civil Writ Petition No. 17633 of 1995 (Surinder Singh v. State of Haryana and others) on December 20, 1996, by a Single Bench of this Court, contended that since the petitioner's father had submitted application seeking appointment of his son (petitioner) when old ex gratia employment policy, Annexure P-1, was in vogue and the respondent-Board after obtaining opinion of the special medical board that the petitioner's father was totally incapacitated from rendering any service to the Board retired him and the petitioner's case for appointment on compassionate grounds was recommended by the officers of the respondent-Board vide their letters, Annexures P-6 and P-7, hence his father's application, annexure P-5, could not have been rejected under the amended policy, Annexure P-9. The rejection order, Annexure P-8, was passed on July 12, 1996, whereas the new policy, Annexure P-9, was implemented with effect from August 31, 1995. The petitioner's case was required to be decided under the old policy, Annexure P-1. In the old policy there was no condition that if a Class I, II or III Government servant retired due to his becoming blind, incapacitated from rendering any service to the Department on or after attaining the age of 55 years, then the facility of compassionate employment to his/her dependent will not be available. This new clause has been incorporated in the new policy, Annexure P-9. This new condition in the new policy is arbitrary and discriminatory as Government employees other then Class IV employees retire at the age of 58 years and Class IV employees retire at the age of 60 years. If before the date of attaining this age, a Government employee suffers any such disability, then he would not be entitled to get relief of this policy. Hence, this condition in the new policy, Annexure P-9, has no nexus with the object for which this policy is formulated.  9. The respondents' learned counsel contended that petitioner's father's application, Annexure P-5, was under consideration and in the meantime, new policy Annexure P-9, was issued modifying the earlier policy Annexure P-1. Therefore, application, Annexure P-5, was to be considered in the light of the directions given in the new policy, Annexure P-9, When petitioner's father, Chetan Singh retired, he was more than 55 years of age; therefore, his son (petitioner) had no legal right to seek compassionate employment under the new policy, Annexure P-9. Hence, Annexure P-8, was rightly passed and the prayer was declined.  10. The respondents' learned counsel also submitted that Clause 5 of the new policy, Annexure P-9, has a rationale behind it. If a Government employee of Class I, II or III service retired at the age of 55 years, he is entitled to get full pension and other retrial benefits. Therefore, his family does not face any financial crisis. Hence the condition of age limit was incorporated in the new policy, Annexure P-9.  11. Only two points arise for consideration in this writ petition :(1) Whether application, Annexure P-5, was required to be decided in terms of the old ex gratia employment policy, annexure P-1, or in terms of the new policy, Annexure P-9; and (ii) whether clause (5) of the new policy, Annexure P-9, is arbitrary and discriminatory and has no nexus with the object for which this policy is formulated ?  12. So far as the first point is concerned, in Smt. Sushma Gosain's case (supra), the Apex Court has held :-  "....... that in all claims for appointment on compassionate grounds, there should not be any delay in appointment. The purpose of providing appointment on compassionate ground is to mitigate the hardship due to death of the bread earner in the family. Such appointment should, therefore, be provided immediately to redeem the family in distress. It is improper to keep such case pending for years. It there is no suitable post for appointment, supernumerary post should be created to accommodate the applicant." 13. A single Bench of this court in Rajesh Chander Sharma's case (supra) has also considered this aspect and held that case of the petitioner for compassionate appointment has to be decided according to the instructions which were in force on the date when he had submitted the application.  14. In Tarun Chakraborty's case (supra), a Single Bench of the Calcutta High Court has held that dependent of the deceased employee was entitled to compassionate appointment on the date of death of the deceased employee. Policy of compassionate appointment if changed later on in one time financial benefit in lieu of employment, the dependent has a legal right to get appointment as per the existing policy at the time of death of the deceased employee. If there is a policy decision in force for the benefit of the employees, deviation or departure from such policy decision attracts the wrath of Article 14 of the Constitution. Executive instructions unless issued for the benefit of the employees cannot be given retrospective effect.  15. Surinder Singh's case (supra) reported in 1996(2) S.L.R. 230 : 1996(1) SCT 767, was decided by a Division Bench of this Court. In that case also, petitioner had applied for appointment on compassionate ground in view of the ex gratia scheme. He was considered eligible to the appointment as dependent of the deceased employee and was placed at serial No. 463 in the priority list as on May 9, 1994. A post of Chowkidar-cum-Mali was available for his appointment under the ex gratia scheme, but on account of laxity on the part of the concerned authorities, no decision could be taken till the issuance of instructions dated May 8, 1995, providing that a married dependent of deceased employee would not be entitled to compassionate appointment. The Division Bench held that the instructions issued on May 8, 1995 could not be applied retrospectively so as to prejudicially affect the right of the petitioner to be considered for appointment on compassionate grounds, particularly when the post was available for him before the issuance of the new instructions.  16. In the present case, it is obvious that the petitioner's father Chetan Singh met with an accident during the course of the employment on July 1, 1993, which resulted in seriously injuring him and later on because of these injuries he was incapacitated to render any service to the respondent- Board, On April 20, 1994, he made application (Annexure P-5) to the Sub- Divisional Officer, Operation Sub Division (East), H.S.E.B., Ambala City, that due to his incurable disease he wants retirement on medical grounds; after his retirement there will be no source of income in his family; therefore, he requested that his son-Gurdeep Singh (petitioner) may be given employment in the Haryana State Electricity Board on compassionate grounds in view of Haryana Government's instructions dated 23.11.1992 adopted by the H.S.E.B. on 26.4.1993. In pursuance of letter dated 7.7.1994 (Annexure P-6) when this application was under consideration, Chetan Singh was medically examined by a special medical board constituted by the Chief Medical Officer, Ambala, on August 5, 1994, and vide order dated March 20, 1995 (Annexure P-3) passed by respondent No. 2, Chetan Singh was retired from service with effect from August 5, 1994. Chetan Singh's application, Annexure P-5, was considered and recommended by the Chief Engineer, `OP' Z-1, Panchkula, vide letter dated 5.10.1995 (Annexure P-7), but this prayer was declined by the respondent-Board vide order dated July 12, 1996 (Annexure P-8). In the letter, Annexure P-8, there is no reference to the new policy, annexure P-9. It is completely a non-speaking order showing total non-application of mind.  17. In view of the aforementioned authorities, Chetan Singh's application for appointment of his son (petitioner) on compassionate grounds submitted on April 20, 1994, should have been considered immediately in compliance of the Government's instructions, Annexure P-1. In compliance of letter, Annexure P- 6, he was examined by the medical board on August 5, 1994, and on having been declared invalid/disabled to perform duties, he was retired from service with effect from August 5, 1994, vide order dated March 20, 1995 (Annexure P-3), but till then, his application (Annexure P-5) was not decided by the officers/officials of the respondent-Board. If Chetan Singh's application had been considered by the officials of the respondent-Board in view of the recommendatory letter (Annexure P-7), the petitioner would have been appointed by the respondent-Board on compassionate grounds in pursuance of the policy (Annexure P-1). Hence, in my considered view, the application (Annexure P-5) filed by the petitioner's father before issuance of the new ex gratia employment policy, Annexure P-9, was required to be considered under the old policy (Annexure P-1). For deciding this application, the modified policy (Annexure P-9) cannot be applied retrospectively.  18. Since the writ petition is being allowed while deciding point No. 1, it is not necessary to decide point No. 2.  19. For the reasons mentioned above, the writ petition is allowed, the respondents are directed to consider the petitioner's case for his appointment on compassionate grounds and pass a speaking order within two months from the date of submission of certified copy of this order. The parties are left to bear their own costs.  Petition allowed.
summary: Constitution of India, Articles 21 and 14 - Compassionate appointment - Permanent disability - Appointments for dependents of disabled/blind/deceased employees - Haryana Government's instructions as of 31.8.1995 state that no appointment will be given if the employee dies or becomes disabled/blind after the age of 55 - Petitioner's case recommended for appointment under the instructions of 23.12.1992 - Court directs petitioner's case must be considered under the instructions applicable at the relevant time, and subsequent instructions cannot be applied to him since his case has already been recommended - Respondent ordered to consider the case and give a speaking order. [Paras 16 to 19]

text: Viney Mittal, J. - Making a grievance against the order dated July 8, 2002 (Annexure P.6) passed by the Director of Secondary Education, Haryana respondent No. 2 and the order dated July 31, 2002 (Annexure P.5) passed by the Head Master, Government High School, Kankrola respondent No. 4, the petitioner Gopi Chand has approached this Court through the present petition under Articles 226/227 of the Constitution of India. The prayer made in the petition is for the issuance of a writ in the nature of Certiorari for quashing the aforesaid orders which have been appended as Annexures P.6 and P.5 respectively.  2. Facts :  The petitioner is an ex-serviceman. Vide order dated August 25, 1994 he was appointed by the District Education Officer, Gurgaon respondent No. 3 as Social Studies Master on adhoc basis through Zila Sainik Board, Gurgaon against a vacancy meant for ex-serviceman. Accordingly, the petitioner joined his duties with effect from September 1, 1994. A copy of the appointment letter issued to the petitioner has been appended as Annexure P.2 with the petition. It was stipulated in the petition that the services of the petitioner were liable to be continued till the end of "Current Academic Session", namely, 1994-95 or till the regular candidate selected through the Subordinate Selection Board Haryana/Departmental Selection Committee/Promotee candidate was available. After the aforesaid academic session was over the services of the petitioner was sought to be dispensed with. The petitioner and some other similarly situated incumbents approached this Court through Civil Writ Petition No. 3997 of 1995. A direction was sought against the respondents to permit them to continue in service till their services were replaced by the regularly selected candidates. Vide judgment dated May 31, 1995 a Division Bench of this Court directed the respondents' department to permit the petitioners to continue in service and till the time they were replaced by regular incumbents or their posts were abolished or till anyone of them was involved in disciplinary proceedings. A copy of the aforesaid judgment dated May 31, 1995 has been appended as Annexure P.3 with the petition. The petitioner maintains that thereafter an advertisement for regular selection was made but no steps to fill the vacancies were taken by the department with the result that the petitioner continued to serve on the aforesaid posts. On July 31, 2002, the petitioner received a communication from the Head Master of the Government High School, Kankrola respondent No. 4 informing the petitioner that since he had attained 55 years of age and was working on adhoc basis, therefore, he was relieved of his duties on the evening of the aforesaid date i.e. July 31, 2002. It was informed by the Head Master that the Director Secondary Education, Haryana had issued order dated July 8, 2002 to the District Education Officer, Gurgaon in this regard. A copy of the aforesaid communication received by the petitioner from the Head Master is appended as Annexure P.5 with the petition. The petitioner has also appended the copy of the order dated July 8, 2002 issued by the Director Secondary Education, Haryana respondent No. 2 to District Education Officer, Gurgaon respondent No. 3 as Annexure P.6 with the petition.  The orders Annexures P.5 and P.6 have been challenged by the petitioner on various grounds. It is stated by the petitioner that no notice or opportunity of hearing was ever provided to the petitioner before passing the aforesaid orders Annexures P.5 and P.6. A further grievance is made that the petitioner had been working in the department of the respondent Government since September 1, 1994 and, therefore, he was entitled to continue in service till the age of superannuation. It was further maintained by the petitioner that all his ACRs from 1994-95 till 2001-02 were good and, therefore, there was no cause to retire the petitioner on attaining the age of 55 years.  3. Upon a notice, the respondents have put in appearance. A joint written statement has been filed by the respondents No. 1 to 4. Passing of the orders Annexures P.5 and P.6 has been defended. The defence put up by the respondents is that since the petitioner was working on adhoc basis, therefore, there was no provision for the grant of extension to adhoc employees beyond the age of 55 years which was only available to regular Government employees. On that basis, it is maintained by the respondents that he was rightly relieved from service vide order dated July 8, 2002 (Annexure P.6). The respondents have further maintained that the provisions of Rule 3.26 of the Punjab Civil Services Rules, Volume I Part I (hereinafter referred to as the Rules) are not applicable to the adhoc employees.  4. We have heard Shri Ravi Verma, the learned counsel for the petitioner and Shri Raghubir Chaudhary, the learned Senior Deputy Advocate General, Haryana for the respondents and with their assistance have also gone through the record.  5. Shri Ravi Verma, the learned counsel for the petitioner has submitted that the petitioner had joined the service of the respondents department with effect from September 1, 1994 in pursuance to the appointment order Annexure P.2. Subsequently, in view of the directions dated May 31, 1995, the petitioner was to continue in service till the decision of a regular incumbent or till an action was taken against him for some disciplinary proceedings or still the post in question was abolished. According to Shri Verma, none of these three eventualities had happened and, therefore, the petitioner was rightly continuing in service. According to Shri Verma, the retirement age as provided in Rule 3.26 of the Rules (as applicable to the Haryana) provides that every government employee shall retire from service on the afternoon of the last day of the month in which he attains the age of fifty-eight years. On that basis, it is maintained by Shri Verma that the petitioner was also entitled to serve till he had attained the age of fifty-eight years. According to Shri Verma, the only eventuality envisaged under the Rules in which a person could be retired at the age of 55 years was when "the appointing authority was of the opinion that it is in the public interest so to do". Since no such opinion had been expressed by the appointing authority/any competent authority, therefore, the services of the petitioner could not have been dispensed with on his attaining the age of 55 years.  6. On the other hand, Shri Raghubir Chaudhary, the learned Senior Deputy Advocate General, Haryana has submitted that the petitioner was admittedly an adhoc employee and, therefore, there was no provision regarding the grant of extension to adhoc employees in terms of the Rules. On that basis, it is maintained by Shri Raghubir Chaudhary that there was a criteria for granting the extension of service to employees beyond the age of 55 years but the aforesaid criteria was not applicable in the adhoc employees such as the petitioner. Thus, Shri Chaudhary has submitted that the claim made by the petitioner was not supported under the Rules.  7. We have given our thoughtful consideration to the entire matter and in our opinion, the present petition deserves to succeed.  8. It is not in dispute that the petitioner has been in continuous service with effect from September 1, 1994. Although he was appointed in terms of the appointment order Annexure P.2 but subsequently because of the directions issued by this Court vide judgment dated May 31, 1995 his services could only be terminated on his replacement by regular incumbents or abolition of the post or in case of his involvement in disciplinary proceedings. Since the services of the petitioner have not been dispensed with in any manner on account of the aforesaid eventualities therefore, he was to continue in service till the date of superannuation meant for regular government employees.  9. We have noticed that under the provisions of Rule 3.26 of the Rules, every Government employee shall retire from service on the afternoon of the last day of the month in which he attains the age of fifty-eight years. Under the provisions of clause (d) of the aforesaid Rule 3.26, an appointing authority has the discretion to retire a government employee at the age of 55 years by serving a notice of not less than three months to him, if it is of the opinion that it is in the public interest, to do so. Thus, we find that the normal tenure of an employee shall be upto to the date of his attaining 58 years of age. However, a discretion has been provided to the appointing authority to curtail the aforesaid period if the aforesaid appointing authority was of the opinion that it was in public interest to do so. In such a situation, the employee could be retired at the age of 55 years by giving him a notice of not less than three months. Even if we accept the stand adopted by the respondents that the Rules are not applicable to the case of an adhoc employee. Still, the normal Rule would be to treat an adhoc employee at par with a regular Government employee as far as the date of superannuation is concerned.  10. Nothing has been pointed out by Shri Chaudhary that the appointing authority of the petitioner had taken any decision under clause (d) of Rule 3.26 of the Rules to the effect that it was not in public interest to retain the petitioner beyond the age of 55 years. In the absence of any such decision the petitioner is entitled to continue till the age of superannuation which is the date on which he attains the age of fifty-eight years.  11. In this view of the matter, we do not find that the action of the respondents in retiring the petitioner at the age of 55 years was supported by any rule or was in any manner justified. Accordingly, we quash the order dated July 8, 2002 (Annexure P.6) passed by respondent No. 2 and the second order dated July 31, 2002 (Annexure P.5) passed by respondent No. 4 and declare that the petitioner would be entitled to continue in the service of the Government till he attains the age of 58 years. Of course, the respondents would be at liberty to dispense with the services of the petitioner earlier also in terms of the judgment dated May 31, 1995 passed by a Division Bench of this Court earlier, in case any of aforesaid eventuality arises.  There shall be no order as to costs.  Petition allowed.
summary: In accordance with Constitution of India, Articles 14 & 16 and Punjab Civil Services Rules, Vol. I, Part I, Rule 3.26(d), the appointing authority holds the power to retire a Government employee at the age of 55 years after a notice of no less than three months, if it believes it is in public interest. Adhoc employees are typically treated as regular Government employees in terms of their superannuation date. There is no indication of how it was not in the public interest to keep the petitioner beyond the age of 55 years. As a result, the petitioner is authorized to continue in service until he reaches the age of 58 years. [Paras 9 & 10]

text: G.C. Garg, J. - This order will dispose of Civil Writ Petition Nos. 1694 and 20583 of 1992, the point involved being the same. The facts hereinafter mentioned have been taken from Civil Writ Petition 1964 of 1992.  2. The petitioner herein seeks migration in the 2nd Year of Bachelor of Dental Science from Dental College situated outside the State of Punjab to Dental College and Hospital, Amritsar affiliated to the Guru Nanak Dev University, Amritsar.  3. The petitioner who is undergoing her studies in Dental Course in Bapuji Dental College, Dawangiri (Karnataka), applies for migration to Punjab Government Dental College and Hospital, Amritsar, a college affiliated to Guru Nanak Dev University, Amritsar. Admission in Bapuji Dental College, Dewangiri is not regulated on the basis of entrance test as is the case in Punjab Government Dental College and Hospital, Amritsar. Students, who had applied for migration to Dental Colleges in the State of Punjab before February 15, 1991 and were eligible, were being permitted to migrate irrespective of the fact, whether they got admission in the Dental/Medical Colleges on the basis of entrance test or otherwise. The situation for migration in the Colleges affiliated to Punjabi University continues to be the same, but Guru Nanak Dev University amended its regulations to provide that in the Colleges where the students are admitted on the basis of entrance test, migration be allowed to other students in these colleges, if otherwise eligible, if the student was admitted to that college on the basis of an entrance test and had secured at least the percentage of marks in the entrance test equivalent to that secured by the last candidate admitted to the course.  4. The petitioner applied for migration on October 19, 1991 and her request is not being considered because of change in the regulations of Guru Nanak Dev University though the Director, Research Medical Education, Punjab recommended to the Principal, Dental College, Amritsar vide letter, Annexure P-3, to approach Guru Nanak Dev University for allowing migration in relaxation of conditions before admitting the students. Seven seats are, admittedly, lying vacant in the Dental College, Amritsar where the petitioner and others seek migration and can be accommodated.  5. Challenge to the validity of the Regulation amended by Guru Nanak Dev University being on the ground that there was no rationale behind it and is hit by the provisions of Articles 14 and 15 of the Constitution of India is not sustainable. Learned counsel for the petitioner further contended that once a student is eligible to be admitted to a Dental College and has been so admitted, Regulations could not be made by the University so as to debar the students of other colleges to migrate to college affiliated to it on the ground that the admission to that college was not on the basis of entrance test.  6. Guru Nanak Dev University is a statutory body incorporated under an Act of State Legislature. It is free to regulate its own affairs and frame regulations. Similarly, Punjabi University, Patiala is entitled to frame its own Regulations relating to admission and migration to Colleges affiliated to it. Merely because the two Government Dental Medical Colleges situated in Amritsar and Patiala are governed by different set of Regulations, one of Punjabi University and the other of Guru Nanak Dev University is not enough to sustain the claim of the petitioner seeking annulment of the Regulations providing that only those students could be allowed to migrate who had been admitted in the other Colleges on the basis of entrance test. Dental College at Patiala is affiliated to Punjabi University and Dental College at Amritsar is affiliated to Guru Nanak Dev University though admissions to the two Colleges are controlled by the State Punjab. It cannot be said as a matter of law that Regulations relating to admission and migration to a particular course should be same either throughout the country or at least in the Universities situated in a particular State. Each University, as noticed earlier, is a statutory body and can have its own Regulations. Admission to these Colleges is not made by the Universities but by the Government on the basis of entrance test which the Universities in rotation conduct on behalf of the State Government. Thus, simply because the students are admitted on the basis of a joint entrance test, it cannot logically be concluded that Regulations for migration should be the same in the two Universities.  7. Recognition granted by the All India Dental/Medical Council to Bapuji Dental College, Dewangiri again, in no way, helps the petitioner. All India Medical Council operates in a different field whereas the University which is the examining body, governed by its Regulations, has a different function to discharge. Mere grant of recognition to a Dental College by the All India Medical Council cannot clothe the students of one College with a right to seek migration to another College of their choice. Its functions are advisory. The contention of the learned counsel, if accepted, would mean that regulations of all the Universities in the country imparting medical education should be the same not only regarding migration but in other respects also.  8. Again, relief cannot be granted to the petitioner only on the ground that Punjabi University is still allowing migration to students like the petitioner but Guru Nanak Dev University is not allowing migration because of the amended Regulation noticed above. The two Universities are independent of each other and can frame their own Regulations depending upon their requirements. Regulations thus, cannot be said to be violative of Articles 14 and 15 of the Constitution of India, only on the ground that all three Universities in the State do not have a uniform criterion for migration to Colleges affiliated to them.  9. The other challenge of learned counsel for the petitioner is about retrospective amendment of the Regulation. The Regulation as amended is prospective in nature. Simply because the petitioner got admission in the Dental College in the year 1990 and the amendment has been made by Guru Nanak Dev University in its Regulations in the year 1991, it cannot be said that it is retrospective. The petitioner applied for migration in October, 1991 and the Regulation had already been amended in February, 1991.  10. Migration is not a right, it is rather a concession to a student to migrate from one college to another or from one university to another, if his case is covered by the Regulations framed by the University. Each University is entitled to maintain is own standard and frame its own Regulations in that behalf. Though I have upheld the validity of the Regulation and that the petitioner is not entitled to any relief on that basis, yet there is another aspect of the matter. In the case of Devinder Pal Singh, application for seeking migration was submitted on May 6, 1991, i.e. after February 15, 1991. He was denied migration by the University. He approached this Court by way of Civil Writ Petition No. 7999 of 1991 and Guru Nanak Dev University without waiting for the verdict of this Court, permitted him to migrate from a College affiliated to Mysore University, to Dental College, Amritsar affiliated to it. Learned counsel for the respondents could not dispute this fact, but stated that migration was allowed to him by mistake and by wrongly construing the interim order of this Court.  11. Medical education is imparted by spending huge public funds. Should the available seats be permitted to go abegging. It is not a case where the University is going to create extra seats for these students but it is a case where the seats are already in existence and are lying vacant. No body would gain if these seats are allowed to remain vacant. Out of the seven petitioners, in the two petitions, seeking migration, six are girl students from whom special provision has been made in Article 15 of the Constitution of India. Keeping in view the fact that seats are lying vacant and Guru Nanak Dev University has already allowed such a migration earlier in the case of Devinder Pal Singh, a candidate similarly situated, a factor which has weighed with me in concluding that the petitioners are entitled to some relief in equity. After effecting migrations under the Regulations, as amended, if some seats still remain vacant, then these should not be permitted to go waste. Under these circumstances, it would be appropriate to direct the University to consider the cases of the petitioners and other similarly situated students for migration on their own merits against the available seats, as expeditiously as possible.  12. In the matter of admission to Medical Colleges, the apex Court has also indicated on several occasions that the seats should not be permitted to remain vacant. The same view was taken by this Court in Miss Sumedha Kalia v. State of Haryana, 1990(4) SLR 122.  13. Dismissal of Civil Writ Petition No. 14543 of 1991 in limine by a Division Bench of this Court on January 15, 1992, in no way helps learned counsel for the respondents, as that was a case where application for migration was moved on February 12, 1991 and the only challenge was to the validity of Regulations.  14. For the reasons aforesaid, I direct the respondent-University to consider the cases of the petitioners and other similarly situated students seeking migration to Govt. Dental College, Amritsar on their own merits against the available seats, as expeditiously as possible. The writ petitions are disposed of in the above terms and directions. This order will, however, be not taken as a precedent as the direction has been issued in the peculiar facts of this case. The parties shall, however, bear their own costs.  Petition allowed.
summary: A. The Medical Council of India's recognition of a college does not grant students the right to seek migration to another college of their choice. Amendment in the regulations allows only admitted students who passed the entrance test held by the university in rotation to be allowed migration. Petitioner is not entitled to migration. [Paras 6 and 7] B. Universities have the independence to frame their own regulations depending on their own requirements, and regulations cannot be deemed violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. [Para 8] C. Amendment of regulations of the University cannot be considered retrospective only because a student seeking migration from an outside college had already taken admission. The petitioner applied for migration after the amendment. Amendment for him is not in any manner retrospective. [Para 9] D. Migration is a concession, and each university is entitled to maintain its own standard. The university should consider all cases on their own merits keeping in view the available seats, and should not go to waste. Petitioners being girls are on better footing than that of the boy student for migration as they are protected under Article 15 of the Constitution. The university is directed to consider their cases along with others on their own merits to the extent of availability of seats. [Paras 10, 11 and 13]

text: G.S. Singhvi, J. - Shri S.P. Gupta and four others sought this Court's intervention by filing Civil Writ Petition No. 15652 of 1992 for quashing the letter dated September 6, 1990 written by the Home Secretary, Chandigarh Administration to the Secretary, House Allotment Committee to take action for eviction of those Journalists/Press Correspondents who had attained the age of 60 years or who were transferred outside Chandigarh. They also prayed for quashing orders passed by the House Allotment Committee for cancellation of allotments of houses made to them and the notices issued by the Sub Divisional Magistrate, Chandigarh-cum-Estate Officer under the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971 (hereinafter referred to as the Act). By an order dated September 6, 1993, a Division Bench dismissed the Writ Petition on the ground that the Journalists/Press Correspondents are not entitled to allotment of residential houses under the Government Residences (Chandigarh Administration Pool) Allotment Rules, 1972 (hereinafter referred to as 1972 Rules). While doing so, the Division Bench referred to the decision taken in the meeting held on July 5, 1968 under the Chairmanship of the then Chief Commissioner, Chandigarh, Shri M.S. Randhawa as well as 1972 Rules. Some of the observations made in the order dated September 6, 1993, are extracted below :-  "It will be seen that as per this decision the quota of houses for Press Correspondents had been fixed at 33, a number which has since been exceeded by almost three times, inasmuch as according to the affidavit of the Secretary, House Allotment Committee, Chandigarh, the number of houses already allotted to Journalists or Press Correspondents is 94. There is no material on record to show how, why and when any decision was taken raising the limit of the number of houses to be allotted to Journalists or Press Correspondents to this figure. To the pointed query put to the Standing Counsel for the Chandigarh Administration, in this behalf, no answer was forthcoming. It was the plea of the petitioners that allotment of Government Residential Houses to Journalists or Press Correspondents was governed by the provisions of Government Residences (Chandigarh Administration Pool) Allotment Rules, 1972 (hereinafter referred to as the "Allotment Rules") while the Standing Counsel for the Chandigarh Administration, Mr. Ashok Aggarwal, sought to trace the exercise of the power of allotment of such houses to Journalists or Press Correspondents, to rule 26 thereof. Neither of these contentions can, however, stand scrutiny. A plain reading of the allotment rules would show that they deal with and are concerned merely with the allotment of Government Residential Accommodation to government servants. Journalists or Press Correspondents clearly do not come within their ambit. As regards to rule 26 of the Allotment Rules, this reads as under :- "Relaxation of Rules - S.R. 317 - A.M. 26 - The Chief Commissioner may, for reasons to be recorded in writing, relax all or any of the provisions of these rules in the case of any Government servant or residence or class of Government servants or types of residence." Here too, it will be seen that the power of relaxation contained therein is only concerning and with regard to Government servants and residences for them. Journalists and Press Correspondents cannot possibly be brought thereunder. Such being the situation, there can be no escape from the conclusion that the allotment of Government Residential Accommodation to Journalists or Press Correspondents is not a matter covered either by the allotment rules or even by the power of relaxation contained in rule 26 thereof. In other words, there are no rules, regulations or guidelines governing such allotment. Such being the settled position in law and the circumstances being as narrated, no other conclusion is possible except that the allotment of government residential accommodation, by the Chandigarh Administration, to Journalists and Press Correspondents has been an exercise of unbridled power and discretion and cannot, therefore, be sustained. Journalists and Press Correspondents are not entitled to allotment of government residential accommodation and, consequently, it follows that all such allotments made, lack legal sanction and therefore, no further allotment be made to Journalists or Press Correspondents. The Chandigarh Administration would, no doubt, now take all the necessary consequential action in the matter. In making this order, we are conscious of the fact that persons to be adversely affected by it, namely, Journalists and Press correspondents, who have been allotted government residential accommodation, are not before us. The issue raised being of general public importance could not, in our opinion, brook undue delay, which would inevitably have occurred if all the 90 odd allottees were to have been personally served. In order, however, to get their view point, in a representative capacity, we impleaded the Press Club of Chandigarh, which unfortunately came forth with no such view. Be that as it may, we leave it open to any aggrieved allottees to seek review of our order, if they can show any legal infirmity in it, warranting a different view being taken. In the context of what has been held, no occasion survives to grant to the petitioners the relief claimed. At any rate, both the petitioners have vacated the houses allotted to them and neither of them appeared later either in person or through counsel to press their claim. Mr. R.S. Surjewala, counsel for the petitioner Shri S.P. Gupta did appear but stated that he had no instructions. Be that as it may, the challenge of the petitioner Shri S.P. Gupta to the policy decision of the Chandigarh Administration regarding cancellation of the allotment of the allottees on attaining the age of 60 years or being transferred out of Chandigarh, stands rendered infructuous by the very entitlement of Journalists and Press Correspondents to allotment of government residential accommodation being held to be contrary to law. Similarly, Waryam Singh Dhotian, the other petitioner cannot now be heard to complain of allotment not being made in his favour. As regards penal rent charged from him, he having continued in occupation beyond the permissible period, clearly rendered himself liable to it." 2. Several issues relating to allotment of residential houses in Chandigarh were considered by a Full Bench of this Court while deciding Civil Writ Petition No. 16863 of 1994 which was registered on suo motu cognizance taken by the Court. By a detailed judgment dated June 1, 1995, the Full Bench gave directions to the Administration to make allotments in terms of directions given by the Court. The conclusions recorded by the Full Bench are extracted below :-  "I) The judgment in K.G. Verma's case (CWP No. 12688 of 1993 decided on February 4, 1994) is overruled and it is held that allotment of residential accommodation in Chandigarh is to be made under rule 5 of the Rules and only in exceptional cases out-of-turn under Rule 26; II) In making allotments to the State Government employees the recommendation or concurrence of the respective State Government would not be required; III) Only eligible persons, as defined in Rule (2)(e), would be given government accommodation but those who are already occupying such accommodation will not be disturbed with the exception of Journalists and Press Correspondents who are covered by S.P. Gupta's case (supra); IV) Rule 7 is struck down as being arbitrary; (V) The allotment in favour of Mr. A.R. Talwar is quashed and a direction is issued that he will vacate H. No. 11, Sector 7 Chandigarh within three months but in the light of his security considerations, he is allowed allotment of a type 6 house instead of category 8 which is his actual entitlement; VI) Some guidelines be framed to ensure that the budget for maintenance of government accommodations in Chandigarh is spent fairly amongst the various types of accommodation covering different strates of the population; VII) Rule 3-A of the Rules is to be strictly enforced as it remains on the statute book; VIII) No allotment be made on the basis of instructions in favour of a government employee who is a member of the family of a superannuated government servant occupying a government accommodation; IX) Steps be taken to ascertain and if necessary, to recover government accommodation that has been sub-let by the allottees and to ensure that residential accommodation is not used for any other purpose; X) The directions of the Supreme Court in the All India Judges' case be strictly complied with within the time frame fixed by the Court; XI) High Court Judges who have not been allotted government residential accommodation so far be provided such accommodation on a priority basis." 3. Shri Ramesh Gautam and others, Journalists/Press Correspondents as also Shri B.R. Jatley, whose Writ Petition (Civil Writ Petition No. 75 of 1996) is being disposed of by this order, who were likely to be affected by the order of the Division Bench dated September 6, 1993 filed petitions for Special Leave to Appeal questioning the correctness of the directions given by the High Court in S.P. Gupta's case. These appeals were disposed of by the Supreme Court on May 7, 1996 i.e. the day on which the Petition for Special Leave to Appeal filed by the Chandigarh Administration against the order of Full Bench was disposed of. Their Lordships reversed the order of the Division Bench on the ground of violation of principles of natural justice and remitted the case to the High Court for deciding the larger question, whether the Administration was justified in allotting Government residential quarters to the Journalists/Press Correspondents on the basis of discretionary quota. The relevant portion of the order of the Apex Court and the directions given by the Apex Court are reproduced below :-  "We are, therefore, of the opinion that the order passed by the Division Bench of the High Court in S.P. Gupta's case which we have extracted earlier was clearly in violation of the principles of natural justice. Reserving to the Journalists the right to seek review of the order, after expressing strongly against the allotment of quarters to them, would hardly serve the principles of natural justice. The Full Bench of the High Court has merely endorsed the view of the Division Bench and interpreted it to mean that the allottees are liable to be evicted forthwith from the premises occupied by them. If the main order passed by the Division Bench suffers from the infirmity pointed out by us, the decision of the Full Bench would also suffer from the same infirmity. We, therefore, set aside the decision of the Full Bench also in this behalf. We may mention that the learned Solicitor General appearing on behalf of the Chandigarh Administration stated before us that no fresh allotments have since been made or shall be made hereafter to Journalists or Press Correspondents. We any also state that we have, in Civil Appeals arising out of S.L.P. (Civil No. 16919, 18950-18951 and 23225/95) disposed of today, finalised the revised rules for allotment of Government quarters and those rules do not provide for allotment of Government residential quarters to Journalists. Therefore, the question of any further allotment to Journalists from Government residential quarters is ruled out. Secondly, the rules regarding eviction from Government residential accommodation of the Journalists attaining the age of sixty years has not been set aside since both the Division Bench and the Full Bench went into the larger question regarding allotment of Government residence to Journalists/Press Correspondents. That rule stands and can be implemented unless there is any stay in that behalf from any court. So far as the appellant B.R. Jaitely is concerned, we are told that he has not paid the occupation charges which exceed a lakh and he has also not vacated the quarters, even on attaining the age of sixty years. It will, therefore, be open to the Administration to proceed to evict him from the quarter unless he pays up the entire dues within two weeks from today and unless there is any order in his favour to continue in occupation even after attaining the age of sixty years. On the larger question whether the Administration was justified in allotting Government residential quarters to Journalists/Press Correspondents on the basis of a discretionary quota, the High Court may consider the same de novo after issuing a public notice in two local newspapers, one in English and the other in the regional language and thereafter proceed to consider whether the existing Journalists allottees should be allowed to continue in occupation upto or beyond the age of sixty years as per the policy and if any Journalist questions the policy, to consider whether the policy, is supportable in law. We must make it clear that for the present since there is no interim order which has been brought to our notice prohibiting eviction after the Journalists have completed the age of sixty years, it would be open to the Administration to proceed to enforce that policy unless precluded from doing so. 4. After taking on record the list produced by the respondents, the Court, on July 22, 1997, directed the publication of notices in accordance with the directions given by the Supreme Court.  6. In response to these notices, Shri Ramesh Gautam and 52 others allottees/Journalists filed a joint written statement which was taken on record by an order dated September 10, 1997 passed in Civil Miscellaneous No. 20304 of 1997. Written statements filed by Shri Jagmohan Futela, Miss Reeta Sharma, Shri U.K. Bhanot and Shri P.P.S. Gill were also taken on record by separate orders passed in Civil Miscellaneous Nos. 21555, 21300, 11308 and 21313-14 of 1997. Reply filed on behalf of Chandigarh Administration to the Written Statement of Shri Ramesh Gautam and others was also taken on record.  7. Arguments in these cases were heard and the order was reserved on September 24, 1997. However, before the order could be pronounced, Shri P.C. Punnen claiming himself to be a public spirited person filed Civil Miscellaneous Nos. 4161-62 for bringing to the notice of the Court that a large number of Journalists/Press Correspondents were illegally occupying Government houses without paying rent. On October 24, 1997, his application was ordered to be listed alongwith the record of the main case. Due to non-constitution/non- sitting of the Bench, the case could not be taken up for consideration of his application for the next about nine months. When it was finally taken up for consideration, neither Shri Punnen nor anyone on his behalf appeared. Counsel appearing for Shri Ramesh Gautam and others and counsel for the Administration stated that they do not have anything to add in the context of the application of Shri Punnen.  ARGUMENTS.  8. Shri S.P. Jain, learned Senior Counsel appearing for Shri Ramesh Gautam and others Journalists/Press Correspondents strenuously urged that the allotments made prior to September 6, 1993 i.e. the date on which the writ petition filed by S.P.
