By not writing the report in accordance with the Government instructions and not disclosing the material on the basis of which the adverse report was formed, the Government servant is denied the opportunity of representation against the same and, therefore, such reports have got no value as the same have been recorded in complete contravention of the mandatory provisions of the instructions, as also the principles of natural justice. It is very unjust, unfair and arbitrary to condemn the Government servant and doubt his integrity without giving the reasons and the material as required by the instructions, So adverse report for the year 1984-85 is liable to be expunged.  15. The petitioner also challenged the validity of the Government instructions which permit the Government to retire a Government servant even on the basis of a remote or solitary report concerning his integrity. The power to compulsorily retire the Government servant is to be exercised in public interest. It is incumbent that for assessing whether the Government servant should be allowed to continue in service, the Government has to come to the conclusion that the officer is a dead wood. The power is intended to be exercised only to chop off the dead wood. For this purpose it is necessary that the entire service record of the officer should be reviewed. Precisely for this reason the instructions of the Haryana Government provide that if 70% of the reports of the officer are good, he should be allowed to continue beyond 55 years of age. But an exception has been made in the case of report concerning the integrity of the Government servant. According to the instructions, even a remote or a solitary report doubting the integrity of the Government servant is enough to retire him from service. Recently, the Supreme Court in Hans Raj v. State of Punjab, A.I.R. 1985 S.C. 69 has laid down that an officer cannot be compulsorily retired on the basis of stray entry. In the present case, the overall record of service of the petitioner is satisfactory. There is only one stray entry on the basis of which the petitioner had been compulsorily retired. In my opinion, reliance on such an entry is not enough to retire the Government servant prematurely. In my opinion, these instructions run contrary to the statutory rules according to which on a review of the record, the Government has to come to the conclusion that it would be in the public interest to retire the Government servant. This opinion can be formed only if the entire record of service of the Government servant is reviewed. This opinion can be formed only if the entire record of service of the Government servant is reviewed. The servant record in the form of ACRs contains the views of different officers under which the Government servant had the opportunity to work and their respective views. The Government servant cannot be retired merely on the basis of a solitary or remote report affecting his integrity, because such an action will be just arbitrary.  16. The instructions do not provide that stale or stray entries should not be used against Government servant. A Division Bench of this Court in 1989(3) SLJ 110(SN), J.V. Gupta and Amarjeet Chaudhary, JJ., held that the Government servant cannot be allowed to retire on the basis of an adverse report regarding his integrity if such a report was recorded ten years ago. Amarjeet Chaudhary, J., took the same view in 1989(5) SLR 343. So, in my view the instructions are too widely worded and an officer cannot be retired just on the basis of a solitary remote report regarding his integrity. Retirement on the basis of such a report would amount to removal from service and, therefore, these instructions would clearly be violative of the provisions of Article 311(2) of the Constitution as these instructions provide for compulsory retirement without any enquiry. I am further of the view that these instructions are also arbitrary, unfair, unreasonable, capricious and discriminatory. The main instructions provide for a review of the entire service record of the Government servant, and if on such a review it is found that 70% reports of his are good, he shall not be retired. On the other hand, if there is any adverse report regarding the integrity of the Government servant, one such single instance is enough to retire the Government servant. In my opinion, the instructions are arbitrary and discriminatory and, therefore, violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution of India.  17. In the present case, the petitioner submitted representation against the adverse report but the said representation was rejected by three words order i.e. "considered and rejected". In a case where the competent authority considers a representation against the integrity report, it is not sufficient to dispose of the representation by a non-speaking order. This Court in Lalit Kumar Gupta v. State of Haryana, 1988(5) S.L.R. 9 agreed with the judgment of the Andhra Pradesh High Court in M.S. Sharma v. State of Andhra Pradesh, 1981(3) S.L.R. 760, disapproved such practice and quashed the order disposing the representation by a non-speaking order. In the present case also, the order dated 11.4.1986 shows that the representation against the adverse report was disposed of by a non-speaking order. For this reason also, the report for the period from 1984-85 cannot be taken into consideration for compulsorily retiring the petitioner from service. A Division Bench of this Court in 1989(1) Northern Law Reporter 328 has taken the view that if the overall grading of the Government servant's performance is average, describing the entry of such an officer as doubtful integrity is not enough for compulsorily retiring him from service. As already discussed, in the present case, the entire service record of the petitioner is very good except a stray entry in the report for the year 1984-85. So, in my view, the petitioner could not be compulsorily retired on the basis of the said report. In this case, the service record of the petitioner shows that the earned Very Good reports besides a number of appreciation letters, awards and merit certificates etc. but the reviewing authority did not take into account all this. The review in the present case seems to be on extraneous consideration, and for that reason also the impugned order of compulsory retirement is bad in law.  18. The power of compulsory retirement is an extraordinary power conferred on the Government to be exercised only sparingly in appropriate cases. The Government servant at the age of 55 years is at the crucial stage of his career. The period of service at 55-58 years is very important from the point of view of the Government servant as he has to settle his children during this period. This power should be exercised only in rare cases where it is established that the officer concerned is a deadwood and deserves to be chopped off. The power should be exercised very carefully keeping in view the principles laid down by the Supreme Court from time to time.  19. In view of the foregoing discussion, the writ petition is allowed. The impugned order is set aside. It is held that the petitioner always remained in service as Tehsildar and shall be deemed to have retired on attaining the age of 58 years. Accordingly, he shall be entitled to all arrears of pay and allowances alongwith interest @ 12% p.a. besides all retirement benefits, including leave encashment and enhanced pension, gratuity etc. The arrears of pay and allowances granted above along with interest thereon shall be paid within a month from today. No costs.  Petition allowed.
summary: A. Constitution of India, Article 311, Punjab Tehsildari Rules, 1952, Rules 25(2)(c)(i) and 25(2)(c)(a) - Petitioner represented against the adverse remarks - Order of compulsory retirement passed on the same adverse remarks during the pendency of representation - Order of compulsory retirement illegal. [Para 7] B. Punjab Tehsildari Rules, 1952, Rules 25(2)(c)(i) and 25(2)(i)(a) - Financial Commissioner recording confidential report and also disposed of appeal against the same - Financial Commissioner not competent to decide the appeal against the confidential reports recorded by him - Representation should have been placed before the higher authority i.e. Revenue Minister, for disposal. [Para 7] C. Constitution of India, Article 311(2) Punjab Tehsildari Rules, 1952, Rules 25(2)(c)(i) and 25(2)(i)(a) - Confidential report/Compulsory retirement/Doubtful integrity - Order of compulsory retirement passed on the basis of confidential reports recorded with the remarks integrity doubtful amounts to punishment from removal of service - Such report will be of no value - Remarks expunged. [Para ] D. Confidential reports/Adverse remarks/Doubtful integrity/Natural justice - Confidential reports containing remarks of doubtful integrity must be followed by reasons - Reasons for recording remarks of doubtful integrity should be disclosed to the employee - Depriving the employee of making representation against such remarks - Such report will be of no value - Remarks expunged. [Para 14] E. Constitution of India, Article 311 - Compulsory retirement/Confidential reports/Solitary adverse report - Solitary/Remote adverse report against the integrity of an employee - Such report cannot be made the basis of compulsory retirement. [Paras 15 and 16] F. Constitution of India, Article 311 (2) - Representation against the adverse remarks affecting the integrity of an employee - Representation against such remarks should be decided with a speaking order - Representation decided with non-speaking order "considered and rejected" - Order rejecting any representation not proper - Such reports cannot be made the basis of compulsory retirement. [Para 17] G. Constitution of India, Article 311 - Compulsory Retirement/Age of superannuation - Power of compulsory retirement at such stage should be exercised with full care and only in such cases where the employee is found to be dead wood. [Para 18]

text: S.S. Nijjar, J. (Oral) - The petitioner has filed this petition under Article 226 of the Constitution of India with a prayer for issuance of a writ in the nature of certiorari quashing the order dtd. 28.10.2002 (P/11) to the extent that the petitioner has been given deemed dtd. of promotion as Assistant Engineer (Civil) w.e.f. 14.12.2001 instead of 20.3.1990. The petitioner belongs to reserved category of Scheduled Caste. He was appointed as Junior Engineer on 25.3.1985 in the Punjab State Electricity Board (hereinafter referred to as the `respondent-Board'). He was due for promotion as Assistant Engineer in the year 1989. However, the respondents passed an order on 18.1.1989 that the petitioner could not be promoted as he had not passed the departmental examination. Instead one Sumesh Bansal belonging to general category was promoted as Assistant Engineer. In the order of promotion of Sumesh Bansal, condition No. 9 provided as follows :-  "9. Further the promotion of Sh. Sumesh Bansal is purely on ad hoc basis against quota of SC category as no SC candidate belonging to SC category is eligible for promotion. He is liable to be reverted without notice as soon as a candidate belonging to SC category attains eligibility". 2. The petitioner passed the necessary departmental examination on 20.3.1990. In view of condition No. 9 in the promotion order, Sumesh Bansal had to be reverted to make room for the petitioner on 20.3.1990. Petitioner brought these facts to the notice of the respondent-Board, which seemed to have fallen on deaf ears. Ultimately, Sumesh Bansal filed a civil suit for injunction on 19.5.1994 restraining the respondent-Board from reverting him to the post of Junior Engineer (Civil). The respondents filed a written statement in the civil suit and pleaded that the petitioner was entitled to be promoted. It was stated as under :-  "In reply to para No. 5 of the plaint it is submitted that the plaintiff was promoted as AE/Civil purely on ad hoc basis against the vacancy reserved for promotion to JE/Civil belonging to SC category against 14% reservation available in promoting to class I and II services due to non- passing of DAE by JE/Civil belonging to SC category at that time with the specific condition incorporated in his promotion orders that he will be reverted as soon as candidate belonging to scheduled caste category attains eligibility for promotion as JE/Civil. Now Shri Kuldeep Singh seniormost JE/Civil belonging to scheduled caste category and possessing the qualification of BE/Civil has claimed promotion as Assistant Engineer/Civil after qualifying DAE and acquiring eligibility for promotion policy. Therefore, the defendant board has initiated a proposal for promoting the scheduled caste JE/Civil as AE/Civil by reverting the plaintiff. This proposal is based on natural justice and is in line with the reservation policy and also in accordance with the conditions attached in the promotion orders of the plaintiff." 3. The civil suit filed by Sumesh Bansal was dismissed on 21.10.2000. Still the petitioner was not given promotion compelling him to move this Court by way of C.W.P. No. 6891 of 2002. The writ petition was disposed of on 3.5.2002 by directing the respondents to take a decision on the grievance of the petitioner. Consequently the respondents have now passed an order dtd. 26.9.2002 (P/10) promoting the petitioner w.e.f. 14.12.2001 instead of 20.3.1990. The respondents have filed the written statement. It has been stated that Sumesh Bansal could not be reverted due to changed circumstances. It is submitted that during the year 1989 there were 104 cadre posts of Assistant Engineers (Civil) available with the Board. On the basis of the prevalent regulations, 9% of the posts were to be filled from graduate Junior Engineers (Civil). As such 9 posts came to the share of graduate Junior Engineers and 7 posts were already held by graduate Junior Engineers. Therefore, 2 more promotions were required to be made. Out of these two posts, one post was to be filled by promotion from Engineering Subordinates belonging to Scheduled Caste category. There was 14% reservation in favour of the Scheduled Caste at the relevant time. Since the petitioner was not available, the post was offered to Sumesh Bansal.  4. The respondents have, however, categorically admitted that Sumesh Bansal was promoted purely on ad hoc basis against the post reserved for the Scheduled Caste category with clear stipulation that he will be reverted without any notice as soon as a candidate belonging to the Scheduled Caste category attains eligibility. But to justify denial of promotion to the petitioner, it is stated that before the bio-data of graduate Junior Engineers (Civil) could be called on 27.3.1990, some posts in the Cadre of Assistant Engineers (Civil) were rendered surplus, therefore, there was no necessity for considering any-body further for promotion. Also on 25.7.1991, the Board issued a policy decision whereby the promotion share of the category of graduate Junior Engineers (Civil) was reduced from 9% to 5%. Direct recruits share was also reduced by 6%. Consequently, no post was available against which the petitioner could have been promoted.  5. Replication has been filed by the petitioner. The plea taken by the respondents has been controverted.  6. Mr. R.S. Bajaj, learned counsel appearing for the petitioner has submitted that the plea taken by the respondents is only one of convenience and an effort has been made to protect the wholly illegal promotion of Sumesh Bansal. He further submitted that even if there has been amendment in the Rules, the same could not have affected the right of the petitioner which had accrued on 20.3.1990. In support of his submissions, learned counsel relied upon judgment of the Supreme Court in case of Y.V. Rangaiah and another v. J. Sreenivasa Rao and others and State of A.P. and another v. J. Sreenivasa Rao and others, AIR 1983 SC 852.  7. Mr. R.L. Sharma submits that the petitioner became eligible to be considered for promotion on 20.3.1990. There was no post available to promote the petitioner, as a number of posts had been rendered surplus on 27.3.1990. So the petitioner could not have been considered for promotion.  8. Having considered the entire matter, we are of the considered opinion that in view of condition 9 imposed in the promotion order of Sumesh Bansal, the petitioner had to be considered for promotion with effect from 20.3.1990. The respondents have admitted in the written statement that the petitioner attained eligibility for promotion on 20.3.1990. He was not promoted, as there was non-compliance with condition No. 9 contained in the promotion order of Sumesh Bansal. The respondents have not pleaded any other impediment for denying the promotion.  9. Even otherwise a perusal of relevant part of para 5 of the written statement (reproduced above) filed in the civil suit by the respondent-Board in response to the plaint of Sumesh Bansal would clearly show that claim of the petitioner was fully supported by the respondent-Board. It was categorically stated that Sumesh Bansal had been promoted purely on ad hoc basis as Assistant Engineer (Civil) against the vacancy specifically meant for Scheduled Caste Junior Engineer (Civil). This vacancy was filled by promotion of Sumesh Bansal due to non-availability of eligible Junior Engineer belonging to SC category with specific condition for his reversion as soon as Scheduled Caste employee attains eligibility for promotion. The plea taken by the respondent-Board was accepted by the Civil Court as follows :-  "After going through the evidence and the submissions of the learned counsel for the parties, I am of the view that there is no merit in the case of the plaintiff. As stated above, the plaintiff was promoted to the post of AE Civil purely on ad hoc basis against the quota of scheduled caste category because no scheduled caste candidate was eligible to that post at that time with the order that the plaintiff will be reverted without notice as soon as candidate belonging to scheduled caste category attains eligibility. The plaintiff after admitting all the terms and conditions of this promotion order joined as AE (Civil) vide letter Ex. D-1. As such now the plaintiff cannot claim this post as a matter of right. The defendant No. 2 who belongs to scheduled caste category has already cleared his departmental accounts examination in March, 1990. As such, it is he who is entitled to the post on which the plaintiff is working as per clause 9 of order Ex. D-1. The granting of injunction to the plaintiff would defeat the right of defendant No. 2 for promotion for ever. As such, to my mind no injunction as prayed for can be granted to the plaintiff." 10. Even the appeal filed by Sumesh Bansal against the judgment of Civil Court has been dismissed. We are of the opinion that the respondent-Board has acted unfairly and unreasonably by denying the due benefit of reservation to the petitioner. Having defended the right of the petitioner in the civil suit, the respondent-Board cannot now be permitted to take a contrary stand.  11. Further, any subsequent amendment in the Rules cannot take away the accrued right of the petitioner on 20.3.1990. The ratio of law laid down by the Supreme Court in the case of Y.V. Rangaiah (supra) is fully applicable to the facts of the present case. The petitioner has to be given the promotion w.e.f. 20.3.1990, the date when he became eligible for promotion, and Sumesh Bansal was permitted to continue on the post clearly reserved for the Scheduled Caste category. The plea of subsequent reduction in posts is wholly irrelevant so far as the claim of the petitioner is concerned. We are conscious that it may not now be possible to revert Sumesh Bansal, after lapse of such a long period. In that event a supernumerary post can be created for him. But this cannot be used as an excuse to deny the deserved relief to the petitioner.  12. In view of the above, we allow the writ petition and modify the order (P/11) and direct that the petitioner shall be treated to have been promoted w.e.f. 20.3.1990 on the post of Assistant Engineer (Civil). The petitioner shall be entitled to all consequential benefits such as seniority and further promotions. The arrears of salary with 9% interest shall be released to him within two months on receipt of a certified copy of this order. No costs.  Petition allowed.
summary: A. Constitution of India, Article 226 - Promotion - Claim from retrospective date - A General candidate promoted on a reserved category post as petitioner did not pass departmental examination - The condition in promotion order will be reverted on availability of an SC candidate - Petitioner eligible from 20.3.1990 - Petitioner promoted from 14.12.2001 - Respondent fully supported petitioner's claim in civil suit by General candidate - Given condition, petitioner had to be considered for promotion from 20.3.1990 - Respondent cannot take contrary stand after defending petitioner's right in civil suit. [Paras 8, 10] B. Constitution of India, Article 226 - Promotion - Claim from retrospective date - Subsequent amendment in rules - Any subsequent amendment in Rules cannot take away accrued right of petitioner - Referring to Supreme Court judgment in case of Y.V. Rangaiah - Plea of reduction in posts due to amendment in rules dismissed. [Para 11]

text: Jawahar Lal Gupta, J. (Oral) - The petitioner, a Physical Training Instructor in the State of Haryana, prays for the issue of a writ of mandamus directing the respondents to release the selection grade on his completing 18 years of service viz. October 25, 1978. A few facts as are relevant for the decision of this case may briefly be noticed.  2. The petitioner joined service under the Central Government as an Instructor under the National Discipline Scheme. He was appointed on October 24, 1960. This scheme had been prepared by the Government under the National Fitness Corps Programme. Subsequently, there was a decision to decentralise the scheme. On October 1, 1972, the administrative control over the Instructors who had been posted in various Government/private schools in the State of Haryana was transferred to the State Government with effect from October 1, 1972. On October 14, 1976 the State Government issued an order by which it sanctioned 311 posts of Physical Instructors in the pay scale of Rs. 125-5-150/5-250. It also sanctioned 14 posts of Director, Physical Education in the scale of Rs. 220-8-300-10-400. It was further decided that 15 per cent of the posts for both the cadres will be in the selection grade of Rs. 250-10-300 and Rs. 400-20-600, respectively. It was also decided that all the Instructors under the National Discipline Scheme working in the State Government be absorbed with effect from July 1, 1976, and placed in the scales of pay sanctioned for the different posts. The sanction was subject to certain conditions. One of these conditions was that the employees working in the National Discipline Scheme shall be kept in a separate block without disturbing their inter se seniority and that ``it will be a diminishing cadre___________''. In pursuance of this policy decision, the petitioner was appointed as a Physical Training Instructor (N.F.C.) in the pay scale of Rs. 125-250 with effect from July 1, 1976. A copy of the order dated October 15, 1976, issued by the Director of Public Instruction, Haryana, in this behalf is as Annexure P-2 with the writ petition. The appointment was purely on temporary basis. It was, however, stipulated that ``from the date of absorption in the State service he will be entitled to all allowances as admissible to other State employees of this cadre''.  3. Before the petitioner was actually absorbed as Physical Training Instructor in the State of Haryana, the Government had issued a letter dated January 31, 1975, regarding the grant of selection grade to ``the Provincialised Teachers''. A copy of this letter is at Annexure P-3 with the writ petition. By this letter sanction of the Government of Haryana was conveyed to the Department for the grant of ``selection grade with effect from 1.10.1974 to these Masters/Teachers borne on Provincialised Cadre who have completed 18 years of service on that date and from then onwards to ______''. After his absorption in the State service, the petitioner submitted a representation to the Minister praying that he should also be granted the selection grade in accordance with the letter issued by the State Government on January 31, 1975. The claim was examined but the State Government found no ground to grant any relief. Since the petitioner did not hear anything in reply, he approached this Court through the present writ petition. The petitioner alleges that the action of the State Government in not releasing the selection grade to him is violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. Accordingly, he prays for the issue of a direction to the respondents regarding the grant of selection grade.  4. The respondents contest the petitioner's claim. It has been pointed out that the persons working in the Provincialised Cadre belong to a different class of employees. They have no avenue of promotion. It was due to an undue hardship that a decision to grant selection grade on completion of 18 years of service was taken. Since the petitioner belongs to a different class of employees, he has no claim for the grant of selection grade. Mr. Rathee, learned counsel for the petitioner, submits that even the Instructors under the National Discipline Scheme have no avenue of promotion. They also belong to a diminishing cadre and consequently the action of the State Government in not granting the selection grade to them is violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. The learned counsel has also placed reliance on a decision of the Supreme Court in JBT Rajkiya Adhyapak Sangh and others v. State of Haryana and others, 1991(3) RSJ 111. The claim made on behalf of the petitioner has been controverted by the learned counsel for the respondents.  5. It is the admitted position that the petitioner had been initially recruited by the Central Government. He was working under the National Discipline Scheme which had been prepared by the Central Government. The petitioner and the others like him were absorbed in the State service vide order dated October 15, 1976. This absorption was in pursuance of the policy decision taken by the Government on October 14, 1976. The State Government had taken a conscious decision that 15 per cent posts of the Physical Training Instructors shall be placed in the selection grade. It is not alleged that the State Government has not granted selection grade to the members of the Cadre in accordance with this decision. The only claim made by the petitioner is based on the fact that those working in the Provincialised Cadre had been granted selection grade on completion of 18 years of service while the petitioner has been denied a similar relief. This, the petitioner alleges, is discriminatory. Admittedly, the petitioner does not belong to the Provincialised Cadre. In fact, there were certain schools in the State of Punjab which were being run by the Municipal and District Boards. On September 27, 1957, the State Government had taken an executive decision to take over the control of the schools which were being run by these Boards. The services of even those teachers who were employed in these schools were also taken over. Later on, these teachers were described as members of the Provincialised Cadre and the rules called the Punjab Education Service (Provincialised Cadre) Class III Rules, 1961 were promulgated to regulate their conditions of service. These rules were retrospectively enforced with effect from October 1, 1957. The teachers belonging to the Provincialised Cadre had claimed parity with those working in the State Cadre. This claim was partly accepted by this Court. The decision was challenged by the State of Punjab before the Apex Court. In the State of Punjab v. Joginder Singh, AIR 1963 SC 913, their Lordships ruled that the members of the Provincialised Cadre were totally distinct and different from those belonging to the State Cadre. It was held that the Government which is carrying on the administration is entitled to ``have a choice in the constitution of the services to man the administration ___________''. It can constitute two services ``consisting of employees doing the same work but with different scales of pay or subject to different conditions of service. Constitution of such services is not violative of Article 14. The proposition that ``Article 14 requires that equal work must receive equal pay or that if there is equality in pay and work there have to be equal conditions of service is untenable''. Accordingly, the appeal filed by the State Government was accepted and the decision of this Court was reversed. It was categorically held that the members of the Provincialised Cadre belong to a distinct class and they were not entitled to parity with those working in the State Cadre.  6. In view of this authoritative pronouncement of a Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court, it is clearly settled that the teachers working in the Provincialised Cadre cannot claim parity with their counterparts in the State Cadre. It would be equally true that those who do not belong to the Provincialised Cadre cannot complain of discrimination on the ground that they have been treated differently from those belonging to that cadre. Resultantly, the grievance of the petitioner that he has been treated differently from the members of the Provincialised Cadre cannot be sustained.  7. Mr. Rathee has placed reliance on the decision of the Supreme Court in JBT Rajkiya Adhyapak Singh's case (supra). This case is clearly distinguishable on facts. Nothing has been pointed out in the decision which may be applicable to the facts of the present case.  8. No other point has been urged.  In view of the above, no ground for interference is made out. Accordingly, the writ petition is dismissed. However, in the circumstances of the case, there will be no order as to costs.  Petition dismissed.
summary: According to Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution of India, the Punjab Education Service (Provincialised Cadre) Class III Rules, 1961, state that the government carrying out the administration can decide which services are necessary to man the administration. Teachers in the Provincialised Cadre are not entitled to the same status as those in the State Cadre, and those who are not part of the Provincialised Cadre cannot complain of discrimination. Therefore, the petitioner's claim that he was treated differently from members of the Provincialised Cadre cannot be upheld, and his petition is dismissed. This is in accordance with the ruling in AIR 1963 SC 913. [Paras 5 & 6]

text: S. Rajendra Babu, J. - By interim order dated March 11, 1999, directions were given to work out a scheme to absorb the respondents in C.A. No. 810 of 1998. Pursuant to the said order, the Government framed the scheme and placed the same before the Court. Thereafter, having looked into the scheme framed by the Government, by an order made on September 28, 1999, this Court disposed of the matter finally and gave certain directions. It is now stated that the manner in which the scheme is being implemented is not in conformity with the directions issued by this Court and, therefore, the present contempt petitions have been filed. These petitions are really in the nature of seeking implementation of the order made by this court rather than to punish any of the respondents.  2. In order dated September 28, 1999 disposing of C.A. No. 810 of 1998, this Court stated that there were three conditions in the matter of absorption of the retrenched employees who were working in the Census Department and they were as follows :  "(i) Retrenched employees of the Census Operation in Tamil Nadu with not less than six months service were placed in priority (iii) list under Group II for employment assistance through Employment Exchanges. (ii) A period of three years was ordered to be excluded in computing their age for appointment through the Tamil Nadu Public Service Commission and the Employment Exchanges, provided they had rendered temporary service of at least six months in the Census Organisation of the State. (iii) The rule of reservation was to be followed in making the appointment of retrenched census employees." However, the matter was further clarified in the following manner :  "In the circumstances, we direct the State Government to modify the scheme in respect of these two conditions. It would be appropriate for the State Government to delete these two conditions and all that may be insisted upon is that the retrenched employees of the Census Department should be placed in Group IV and the condition relating to the exclusion of three years from their age shall be deleted. Subject to this modification, the scheme proposed by the State Government may be worked out so as to absorb the respondents in services of the State Government or in any of the Local Authority or Government undertakings as may be feasible as expeditiously as possible." 3. The Government has now stated the manner they have worked out the orders made by this court earlier. The following modification, inter alia, was carried out in G.O. Ms. No. 144, P&AR dated 11.8.1999 :  "(a) All the retrenched employees of Census Organisation shall be placed in priority (iii) list under Group IV for employment assistance through Employment Exchanges for sponsoring against the vacancies arising in State Government, Local Bodies and Public Undertakings. (b) The retrenched employees of Census Organisation shall be exempted from the age limit prescribed in the relevant service rules governing the posts in which they are to be appointed. This concession shall apply only to the retrenched employees of 1991 Census." 4. The order of the extent of clause (a) above is not justifiable to ask the ex-employees to be sponsored again by Employment Exchanges and that condition will not be in conformity with the order made by this Court. We make it clear that the proper course would be to consider their cases as retrenched employees in a separate category and work out a scheme to fit them against appropriate posts in appropriate departments in the State Government, Local Bodies and Public Undertakings without insisting upon such retrenched employees being sponsored by the Employment Exchanges. We also make it clear that clause (b) will remain undisturbed as the same is in conformity with the order made by this Court. Let these directions be complied within three months from today.  5. The contempt petitions are disposed of in terms of the aforesaid directions. No costs.  Petitions disposed of.
summary: The Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 outlines that petitions that seek implementation of a court order should not be used to punish any individuals. In a case regarding the absorption of retrenched employees, directions were given to create a scheme that would fit these individuals into appropriate positions without requiring them to be sponsored by employment exchanges. However, the current implementation of the scheme does not align with the court's directions, as it is not justifiable to require ex-employees to be sponsored again. As a result, new directions were issued to consider these retrenched employees in a separate category and create a scheme that fits them into appropriate departments without the sponsorship requirement. [Para]

text: G.R. Majithia, J. - This judgment disposes of Civil Writ Petition No. 4275 and 6955 of 1993.  1. A challenge has been made to the order of the State Government in the Department of Irrigation and Power (Personnel-II Branch) dated June 16, 1992, whereby the representation dated September 14, 1991 filed by Shri Harjit Singh, Line Superintendent and others was rejected.  2. Civil Writ Petition No. 4275 of 1993 has been filed by the Punjab Electrical Inspectorate Junior Engineers Association, Patiala through its Vice President and Civil Writ Petition No. 6955 of 1993 has been filed by Harjit Singh, Balwant Singh and Ram Rattan, Assistant Electrical Inspectors in the office of the Chief Electrical Inspector to Government, Punjab Patiala. The petitioners have made grievance to the prescription of qualifications for recruitment to the posts of Assistant Electrical Inspectors in these petitions. The qualifications for the said post have been prescribed under the Punjab Electrical Inspectorate (State Service Class II) Rules, 1979. Harjit Singh, petitioner No. 1 in Civil Writ Petition No. 6955 of 1993 moved this Court through Civil Writ Petition No. 1386 of 1991 wherein he made similar grouse as has been made in this writ petition. This court directed that the petitioner should file a representation to the appropriate authority and the writ petition was disposed of on September 7, 1991. Before that the petitioners in Civil Writ Petition No. 6955 of 1993 had made a similar grievance by filing Civil Writ Petition No. 7928 of 1989. The writ petition was dismissed by a learned single Judge of this Court on September 5, 1990. The petitioners unsuccessfully assailed the judgment of the learned Single Judge in L.P.A. No. 1119 of 1990. Being aggrieved, the judgment in the Letters Patent Appeal was challenged in the apex court through special leave to appeal (Civil) Petition No. 4720 of 1991 and the same was dismissed vide order dated July 29, 1991.  3. Through the present writ petitions, third attempt has been made by the petitioners to undo and unsettle what has been already settled.  4. The Governor of Punjab in exercise of the powers conferred by the proviso to Article 309 of the Constitution of India, framed the Rules called the Punjab Electrical Inspectorate (State Service Class-II) Rules, 1979 (for short, the Rules). Clause (f) of Rule 2 of the Rules says that service means the Punjab Electrical Inspectorate State Service Class II and the service's shall comprise the posts shown in Appendix 'A' to these Rules. Appendix 'A' reads thus :  Sr. No., Name of Post, Pay Scale, No. of Posts  1. Class II Assistant Electrical Inspector, Rs. 400-30-700-40-1100, Permanent, Temp. Total  Rule 9 says that no person shall be appointed to the Service by direct recruitment unless he (a) possesses educational qualifications and experience specified in Appendix 'B' to these rules and (b) is a person with a satisfactory character and antecedents, verification in respect of which shall be arranged through the Government agency except in cases where such verification may have already been made at the time of his entry into Government service. In Appendix 'B' qualifications and experience for direct appointment or by transfer from any other Department of the State Government to the post of Assistant Electrical Inspector have been prescribed and these are as under :-  "(a) Possesses a Degree or Diploma equivalent to Degree in Electrical Engineering from a recognised university or qualifications equivalent to such Degree or Diploma;  (b) has been regularly engaged for a period of at least three years in the practice of Electrical Engineering and in the Administration of Act and Rules made thereunder of which not less than one year has been spent in an Electrical or Mechanical Engineering Workshop or in generation, transmission or distribution of electricity or in the administration of Act and Rules made thereunder, in a position of responsibility; and  (c) possesses knowledge of Punjabi language in Gurmukhi script of Matriculation standard or its equivalent."  Rule 8 of the Rules provides for method of appointment to the posts in the service. It says that appointment to the posts in the service shall be made in the following manner :-  (i) 60 per cent by direct appointment;  (ii) 40 per cent by promotion from amongst the Line Superintendents, who have rendered service as such for not less than ten years in the case of Diploma holders and five years in the case of degree-holders in the Electrical Inspectorate;  (iii) By transfer if no suitable candidate is available by the afore- mentioned two methods;  (iv) All promotions to the posts in the service shall be made by selection on the basis of merit-cum-seniority and no person shall be entitled to claim as of right, promotion to such post on the basis of seniority alone."  5. The petitioners are Line Superintendents. 40% posts in the Service have been reserved for the Line Superintendents by promotion and the petitioners are entitled for consideration for promotion against the 40 per cent promotional quota. Concededly, the 40 per cent promotional quota already stands filled.  6. The petitioners' grouse that prescription of qualifications "possesses a Degree or Diploma equivalent to Degree in Electrical Engineering from a recognised University or qualifications equivalent to such Degree or Diploma" is not justified. They say that a Line Superintendent possessing a Diploma in Electrical Engineering should have been permitted to apply for direct quota posts in the service. We find no merit in the submission made for the following reasons :  (i) It is for the appointing authority to prescribe the minimum qualifications for a post in the service;  (ii) The judgment rendered inter parts in Civil Writ Petition No. 7928 of 1989, which was decided on September 5, 1990, has attained finality as it was affirmed by the Letters Patent Bench and the apex Court; and  (iii) The appointing authority can prescribe that a candidate with higher qualifications than the minimum prescribed will be preferred for the post and if such a provision is made, no fault can be found with it.  For the reasons stated above, there is no merit in these petitions. The same are dismissed.
summary: Constitution of India, Articles 14 and 309 - Punjab Electrical Inspectorate (State Service Class II) Rules, 1979, Rule 2 - Minimum qualifications - Appointment - The authority responsible for appointments has the power to define the minimum qualifications required for a position in the service - Also, they have the discretion to state that candidates with higher qualifications will be given preference - Such a condition is legal. [Para 6]

text: R.L. Anand, J. (Oral) - The petitioners through this writ petition under Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution of India have given challenge to the selection proceedings conducted by respondent No. 4 on the basis of which the order Annexure P3 was passed promoting Sarvshri Nand Kishore and Pawan Kumar against the posts of Junior Store Officers from the post of Senior Store Keepers.  2. Before proceeding further in the matter, I would like to state that during the pendency of this writ petition, petitioner Nos. 1 and 2, namely, Satish Uma Chand and Badri Nath Sharma have been promoted as Junior Store Officers w.e.f. 16th January, 2001, but they are still making a prayer before me that they should be considered for promotion from the date when their juniors were promoted.  3. The case set up by the petitioners in short is that in the cadre of Senior Store Keepers they were always senior to respondent Nos. 7 and 8 and, therefore, they could not be ignored for the purpose of promotion by the Departmental Promotion Committee.  4. On the contrary, the short defence of the respondent authorities is that the Selection Committee adopted the criteria of merit-cum-seniority by assessing the record of all the eligible candidates and, resultantly, Sarvshri Nand Kishore and Pawan Kumar Sharma were recommended by the Selection Committee. On this recommendation, the order of promotion Annexure P3 was issued in favour of the respondents.  5. I have heard Shri Rameshwar Sharma, Advocate on behalf of the petitioners, Shri Arun Nehra, Advocate, on behalf of respondent Nos. 1 and 2 and Shri O.P. Sharda Advocate on behalf of the private respondents and with their assistance, have gone through the record of the case.  6. The original record was produced before me. The perusal of the same would reveal that on 24th January, 2000, the Departmental Promotion Committee was consisted of the Director (as Chairman), Dean (Member), Deputy Director (Admn) (Member), Prof. R.N. Kataria (Member), Prof A.K. Banerjee (Member) and Dr. D. Behra (Liaison Officer/Member) as members of the Selection Committee. Since two posts for normal zone were to be filled on the basis of merit-cum- seniority, the Selection Committee considered the record of eight eligible candidates, including the petitioners and the private respondents, the proceedings can be quoted in the following manner :  The records of the above officials have been carefully scrutinised and it is certified that there is no doubt about their integrity except that against Shri Satish Uma Chand, an internal investigation is done by M.S. Office against the shortage for some chemicals in the store. "It is also certified that there is no CBI/Vigilance Inquiry pending or contemplated agasint any of the officials." The matter is placed before the Departmental Promotion Committee for their consideration and recommendations. The promotion will be effective from 1.3.1992 under the 2nd Cadre Review." Following were the recommendations of the Departmental Promotion Committee : "Since the method of promotion as per rules is merit-cum-seniority, the following store keepers are recommended for promotion w.e.f. 1.3.1992 to the post of Jr. Store Officer under the 2nd Cadre Review, in order of their merit : 1. Mr. Nand Kishore. 2. Mr. Pawan Kumar." 7. The frontal argument raised by the learned counsel for the petitioners was that a favouritism has been done by the Departmental Promotion Committee while making the recommendations of Sarvshri Nand Kishoare and Pawan Kumar. So much so, Shri Pawan Kumar was at the bottom of the list of eight candidates who was taken into consideration. It was also submitted on behalf of the learned counsel for the petitioners that there is no rule under which the case of eight candidates was supposed to be considered by the Departmental Promotion Committee. This has been done just to accommodate Shri Pawan Kumar who was at the bottom of the list of eight candidates.  8. On the contrary, the learned counsel appearing on behalf of the respondents submitted that the criteria for slection was merit-cm-seniority and not seniority-cum-merit. In these circumstances, the Departmental Promotion Committee was supposed to assess the annual confidential reports of all the eligible persons. Against the two posts, the names of eight persons have been considered. Mr. Nehra further pointed out that so far as the service record of Shri Nand Kishoare is concerned, either it was Excellent or it was Very-Good. During the last ten years he has obtained two "Excellent and remaining reports were "Very-Good". Similarly, all the reports of Shri Pawan Kumar right from 1988-89 upto 1998-99 were "Very-Good". So far as the annual confidential reports of the present petitioners are concerned, either it was Average or it was Good. In these circumstances, the Departmental Promotion Committee rightly recommended the names of Sarvshir Nand Kishoare and Pawan Kumar. it is a settled principle of law that this Court cannot sit as a Court of appeal over the assessment of the Departmental Promotion Committee which is an expert body. Until and unless some arbitrariness or malafides are shown, this court will not exercise its jurisdiction to interfere with the recommendation of the Departmental Promotion Committee.  9. Resultantly, there is no merit in this writ petition and the same is hereby dismissed with no order as to costs.  Petition dismissed.
summary: A. The Constitution of India, 1950, Articles 14 & 16 - Promotion - The Selection Committee evaluated the records of both the petitioners and private respondents, utilizing "Merit cum Seniority". The DPC was tasked with analyzing annual confidential reports. The court is not able to evaluate the DPC's decisions in this role. [Para 8] B. The Constitution of India 1950, Article 226 - Judicial review - Promotions were based on the criteria of "Merit-cum-Seniority". The DPC was comprised of professional individuals, and the Court cannot evaluate their evaluations. [Para 8]

text: T.H.B. Chalapathi, J. - The petitioner joined the Transport Department of Punjab on June 10, 1974, as Motor Vehicles Inspector. Thereafter, he was appointed as Extra Assistant Transport Controller (Technical) and he was reverted as Motor Vehicle Inspector on June 4, 1987, and posted as such at Bathinda. Without joining at the place of posting, he applied for three months'leave originally on medical grounds. This leave of three months initially applied for, was sanctioned by the Competent Authority. Thereafter, he sent an application on September 24, 1987, for extension of leave again on medical grounds. Then the petitioner was directed to appear before the Chief Medical Officer, Ludhiana, by letter dated October 26, 1987. Civil Surgeon, Ludhiana who examined the petitioner on November 12, 1987, found him fit to resume duties. Accordingly, a communication was sent to the petitioner on December 29, 1987, intimating him that the leave applied for by him in continuation of the earlier leave sanctioned, had been rejected and he was directed to report for duty immediately failing which disciplinary action would be taken against him. In spite of this letter, he did not resume the duty through he was asked to join the duty repeatedly by the department. On the other hand, the petitioner sought for constitution of a Medical Board for his medical examination. Accordingly, on the request of the petitioner, Medical Board was constituted by the Director of Health and Family Welfare, Punjab, and vide his letter dated February 11, 1988, the petitioner was directed to appear before the Standing Medical Board in the office of the Civil Surgeon, Faridkot, either on February 19, 1988, or on February 26, 1988, for his examination by the Medical Board. In spite of his request being acceded to by the department for constituting the Medical Board, the petitioner never appeared before the Medical Board at Faridkot. Thereafter, a charge sheet was issued to him on March 14, 1988. The same was returned with an endorsement that he was not found at the given address. Thereafter, also the petitioner was asked to resume his duties but he did not join duty. Then, Enquiry Officer was appointed to conduct enquiry against the conduct of the petitioner. The Enquiry Officer sent notice to the petitioner at the address given by him but the said registered notice was also returned with an endorsement that he was not found at the given address. Thereafter an ex- parte enquiry was held and the Enquiry Officer found him guilty of wilful absence from duty. Basing on the report of the Enquiry Officer, the Disciplinary Authority, namely, the State Transport Commissioner, Punjab, by his order dated October 3, 1989, dismissed the petitioner from service. The said order was also sent to the petitioner but the same was also returned unserved. Therefore, the same was published in the newspaper namely, The Tribune dated December 27, 1989. Thereafter, the petitioner filed an appeal to the Secretary, Transport, Punjab, on January 30, 1990. The said appeal was dismissed by the Appellate Authority on October 29, 1990.  2. The petitioner thereupon filed this Writ Petition invoking the Certiorarial jurisdiction of this Court under Article 226 of the Constitution of India for quashing the orders of the Transport Commissioner dated October 3, 1989, (Annexure P-1) as confirmed by the Secretary, Transport Department, Punjab, dated October 29, 1990, (Annexure P-2).  3. This Writ Petition came up for admission before the Division Bench of this Court, which issued Notice of Motion. Thereafter, after hearing the learned counsel for the petitioner and the respondents, the Division Bench of this Court by its order dated July 22, 1991, allowed the writ petition and quashed the impugned order of dismissal on the ground that the enquiry report had not been communicated to the petitioner and, therefore, the order of dismissal was liable to be set aside in view of the decision of the Supreme Court in Union of India and others v. Mohd Ramzan Khan reported in 1991(1) SCC 588. Thereafter, the State of Punjab filed a Civil Appeal No. 352 of 1994, in the Supreme Court. The Apex Court took the view that as the order of dismissal was passed before November 20, 1990, the decision of Mohd, Ramzan's case (supra) is not applicable to the facts of the case, in view of the decision of the Constitution Bench in Managing Director, ECIL, Hyderabad v. B. Karunakar reported in 1993(6) JT 1. Therefore, the Apex Court set aside the order of this Court dated July 22, 1991, and remanded the matter to this Court for disposal in accordance with law after considering other points raised in the writ petition. Thus, the matter has come up for final hearing now.  4. It is pertinent to observe that the Supreme Court in its order dated January 13, 1994, observed as follows:-  "Inasmuch as it appears that other points were raised in the writ petition (though it does not appear from the judgment that they were argued as such) we are inclined, in the facts and circumstances of this case, to give an opportunity to the respondent to urge the other points raised in the writ petition, if he so chooses, before the High Court." Thus, it is clear that this court is directed by the Supreme Court to consider the points raised by the petitioner in the writ petition other than the point that he was not supplied the copy of the report of the Enquiry Officer.  5. The learned counsel for the petitioner had raised the following contentions. Firstly, that charge-sheet was not supplied to the petitioner, and without supplying the charge-sheet and without obtaining his explanation to the charges, the appointing an Enquiry Officer to conduct enquiry is bad in view of Rule 8(4) and (5) of the Punjab Civil Services (Punishment and Appeal) Rules, 1970. Secondly, that the petitioner was not intimated that Enquiry Officer had been appointed and he was not given any opportunity to appear before the Enquiry Officer and participate in the enquiry. Third contention is that his request of constituting a Medical Board was not properly considered insamuch as the Medical Board was constituted at Faridkot when the petitioner was residing at Ludhiana and his headquarter happened to be at Chandigarh. According to the learned counsel for the petitioner, the constitution of the Medical Board at Faridkot and directing the petitioner to appear before the Medical Board at Faridkot amounts to negation of opportunity to prove that he was not medically fit to resume duty. It is further contended by the learned counsel for the petitioner that before passing an order of dismissal, the Public Service Commission was not consulted as required under Regulation 5(a) of the Punjab Public Service Commission (Limitation of Functions) Regulations, 1955, and, therefore, the order of dismissal is bad.  6. It is also contended by the learned counsel that it was not established that the petitioner wilfully absented himself from resuming duty.  7. It is also contended that the petitioner was not supplied the report of the Enquiry Officer though in the order of dismissal, the Transport Commissioner has stated that the order of dismissal is in continuation of the enquiry report.  8. The last submission made by the learned counsel for the petitioner cannot be accepted in view of the orders of the Apex Court while remanding the matter. If the petitioner is entitled to a copy of the report of the Enquiry Officer, in spite of the decision of the Supreme Court in Karunakaran's case (supra) holding that the decision in Mohd. Ramzan's case is operative prospectively he should have urged this point before the Supreme Court, while remanding the matter back to this Court, it is not open to the petitioner to contend that he is entitled to the copy of the report of the Enquiry Officer.  9. The learned counsel for the petitioner contended that he was not supplied the charge sheet but it is clearly averred in the written statement that charge sheet was issued on March 14, 1988, and the same was sent by registered post but the same was returned with an endorsement that he was not found at the given address. It is not disputed that the petitioner has given his address at Village and Post Office Beghowal, district Ludhiana. The letters had been sent to the petitioner by the department at the said address. Even in the writ petition, the petitioner has given his address as Village and Post Office Beghowal, District Ludhiana. Therefore, when the department sent the registered letters at the address available with it, it cannot be said that no communication was sent to the petitioner in regard to the charge sheet on March 13, 1988. The record shows that the charge sheet dated March 14, 1988, was sent to the petitioner at the given address and it was returned with an endorsement that he was not available at the given address. Therefore, I am of the opinion that it is not open to the petitioner to contend that the charge sheet was not supplied to him.  10. The petitioner also contended that the appointment of Enquiry Officer is bad in view of Rule 8(4) and (5) of the Punjab Civil Services (Punishment and Appeal) Rules, 1970, but in view of the fact that charge sheet had been sent to the petitioner by registered post at his given address, it cannot be said that there is any violation of Rules 8(4) and (5) of the Punjab Civil Services (Punishment and Appeal) Rules, 1970. This contention of the learned counsel for the petitioner, therefore, fails. The learned counsel for the petitioner has contended that Medical Board at Ludhiana should have been constituted and according for him the constitution of the Medical Board at Faridkot amounts to depriving him of an opportunity to prove that he was not medically fit to resume the duty. The petitioner has not placed before me any communication sent by him requesting the constitution of the Medical Board at a particular place. In fact, on an earlier occasion, i.e. in November, 1987, the petitioner was directed to appear before the Civil Surgeon, Ludhiana, on November 10, 1987. The petitioner accordingly appeared before the Civil Surgeon, Ludhiana, and the Chief Medical Officer, Ludhiana, who was a Civil Surgeon, opined that the petitioner was found fit to resume his duties. Therefore, there is no question of constituting any Medical Board at Ludhiana as the Civil Surgeon at Ludhiana had already come to the conclusion that the petitioner was found fit to resume duty. Therefore, the department is right in not constituting the same person who was working at Ludhiana as Civil Surgeon as the Medical Board to examine the petitioner. It is only in the interest of the petitioner himself that Medical Board had been constituted at Faridkot and the petitioner was admittedly intimated of the same and he was asked to appear before the Medical Board on February 19, 1988, or February 26, 1988, but he did not appear before the Medical Board on any of these dates. When the petitioner having knowledge of the constitution of the Medical Board at Faridkot chose not to appear, he has to blame himself. He has no right to say that the Medical Board has to be constituted at a particular place of his choice. No rule has been brought to my notice that the Medical Board of the choice of the petitioner or delinquent official has to be constituted. I do not, therefore, find any merit in this contention of the learned counsel.  11. The learned counsel for the petitioner further argued that the Punjab Public Service Commission was not consulted, therefore, the order of dismissal is bad in view of Rule 5 of the Punjab Public Service Commission (Limitation of Functions) Regulations, 1955. Rule 5(c) reads as follows:-  "5. It shall not be necessary to consult the Commission: (c) "on any order proposed to be made by the Punjab Government on appeal other than an order enhancing the penalty to that for which consultation with the Commission would have been necessary in case the enhanced penalty had been imposed in an original order appealed against is one of - (i) censure; (ii) suspension for not more than one year; (iii) withholding of increments or promotion including stoppage at an efficiency bar, for not more than one year with non-continuing effect." The learned counsel for the petitioner had relied on Rule 5(c) of the Punjab Public Service Commission (Limitation of Functions) Regulations, 1955. The reading of Rule 5(c) in my opinion does not apply at all. According to Rule 5(c), it shall not be necessary to consult the Commission on any order proposed to be made by the Punjab Government on appeal other than the order enhancing the penalty to that for which consultation with the Commission would have been necessary in case enhanced penalty has been imposed in an original order or appealed against the order of censure or suspension for not more than one year or withholding of increments of promotion including the stoppage of increment etc. Therefore, Rule 5(c) is applicable only in case Appellate Authority, namely, the State of Punjab, wants to enhance the penalty imposed by the original Authority in which case only consultation under this rule is required. If the Appellate Authority is merely confirming the order of the Original Authority, no consultation is required under Rule 5(c). Further, it may also be mentioned that the petitioner was not appointed through the media of Service Commission. His post does not fall within the category for which appointments have to be made through the Punjab Public Service Commission. I am, therefore, of the opinion that it was not necessary to consult the Punjab Public Service Commission. The learned counsel further argued that simply because the petitioner was absent, he could not be dismissed from service. He relied upon a decision of the Calcutta High Court in Deputy Inspector Gen. Central Industrial Security Force Eastern Zone v. Shiv Kumar Ray reported as 1995(2) SCT 662. But it has not been held in that case that absence from duty does not amount to misconduct. What has been held in that case is that penalty must be imposed proportionate to the gravity of misconduct and that the dismissing authority should have considered the matter compassionately because of the peculiar facts and circumstances of the case disclosed in defence. Thus, it is clear that it cannot be said that there is any hard and fast rule that in case of absence from duty, no penalty of dismissal can be awarded. Each case depends on its own facts and that the quantum of punishment will depend on the nature of the misconduct. The other decision cited by the learned counsel for the petitioner in Shamsher Bahadur Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh and others, reported in 1993(2) SLR 736 is also to the same effect. Therefore, it is to be seen from the facts of the present case whether there is any extenuating circumstance to reduce the punishment of dismissal from service the conduct of petitioner deserves any sympathy from this Court. The petitioner was appointed as Motor Vehicles Inspector in 1974. Later in the year 1985, he was promoted as Extra Assistant Transport Controller (Technical) in his own pay-scale as Motor Vehicles Inspector on a specific condition that he will not claim promotion on the basis of the orders issued in 1985 appointing him as Extra Assistant Transport Controller and that he will not claim seniority or financial benefits. He was working at the time at Patiala. Thereafter, he was transferred and posted as Motor Vehicles Inspector at Bathinda. He did not join the duty at Bathinda. Even according to the petitioner, he felt his posting as Motor Vehicles Inspector, Bathinda, a punishment itself though he was not actually promoted as Extra-Assistant Transport Controller (Technical). Instead of joining at Bathinda i.e. at his new place of posting, he applied three months' leave initially on medical grounds. Thereafter, he applied for extension of leave. Then he was asked to appear before the Civil Surgeon. Ludhiana, who reported that he was fit to resume duty. Therefore, the ground for applying leave on medical illness was no longer available to him but the petitioner insisted on constituting the Medical Board to further examine him. At the instance of the petitioner, the Medical Board at Faridkot was constituted and he was directed to appear before the Medical Board at Faridkot either on February 19, 1988, or on February 26, 1988, but the petitioner did not care to appear before the Medical Board. Thereafter, a charge-sheet was sent to him at the address given by him. The registered letters were returned with an endorsement that the petitioner was not available. This is not the case of the petitioner that he left the village. Therefore, the only irresistible conclusion one can arrive at is that the petitioner was avoiding service of the registered notice sent to the petitioner, to gain time to his own advantage. Thereafter, Enquiry Officer was appointed. Even then he did not participate in the enquiry though according to the petitioner, he did not receive any communication in regard to the enquiry. It is pertinent to note that the petitioner himself had written a letter on August 18, 1988, to the Transport Commissioner wherein he categorically stated that it is a pre- requisite to serve the charge sheet first before appointing the Enquiry Officer and that the Enquiry Officer has been appointed without communicating the charge sheet to him. This letter of the petitioner dated August 18, 1988, clearly shows that the petitioner had knowledge of appointment of Enquiry Officer. The petitioner cannot escape from this conclusion which can be based on his letter itself. A reading of the letter clearly shows that the petitioner was trying to avoid his joining at Bathinda. Therefore, it is a clear case of wilful disobedience and not only wilful absence from duty but wilful disobedience of orders of transfer. There cannot be any doubt that orders of transfer are incidents of service. When a person has been transferred and posted at a place and when his extension of leave is refused, he has no other option except to join the duty and if he does not join the duty, he has to face the consequences. In this case, after considering the entire record, I am of the opinion that the petitioner deserves the punishment of dismissal. I do not find any grounds warranting interference with the orders of dismissal.  12. Writ Petition is, therefore, liable to be dismissed and is accordingly dismissed but without costs.
summary: Respondent D.S. Dhillon, DAG of Punjab, argued that under Constitution of India, Articles 226/227 and Punjab Civil Services (Punishment and Appeal) Rules, 1970, Rule 8(4) and (5), orders of transfer are an essential component of employment. The petitioner, who had been transferred and posted at a new location, applied for leave on medical grounds and for an extension of that leave. However, upon being contacted by the Civil Surgeon and declared fit for duty, the petitioner refused to report for duty and insisted instead on constituting a Medical Board to re-examine him. The petitioner appeared to be avoiding service and delaying the proceedings to his advantage. The Enquiry Officer appointed to investigate these charges was not communicated with by the petitioner, who had himself previously argued that a charge sheet must be served before an Enquiry Officer is appointed. The impugned order of dismissal was therefore upheld. [Para 11]

text: A.K. Shrivastava, J. - By this petition under Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution of India, the petitioner is seeking relief for quashment of Annexure P/5 dated 9-3-2005, since it is not accordance with the direction dated 21-1-2004 of the State Government. The petitioner has further prayed for his reinstatement.  2. The case of the petitioner is that vide Annexure P/6 dated 21.1.2004 the State Government took a decision that the employees whose services were terminated after 31-12-1988 they may be taken back in the service. The contention of learned counsel for the petitioner is that the petitioner was appointed after the cut off date i.e. 31-12-1988 and his services were terminated after January, 2000. After the Government had taken the decision vide Annexure P/6 dated 21-1-2004 to reinstate all those employees whose services were terminated after cut off date, thereafter clarification was also issued vide Annexure-P/7 dated 15th April, 2005. The contention of learned counsel for the petitioner is that in terms of Annexure-P/6 since the petitioner is an employee appointed after cut-off date and his service was terminated, he is entitled for reinstatement in accordance to Annexure-P/6.  3. On the other hand, it has been contended by Shri Vinod Mehta, learned Govt. Advocate, that vide Annexure-P/7 clarification was made by the State Government. It has also been put forth by him that the petitioner has not served for 240 days, therefore, vide impugned order Annexure-P/5 he was not taken back in service.  4. After having heard learned counsel for the parties, I am of the view that his petition deserves to be allowed.  5. On going through Annexure-P/6 which is a circular of the State Government dated 21-1-2004, it is gathered that the services of those employees who are the appointees after 31-12-1988 and whose services were terminated later on, their services were directed to be reinstated. Thereafter, on 12-4-2004 another circular was issued by the State Government and it was directed that the direction of the earlier circular (Annexure-P/6) may be complied with positively on or before 30th April, 2004. There is a specific averment of the petitioner in his petition in para 5.2 that he was appointed after 31-21-1988 and on the basis of the circular of the State Government of January, 2000 since he was an appointee after 31-12-1988, his services were terminated. It be seen that vide Annexure-P/6 dated 21-1-2004 the State Government took a decision that the class-IV employees who were appointed after 31-12-1988 and whose services were terminated, they be reinstated and further it was made clear vide Annexure-P/7 dated 12-4-2004 that the order should be complied on or before 30th April, 2004. There is no merit in the contention of learned Govt. Advocate that since the petitioner has not served for 240 days, therefore, by the impugned order Annexure-P/5 he was rightly not reinstated. On going through para 11 of the return, it is -found that petitioner had worked for more than 240 days. On x-raying Annexure-P/6 nowhere it is gathered that this was the condition stipulated that the employees should have served for 240 days. The clarification which has been made on 15-4-2005 also does not indicate that the employees should complete 240 days of their service. Therefore, the decision taken by the respondents vide Annexure-P/5 not to reinstate the petitioner on the ground that he has not completed 240 days is arbitrary in nature in para 11 of the return, it has been admitted that the petitioner had worked for more than 240 days. Learned counsel has also invited my attention to Annexure-P/1 in which it has been mentioned that he is serving since 1994. The petitioner has also made specific pleading in that regard in para 5.1 in his petition. In the return though the averments made by the petitioner in para 5.1 have been denied by the respondents and it has been further stated that the petitioner never engaged against the sanctioned post and it has been mentioned that he was engaged only as daily rated muster roll employee as per the job requirement and budgetary provision in the department, but the authenticity of Annexure-P/1 has not denied. Even otherwise the reinstatement of the petitioner has been denied by the impugned order Annexure-P/5 only on the ground that he was not served for 240 days which according to respondents own showing is erroneous. Since this is not the criteria in the circular of the Government Annexure-P/7 dated 12-4-2004 and the clarification dated 15-4-2005 the view of this Court is that the petitioner has made out a case for his reinstatement. The decision of the Apex Court in the case of Mehendra L. Jain v. Indore Development Authority and others, AIR 2005 SC 1252 is not applicable in the present case because in this case the circulars Annexures-P/6 and P/7 were not the subject matter.  6. For the reasons stated hereinabove this petition is allowed. The respondents are hereby directed to give appointment to the petitioner in accordance to the circular Annexure-P/6 dated 21-1-2004. However, the petitioner shall not be entitled for any back wages. But, he will be entitled for the wages from today. Annexure-P/5 dated 9-3-2005 is, accordingly, quashed. The parties are directed to bear their own costs.  Petition allowed.
summary: Constitution of India, Articles 14 and 16 - Reinstatement - Cut-off date - State Government circular dated 21.1.2004 declares the reinstatement of employees appointed after the cut off date and terminated later on - A subsequent circular directed compliance with the previous circular - However, no mention made in either circulars that 240 days of service is a requirement for reinstatement - Refusal to reinstate petitioner appointed after cut off date based on non-completion of 240 days of service is improper - Direction to appoint the petitioner without back-wages issued. [Para 5]

text: K. Ramaswamy, J. - Leave granted.  2. We have heard learned counsel on both sides.  3. The appellant appointed to a substantive post in State Police Service was promoted as a Superintendent of Police in senior time scale on May 11, 1976. He was brought on select list for the year 1977. He was given seniority in the All India Police Service from promotee quota w.e.f. April 30, 1978. Since he was brought on the select list on the said date under Rule 3(3)(b) of the IPS (Regulation of Seniority) Rules, 1954 (for short, the 'Rules'), the appellant claimed the year of allotment, i.e., 1972 under IPS (Regulation of Seniority) Rules, 1954, which was rejected by the Tribunal in the impugned order dated August 18, 1995 in OA No. 557/90.  4. Notice was issued confining to the question as to what would be the consequence of failure to convene a meeting for selection of the candidates and preparation of the annual seniority list.  5. It is stated in the counter affidavit that on November 23, 1976 in a meeting, Selection Committee considered the claims of a total number of 30 State Police Officers and ultimately found 9 officers to be brought on the select list. Notification was issued by the Government of India on June 17, 1977 to appoint 8 officers from the select list of 1976 under Rule 5(1) of the IPS (Cadre) Rules, 1954. By notification dated August 27, 1977, the list of officers for the selection was to be considered but it could not be considered on account of the strike in the State and the meeting was postponed. Ultimately, a meeting came to be held on February 15, 1978 and the names of 5 persons were listed in the select list of whom the appellant was 5th in the order of merit. The appellant came to be given the seniority from April 30, 1978 when the vacancy from promotee quota had arisen.  6. Shri K. Madhava Reddy, learned senior counsel for the appellant, contended that in view of the decision of this Court in Syed Khalid Rizvi and others v. Union of India and others, 1993(2) SCT 236(SC) : 1993 Supp. (3) SCC 576, it is mandatory on the part of the State to prepare every year the select list of Deputy Superintendents of Police to fill up vacancies which have arisen in the year to the quota and to promote them to the IPS cadre under Rule 9 of the IPS (Appointment by Promotion) Rules, 1954 which was held to be mandatory. It is incumbent upon the State Government to conduct a meeting and select the officers and allot the year of allotment to fulfil the legitimate expectation of the right to consider for promotion. Though explanation has been sought to be given by the Government for failure to hold the meeting, it must be considered that the appellant had lost the chances for promotion and the year of allotment since the appellant has been continuously officiating from the year 1976 and that, therefore, the year of allotment of 1973 is not valid in law. We find no force in the contention.  7. The effect of the inter-play of IPS (Recruitment Rules), 1954, IPS (Cadre) Rules, 1954, IPS (Appointment by Promotion) Regulations, 1955 and IPS (Regulation of Seniority) Rules, 1954 was considered thread-bare in Rizvi's case by a Bench of 3 Judges of which one of us (K. Ramaswamy, J.) was a member. Recruitment to the Indian Police Service is from two sources, namely, direct recruitment and by promotion from the members of State Police Service holding substantive posts. No employee has a right to promotion but has right to be considered for promotion according to Rules. Chances of promotion are not conditions of service but every incumbent of a substantive post in lower cadre has a legitimate expectation for promotion and to be considered for promotion in accordance with the Rules. Unless the officer of a State Police Service is brought on the select list and appointment to a cadre post in accordance with rules, he does not acquire right to assignment of the year of allotment. Eligibility for consideration have been prescribed in IPS (Recruitment by Promotion) Rules. Candidate that fulfils the qualifications requires to be considered for appointment by promotion as per Rule 9 thereof. Preparation of the select list in accordance with the Appointment by Promotion Regulations is a precondition which requires to be prepared every year. It was held to be a mandatory duty. It subserves the object of the Rules and affords an equal opportunity to promote officers to reach higher echelons of the service. It would inculcate dedicated service assiduously discharging the duties with integrity, honesty, exhibiting ability, straightforwardness with missionary zeal of self-confidence. The failure to prepare the list and accord chances of promotion would inhibit efficacy in service and generate dishonesty and manipulation. Preparation of annual list and appointment to service gives, apart from equal opportunity to augment efficacy in service, provides equal chances of promotion to the officers of State Police Service to provide harmony among direct recruits and promotees and make them accountable to proper implementation of law and order. The regulations require preparation of select list annually and revision of the list and review thereof from time to time as adumbrated in the regulations. It was, therefore, held in Rizvi's case that preparation of the select list every year is mandatory. The State Government is enjoined to account for dereliction of the statutory duty satisfactorily to the Court.  8. Regulation 3 of the IPS (Appointment by Promotion) Regulations enjoins the State Government to constitute a committee consisting of all the officers enumerated therein to select the promotees. Under Regulation 5(1), a committee may ordinarily meet at intervals not exceeding one year to prepare a list of the members of the State Police Service as are found to be suitable for promotion to the Indian Police Service.
